THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with Jonah Jones
Sides 1-2
October 26, 1978

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
rfm
P R O C E E D I N G S
Now, then, Jonah, try it and see what you're doing.
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

Okay, very good. Well, now, it's October 26th, 1978, and we're recording Jonah Jones. It's Helen Oakley Dance doing the interview. Jonah, we'll start right at the very beginning, and I'll get you to tell me, you know, where you were born, what year you were born.
Well, I was born on December the 31st, the last day of the year, 1908.
(Laughter)
I was born in Louisville, Kentucky, 16th and Magazine, and I was a pretty -- at that time, you know, kids were ruled by iron hands, you know.
Yes.
And I was there with my mother and grandmother, and my great-grandmother, she was 109 when she died.
My gracious.

And never had a doctor, never knew what vitamins was or nothing, you know. And I used to be tying my shoes to go to school in the morning, and when she'd wake up she started grunting, you know, uh, uh, uh, and it got so, you

know, I was born with that, listening to that, so when she stopped grunting, I knew that was it. I knew she was gone. I was only about six or seven, you know, and I called my mother and said, "Something's wrong with grandma." And she had passed away, straight as a stick, head full of hair, 109.
Fancy that. 109.
Yeah, she was -- she would sit on her bed every night and tell me about slavery times. She was a slave, you know, and she used to tell me about it.
In that area?
No, before.
Yeah, but I mean around there?
Yeah, around in there, yeah, around in Kentucky.
Fancy that.

So, I wasn't too -- I wasn't old enough, really, to grasp it, you know, but she'd sit on the bed every night and talk me to sleep, you know. And I was always surrounded by these women. They wouldn't let you go out of the gate. You couldn't -- they'd tell you to go out in the yard and play, go out and play with your ball, you know, after school and then you went out there in the yard, and if the ball bounced over the fence, you didn't go out there and get it. You'd wait till somebody'd come by and say, "Mister, would you throw me my ball, please?"
Well, Jonah, did you now have brothers and sisters?
Yes, I have a brother. He's eight years younger than I, and played very good trumpet, played very good. And he was in the same band, only he come up later, you see.
I saw what you said in Stanley's piece. You said he was a wonderful trumpet player.

Oh, yeah, he was a good trumpet player, but he's just eight years younger and you couldn't hold him down, you know. He would never be able to play with a band. I was always hoping. Of course I didn't see him much after I left, and then I heard about him, you know. Guys talking, "Hey, your brother's down in Kentucky there blowing a good horn," you know. So I thought well, maybe I'll open a way for him, you know, as best as I can, you know. But he was one of them types of guys, he had to have his way. He could never play with a band like Cab Calloway, which I was with for 11 years. He could never do that because his mind was that -- never mind about how I act as long as I play your music, you know. Well, that'd never go in Cab's band.
Not in Cab's band, would it.

In Cab's band you had to have on the right uniform and the right socks with it, and when you had your hit at 9:00 o'clock, he meant for you to be sitting in your chair at 9:00, not come in at 9:00, you know. So right there I said

no, this'll never work. In fact he played once for us. He was stationed at Fort Bragg in North Carolina, so we played down there, played a dance down there in an auditorium, and he came by the dance and him and a lot of other soldiers, and so Cab saw me talking to him from the bandstand, so Cab says, "Is that your brother?" I said yeah. He said, "Tell him to come up and play one." So I told him to come up and play one. "Do you feel like playing?" He says yeah, so he took my horn and he played, "Stardust," and it was beautiful, you know.

So he broke up the house and Cab says, "Well, you tell him when he comes out of the army he's got a job here," you know. So I was telling him about it, and I said, "But you can't -- you can't be drinking no whiskey and stuff, you have to stay straight. He don't allow that, you know." He was very strict about those things. So he said, "Oh, no, he's not going to tell me how much to drink. As long as I play his music that's all I'm supposed to do." So I let it drop from then on.
(Laughter)

No use in going into that no further, you know. So he played around Cincinnati there with a few bands, and then I think he gave it up. I think he had something wrong with his lungs or something, after he got out of the Army.
Oh. Well, listen, we'll go back. Wait a minute --
Well, let's go back to when the ball went on the other side of the wall. So would your mother -- well, your mother would be working, I guess.

Well, they didn't work so much. My father was working, and well about me, now, to show you how strict they were, they would always keep -- they had a thing about switches that you'd get off of trees. That's what they'd whip you with, you know, and she always had this in a vase, on the mantel, you know, and she'd have some water in there, and she'd always have three or four switches in there she'd got off the tree in the back yard. So you'd come running through the house, you know, and you'd look up and see that, and that'd remind you to slow down.
(Laughter)
But they were really strict on you. They were strict back in those days.
What did your father do?
Well, he was a fireman, worked for the fire department. He was one of the first black firemen in Louisville, and he worked up to be a Lieutenant in the fire department.
Oh, that was quite remarkable, wasn't it?
Yeah, it was really good. The Courier Journal in Louisville, Kentucky, one of the biggest papers, one of the country's leading papers, they gave him about two pages
on that. I went down there to play. They gave him about two pages on that, about him being a fireman, you know. And he could also play a little piano by ear. So --
You had a piano in the house?
Yeah, they had a piano. One of those long flat-tops, you know.
Yeah.
So he could play it by ear, you know, and he bought me a thing once called a Honnher, like a saxophone.
How do you spell that?
I think it's h-o, double-n -- could have been h-o, double-n, h-e-r, could have been. (HONNER)
Oh, yeah.
Yeah. Could have been, you know. It was a funny sounding thing. Nobody played it professionally. I never seen one.
Really? But it was a reed? It was a reed instrument?
I think it was. I think it was. Going back now I think it must have been. I'm not sure.
And he bought that for you?

Yeah, he probably got it cheap somewhere. And then we'd sit around the house and play. He'd play, 'Old Pal, Why Don't You Answer Me,' and he had another one he could play by ear, 'Aggravating Papa.' (Singing). But I had gotten into
the band by that time, and I had gotten into the band. I was getting a little ahead of my story, because --
Yes.

-- the first time I knew anything was we moved from 15th Street to 10th Street. Now I'm about nine years old, nine or ten years old, and then I never paid any attention to music. I hadn't even heard anything about music before that. There used to be a band on the corner that would play, a brass band, adult band, and sometimes I'd hear them rehearse on a Saturday, something like that. But I never paid any attention to it.
But one day, getting into how I got into it, I went down to -- they let me go down to the corner, to see the parade, at Walnut Street and 10th. We were living on 10th then.
What street?
Walnut.
Oh, yeah.
W-a-l-n-u-t.
Yeah.

And I'd go down, and I went down to look at the band and listen to the parade and looking at the band, and then I saw this Booker T. Washington Community Center Band, and it was all kids, you know, all youngsters. And Dickie Wells, he was there.
Oh, Dickie was in it?
He was in it, yeah.
This is the Booker T. Washington Community--
Community Band, yeah.
Community Center?
Yeah, right. All these guys, Bill Beason and all of them, you know. I don't think Beason had come yet. I think I went in before Beason. But Dickie was there.
What was Beason's instrument?
Drums. He played -- when Chick died, he took his place.
That's right, yes.
Also, when Ne'll Spencer died in John Kirby's band, he went with John Kirby.
Oh, did he?
Yeah, uh-huh.
Oh.
So --
What's he doing now, do you know?
I don't know. I've seen him once, in about 12 years.
Oh.
We got together, the Kentucky guys that were in that band, we started a club called the Kentucky Club.
You did?

Dickie called me and said, "Look, give me -- I've got an idea to get the guys together, we're going to start a club." He says, "What I'm going to do, all the fellows here from the band, why I'll get them together. You give me money so I can order space in the Celebrity Club, up on 25th Street, and get a few drinks, and we'll get these guys together." I said okay.
When was that?
Oh, that must have been about -- must --
Eight or ten years ago?
Yeah, a good ten years ago.
Yeah.

And so I gave it to him, then I went up, too, I went up the night when he had it. He gave me -- he was very fair about it, because he gave me the change he had left. I sent him $50.00 and he gave me the change.
Yes.
And they all were there, you know, and --
Well, who all?
Oh, we had a guy named Les Carr, played clarinet and sax. He was out of the band. Of course in the band we had no sax, he played clarinet.
Yeah.
But later he played clarinet and sax. Well, he used to play with a band around there called Furman
Practically everybody --
What's it called?
Furman Tapp.
T-a, double-p?
Yeah. Played in Small's Paradise over there.
Oh, really?
But before that, he was from Louisville, you know.
Yeah.

He was from Louisville and he had a band, he got some of the kids out of the band, Sunday school band, and had an orchestra. So -- but how they got away with -- which was Cecil Scott's band in later years, that was Lloyd Scott's band, his brother, Lloyd Scott.
Oh, Lloyd Scott.
Yeah, Lloyd had it. Lloyd was a drummer.
A drummer?

A drummer. And they took Dickie, come in and they needed a trombone. They needed Dickie Wells. The next day they needed a saxophone so they got Les Carr, alto and clarinet, and they needed a tenor, and they got Hal MacFarland. He's a tenor and clarinet.
MacFarland?
MacFerin, F-e-r-i-n. And then they got

him, and then when -- I think when Cecil left -- when Lloyd left, I think Beason went in there. They had practically -- then they had another bass player in there, Mac Walker. He was out of the band, too, out of the kid band.
Yeah.
He later played with Stuff at the Onyx Club.
Oh, yeah.
So they had half that band almost was out of Kentucky, out of Louisville.
No kidding.
Out of the kids band. So these guys, we got together for the club. We had a guy, we called him Hoggie, his name is Harold McFerlin, but Hoggie we called him.
How would you spell Hoggie?
H-o-g-g-i-e.
Yeah, right.
And Les Carr, and Charlie Bloomer was the drummer.
Yeah.
And he passed away in --
Would that be B-l, double-o, m-e-r?
Yeah, -o-o-m-e-r. Charlie Bloomer.
Yeah, right.
And we didn't play. We just had a get
together.
Yeah.
At the Celebrity Club. Charlie Bloomer --
I guess some of you hadn't seen each other in a long time.
We hadn't seen each other, you know. And so then we had another guy named Isaiah Bland. He played the alto horn (Singing).
Oh, yeah.
Not the alto sax, but the alto horn.
What's his name?
His name was Isaiah Bland, B-l-a-n-d.
Bland.
Isaiah.
Oh, Isaiah. A-i-r --
Yeah, like Isaiah. I know he had a brother named Isaac, so I figured Isaiah and Isaac, maybe they named them biblical names.
Oh, I see, yeah, right.

So he was his twin brother, and both of them played in the band. So he was here, and I hadn't seen him, you know, so that did kind of bring it together, and that night we had a few other guys up there too. Fatha, Fatha Hines. He come by.
Oh, did he?
Yeah, and joined the party.
Oh.

And then we had another guy named Louis Thompson, who was a bass player. He was one of the first. I think he was the first in this Sunday school band at the Booker T. Washington Community Center Band. Because I was talking to him. You know, when you're in there you don't figure out how it started or nothing. You're just there, you know. So we were talking since we've been here, not too long ago, and he says, "You know, I was the first one in that band." And I said, "Is that right?" Says, "Yes. She called me in and had a bin full of instruments, you know, and says pick out one, we're going to start a band." Yes, that was the first --
Well, what was her name?
Mrs. Bessie L. Allen, A, double-l, e-n.
Oh, she was a wonderful woman, wasn't she?
A wonderful woman, and the way she got this money, she started this in Sunday school, and they had about 500 kids that would come there every Sunday.

Yeah, sure. It was a big Sunday school, and you all met in a big room, and then after you -- we played a little bit, the band played, and a little talking here and there, you know, and then you all went off to separate rooms. Some of the boys went to number one room, some of the boys in
number two room. Some of the girls in number one -- I think it was split up. And you'd go up there and they would give you a Bible, you know, and you'd read from the Bible.
Was this Baptist?
No, this was no denomination. It was just --
Just all the children in the neighborhood.
She did this thing. And what a mind she had. I think about it. It's fantastic. The older I get the way I think about it, you know.
Yeah.
I think --
What you really did.
-- what could that woman have been -- you know, how she could think of such --
Yeah.

And a lot of people, you know, there's always somebody that don't like something. So a lot of people would say, 'Oh, no, I wouldn't have my kids go up there. She's a truant officer,' or something like that, you know, and she'll put you in a home, you know. And my mother paid no attention to it and I guess a lot of other mothers didn't either.
She had a home where -- that's right, I want to tell you about that too. She had a home like an orphanage, you know. And she'd have these kids from all over the state of Kentucky,
I imagine, you know. And what happened is when she'd bring them altogether with the other kids that had homes and things, it was a good thing for them, you know?
Of course.
Because -- and then she'd put some of them in the band.
Yeah.

I remember Mac there, Mac Walker, the bass player I was telling you about, he turned out to be a good friend of mine because he couldn't stay out too late, but after rehearsal I'd take him to my house and we'd eat together, you know.
So he had some home life.
Yes. But he had to be back out at the home at a certain time, you know.
Yeah. Was the home right there in the city?
Yeah, right in town. It was only, I guess -- I imagine it would be about 15 blocks.
And she ran that as well.

She ran that. And the way she got the money for the band, she used to go down to the different department stores and the lawyers and doctors downtown, you know, white, you know, and what she thought had money, and she would tell them of the work she was doing in the west end for the
colored kids.
Yeah. Was she white or was she black?
No, she was a black woman.
Yes.
Real light skinned, a light skinned woman.
Yes.
So she would -- some of them would give her $5.00, $10.00, whatever they had. Some of them give her $5.00 to get rid of her, you know.
Yeah.
And then she got down to the department stores, why they'd send her like $500.00 a year, every year, you know.
Really?
To help her, you know.
Would they?
Yes. And she'd in turn take this money and buy instruments, because we'd tear them up as fast as we'd get them. You know how kids are.
Yeah.

And we didn't really know how to take care of the instruments. And she'd take this money and buy instruments and she hired a beginner's teacher, so you had to stay with him about six months, maybe longer. If you were
slow you stayed longer.
Yes.
Maybe nine, but then they'd put you in the band.
Yes?
And she had a conductor for the band. His name was Lockwood Lewis.
Who was he? Was he a school musician?

Yeah, he was a wonderful guy. A big guy, looked like Adam Powell, you know, and about that height and everything, you know. And he would -- they'd make you read all the -- make sure you were reading your parts right, you know, and rehearse after school, after public school, then you'd come over there and rehearse, you know. Overtures, like, "Morning, Noon and Night," "Poet and Peasant," "Light Cavalry," "1812."
Well, how many would be in the band?
Well, we'd have anywhere from 45 to maybe 60, you know, because --
And this would be trumpets, trombones, --
Trumpets, trombones.
Tuba?
At one time we had three bass, three tubas. And then about two snare drums and a bass drum. And then the clarinets, I don't know, about 18 clarinets, maybe. And around about --
Really?
Yeah, and about 14 trumpets and 4 alto horns, and a baritone horn, a euphonium, which is the same thing as a baritone.
Oh, yeah? Is it? I didn't realize that.

Only the baritone is a single bell. The euphonium has got two bells on it. It's got one big one and one little bell, where you press a valve in, and it sounds like a trombone coming out, with a little valve, you know.
Does it?
Yes.
Did you ever play that?
That's an euphonium. No, but I was around them, you know, so --
Is that right. Were they hard to play?
No, I don't think they were any harder than the --
Than the tuba?

Than the baritone horn. But they say you could take one baritone horn and put it in an 80 piece band and you can hear it all over. (Singing). Like that, you know. It wouldn't be as low as a bass, see, but it would be the middle of that.
It penetrates.
Yeah. And they used to write in them K. L. King marches, and Sousa marches. We'd play all of those. And you could hear that baritone running all through there, you know.
Fancy that.
That obligato.
How many would they have of the baritone?
Well, we wouldn't have but one baritone, because they said -- 80 pieces you could hear it, you know.
Isn't that something. What does it look like?
Well, it looks like, you know, an upright bass.
Yes.
It looks like an upright bass.
It does.
Not a bass, not a Sousaphone.
No.
It looked like an upright bass, only smaller.
Only smaller.
Yeah. Hank Duncan, the piano player, do you remember him?
Yeah.
His brother was great with that. He had

a young brother that played in that band, and he was real great on this baritone horn. Because they -- and outside of that he was an outstanding reader. You had to read in that band. Because sometimes, if we couldn't get the idea of the phrase, he'd say, "Dunc, play that over for the fellows. Let them hear it," you know, and he'd go right through it, you know. He was beautiful with that.
Well, when you -- well, let's go back a little bit to -- well, let's go back to when you first heard it then, and what happened?
Well, I went down to hear the parade, and then I saw these trombones in front, gold, and these little guys playing all these different instruments, you know.
And marching.

Yeah, and marching, you know, with their uniforms on and things like that. And I was wearing short pants, you know. At that time they made you wear short pants. You wouldn't think of putting on long pants.

But I saw this band and I said, "Wow, there are some guys in there no older than me. If they can do that I can do it, you know." And I kept looking, and I went running back to my mother and grandmother, saying, "I want a trombone. I want a trombone." You know, the trombones looked so pretty down front there, you know. Sliding and -- and so my grandmother said, "What's wrong with you, are you crazy?" "Who's he think
has got money to buy a trombone? We can hardly buy bread and he wants a trombone." So they thought I'd get over it in two or three days or something, you know.
What were you, about nine?

I was about -- I'd say about 10 or 11 at that time. About 10 or 11, I guess. And so I kept it up and they thought I'd get over it, and I kept this up, day after day after day after day, "I want a trombone. I want a trombone." Every chance I'd get I'd put that on them, you know. And things was hard back there, during the Depression times.
Yes.
And things.
Sure. There wasn't money for a musical instrument.
Yeah. So finally they called a fellow up in time, his name was Hence Grundy. He was one of the top trombone players.
How do you spell that, Hence?
Hence. H-e-n-c-e.
Oh.
He played with a band called the Noble Blue Guitar Stompers, and he played with a jug band. We used to have a jug band. You know, how you blow on the jug? (Singing).
Oh?
Yeah, it was like a bass. It was a jug band. And I used to see him play on a corner, you know.
Yeah.

And so she called him. I think she knew him, and she called him and asked him how much does a trombone cost and how much is a lesson. So he said, 'Well, Mrs. Jones, trombones are pretty expensive and the lessons are pretty expensive, and I know you don't have the money to throw away like that. You don't know if he'll want to keep it up or not.' Said 'But that band he was talking about that he seen in the street parade, that's called the Booker T. Washington Community Center Band, and if you take him over there they'll give him a trombone and teach him free.' So --
You nearly --

Yeah. Oh, wow. So she said, 'I'm going to take you over there.' 'Good.' So she took me over and Mrs. Allen asked me, 'What kind of horn would you want, son?' So I said, 'A trombone.' I didn't know what the hell I was asking for. I'm glad I didn't get it now, because those things are hard to play.
(Laughter)

So she gave me this trombone, so she said, 'Let's see if you can fill it,' and I had no idea of how to fill it, so she showed me how to fill it, was telling me, and the beginners' teacher was there. So I tried and he said,

"Now, pucker your lips up." And said, after I got a sound out, "Now, see if you can reach the seventh position." Well, I tried and I tried to reach that seventh position. That was the last note on the horn, you know.
Yeah.

So, she says, "Oh, that's a shame. His arms are too short. But we have another horn here for you." So I said, "Which one is that," and she said, "The alto horn." Well, I had enough sense to know that I didn't want that alto horn, you know, because all it was was (Singing). But I didn't want that, but I'd settle for anything to get in the band.
Well, what does that alto horn look like, Jonah?
That's something like what I was telling you about, the upright bass. And then the baritone is next in size to it.
Yeah.
And then the alto horn is smaller.
So it's sort of the bell comes out like that?
No, the bell's straight up.
Oh, the bell's straight up.
Straight up, yeah.
I see what you mean, yeah.
And the baritone goes up like that too.
And the bass is straight up there too, see?
I see, yeah.
So they gave me this, and I stayed on it, I guess, about -- I stayed on it for two years.
Well, you learned to read.
Yeah, that was the great thing about it.
Yeah.
Because I still didn't realize what it meant. See an alto is to a trumpet player as a clarinet has a meaning to a saxophone.
To a saxophone.
See, you can get a good clarinet player and he can play the heck out of the saxophone.
Yeah.
But the other way around, no. A good tenor sax player, he wants to stay away from a clarinet.
That's right.
He won't be bothered with that. So that's why the alto kind of helps the trumpet out, because the mouthpiece is not big, but it's a little bigger than the trumpet, you know.
Yeah. So you can sort of ease into it.
Yes. And then by playing that alto for two years it gave me a nice -- it built up my muscles in my lip for the trumpet, and also made me know how to read good.
That's right. Well, would you -- would he send you all home to practice at home, reading?
Oh, yeah. You'd take your horn home and you'd practice.
And he gave you music books?

Yeah, you'd have your music book. You'd go home and practice you know, and run over it, so you could get it right when you came back. But he didn't allow you to play jazz. No, he didn't like you to play jazz. Anytime he caught you playing jazz he'd crack you on your fingers, you know.
Why? What did he tell you?

Well, he just said, 'No, don't play that. What is that? You don't see that on your music do you? So don't put that in there.' You know, some guys would slip in an extra note every now and then. Some guys had got smart, you know, had got out and heard somebody play or something, you know. And he'd come back and he'd try to slip it in, you know. And --
And he's say, 'That's not on the music,' huh?

Yeah. 'That's not on the music. Where do you see that? Don't put that in there. What are you doing?' And -- but we all liked him because he had little jokes, little sayings, he would carry on with us, and he was

a big, fine guy. They used to give him the devil because the older guys that was in that band, the older musicians, said, "They've only give him a stick to break your back," because those guys are going to come up some day and take your place, you know? Which they did. Which they did. They came out of there. It was like a turnover. You see, so many guys would leave, maybe, this year, because in the big band era it was, you know, so guys were looking for guys that could read, you know, band leaders like.
Yeah.
So they would take out two or three of the best men.
Yeah.
This year, then some more would come up, see?
Yeah.
More would join the band. It was like a turnover. Then before I left the band, we had girls in there. We had nice girls, you know, playing trumpet, and about five playing clarinets, you know.
Wasn't that kind of unusual? Didn't the families think that was kind of funny, when the girls wanted to play instruments?
Well, I don't know. We never gave it a thought, you know. All at once we looked up, and here they

come, starting with girls. So you didn't ask no questions, you know, because you're getting all this free training, and you were getting the instruments and stuff, you know. A lot of people -- like anything else, a lot of people didn't think too much of it, you know, but the overall, the -- of the band itself, because a lot of people didn't care for her because they tried to say that she was a truant officer and she would take your kid away from you and all that. Well, you know, all those kinds of things. I remember them saying that, and I remember my mother and them talking about it, you know. And I didn't butt into nothing then, you know, a youngster. I was brought up like that. You never -- you say back and listened, you know.
Yeah.
So whatever happened, you know, went along with the deal.
So about the girls, nobody said a word, and they got so they were in the marching band. They'd march right with us, you know, and travel with us. Sure. See they'd --
What would they be like, 11, 12, 13?
Yeah, something like that.
Yeah.
Sure, 11, 12, you know. Maybe 10, you know.
Well, what did you -- you told Stan that
for her to accept you you had to agree that you'd come after school every day?
Oh, yeah, you had to come to band rehearsal.
Every day she had band rehearsal?
Every day was band -- no, on Sunday you played. Saturday you didn't go. But Sunday you played all day in Sunday school.
Oh.
And you played one overture, one overture, and then you played all the church music. "What a Friend We Have in Jesus," "Abide With Me," and, "Onward Christian Soldiers."
Did you play for the services?
We played while everybody sings, yeah.
Oh, did you?
The whole Sunday school would sing.
Oh, really?
And then we went to different rooms, as I told you about. We'd play, "Onward Christian Soldiers." You know.
Yeah. Yeah.
And then you played an overture, one overture, and -- every Sunday. So you'd practice that during the week and you played it on Sunday.
Did they learn a new piece of music every
Just about, just about, yeah.
Oh, really?
And they were always bringing in new music books, marches, you know, which we didn't play in Sunday School -- we'd play those marches in front of fraternal organizations, you know.
Oh, like the Elks and everything?
Like the Elks and Masons and the United Brothers of Friendship. And sometimes they would go on a convention, and they would take us because they could get us cheaper, see.
Yes.
Once we went to Chicago, and St. Louis. I think the Elks took us to St. Louis. And they could get us -- see the men, they wanted a certain price, you know.
Yeah.
And they could get us cheaper.
Yeah.
Because we didn't belong to no union.
No.
And they'd get the whole gang and put us all in a big dormitory.
Yeah.
They didn't have to worry about no rooms
for us, with all these beds in here, all these cots, you know.
Yeah, sure.
Yeah.
That's where the band was.

Yeah, sure. And I was trying to think were there any girls there. I can't think -- I know they were there, because I have a picture there with them on it. But I -- maybe they stayed somewhere else, because you know how kids are in those days.
That's right.
So I imagine some of the girls' parents wouldn't have agreed to all staying together like that.
Yeah, that's right.
But she was very strict. So things went down right. She was strict, yeah.
It was done just like it should be.
Yes, she was very strict. No -- you couldn't get out of order or nothing, you know. Everything had to be straight.
Well, like with the band, weren't there any bad boys, or were --
Oh, yeah, we had --
TIS2
There we go. All right, Jonah. So we were saying about the girls, they must have been in a different
place.

Yeah. They -- well, it must have been, because she was very strict, as I was saying, you know, and your conduct, she'd watch it. Of course you know how kids are. They always get into something, you know.
Yeah.

They can always study some kinds of things, you know. We were camping out once. We had tents, you know. I don't know why this was, I forget. It's been quite a while. But we had to dig these trenches around these tents, so that if it rained, the rain would go into these trenches, you know, around the tents.
Yeah.

And that was something new to me, you know, because as a kid you're always looking for new things. But then we had another little cat in there, his name was Raymond Tate. He was alto, played the alto horn too, and he went around and hitting on the tents with a stick, you know. Well, there was a saxophone player, sitting on the side of his bunk there, and he hit him in the head, and he fell out, you know, the guy passed out. So these kinds of things were always jumping up, you know. And they raised the devil at him.
Well, Mrs. Allen wouldn't go on the trips, or would she?
No, her husband usually went.
Oh.

His name was Henry Allen. So he would usually go on the trips with us all the time, because she stayed there to keep that Sunday school going, if you were out of town. So that Sunday school still went on you know.
Oh, I see.
And I don't remember her ever missing a Sunday. She was always there.
Always there. Well, that Sunday school, they didn't all play in the band, there would be people that didn't play in the band.
No, as I say, there were about 500 kids, you know.
Yeah, that's right.
So they're out there singing along with the band, you know.
Yeah, I see.
'Onward Christian Soldiers,' in church, you know.
Yeah.
It was a thing to keep the Sunday school going somewhere for the kids to go, for those that maybe their parents wasn't encouraging them to go to church or something, you know.
And keeping them off the streets.
Yeah. And sometimes you'd go to Sunday school and then you went with your mother that night to church, too.
Yes. Did you?
Yeah, sure.
And with your grandmother, too?
And with my grandmother, yeah. We went to church with them.
Yeah.
That was after Sunday school, you know what I mean, so you'd just come up with that.
Yeah, sure. Well, when you switched to trumpet, you were like about two years on the alto?

Yeah, about two years on the alto, and some the guys left. There was a guy named Matthew Holland, he was the first chair man, and he studied very hard at home on his horn, and finally he went out and started playing with the adults around town, you know.
Yeah.
He started to play with them.
What was he, 17 or 18 or something?
Yeah, just about.
Yeah.
And she wasn't too keen on you playing with outsiders like that, you know.
Oh.
Because she'd try to keep you, you know, keep you away from whiskey, and didn't want you to be mixed up in that crowd out there.
Yeah.
And stuff. So he left and he went with a band that was called Howard Jordan's, I think, and then that means that somebody else that was sitting next to him, they'd move up into his chair, you know.
Right.

And then when they'd go, somebody'd move up. So then they come to me once and said, 'Well, we're going to put you on the trumpet, fourth trumpet.' So I was playing -- had about two of us playing fourth trumpet, and about, oh, maybe two or three playing third trumpet and about two or three playing second trumpet. Then you had the first trumpet, one guy played that, then you had a solo trumpet. Some of them overtures had on there, 'Solo trumpet,' you know.
Oh, yeah.
Or, 'First trumpet,' you know. And so it didn't take me long at all to move up to the first chair, because the other guys was leaving.
Well, Jonah, was that -- can you remember was that a thrill when you picked up that trumpet, after the alto horn?
Yeah, well I was glad to get it. I was
glad to get a trumpet so I could play some melody, you know.
Yeah.
I was glad to get it.
Could you -- did you get yourself a tone on it right away?
Oh, yeah. I didn't have no trouble with that, because I'd had the idea of it for two years on that alto horn, you know.
Yeah.

See, what we did was two years on the alto horn, but one year -- just about, not exactly, but one year I played the alto horn, and we were breaking them up so fast, and then we come in one day after about a year and she had four mellophones. See, there was four of us playing alto horn, and she had four new mellophones. Now, this looks like -- the mellophone looks like a French horn.
Yeah.
Only you don't put your hand up in it.
Oh, I see.
And the pitch is E-Flat, same as alto.
Oh, I see.
The French horn is like an F.
Yeah.
See, this is E-Flat, but it looked like a French horn and you play it, you know, with the valves on top
there, and you'd hold it by the bell. So she come up with four of those.
They've got a pretty sound, don't they?
Yeah. Yeah, they've got a very nice sound.
Yeah.
And then I played the mellophone for about a year.
Yeah.
And then after that -- well, I used the same mouthpiece I was using on the alto, see.
Oh.

And then they moved me up to the trumpet. Well, I had the idea then and my lip was pretty strong, so I did pretty good, and I guess in about two years I moved up to first trumpet. Not solo, but first.
No kidding. Well, that was fairly quick, wasn't it?
Yeah, I moved up right fast, you know.
Well, you must have had a good tone right away, I guess.
Yeah, I had a pretty good tone, and --
And power.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, that come from the mellophone, see.
Yeah. Moreso than the alto horn, huh?
Yeah, well, both of them served about the same purpose.
Yeah.
There wasn't much difference in them.
No.
They're both E-Flat.
Yeah.

Pitched to E-Flat, you know. And you played the same music. If the music says E-Flat Alto, you play the mellophone. Yeah, first, second and third. See, in the first place you've got to move up. See, when they put you in there, I started down as third -- I mean fourth alto.
Yeah.
And then you move up to -- maybe another one of the guys goes in the trombone section, see.
Yeah.
Which in our case it did happen. The first man went in the trombone section, and then I'd move up to third, and some other guy would come in and play fourth, you know.
Yeah, right. Right.
Then finally another one would move up to -- maybe he'd go over in the trumpet section and then I'd move up to second.
Yeah. Yeah.
Then pretty soon some other guy would go over -- maybe like when Dunc left, I think Duncan's brother started to play the baritone.
Oh, yeah.
When he left, then -- in fact he died, you know, and then one of the alto players went over there, so then -- the first alto went over there, and I moved up to first.
Yeah, I see. Yeah.
Then later -- you were always moving, you know.
Yeah, that's nice.
Sure.
It'd stimulate your ambition.

I enjoyed it. I really enjoyed it. And with all the kids, if there was something you didn't understand, why they would -- you'd say, 'How does this go here,' you know, and they would show you how it would go.
Yeah, so you didn't have to worry or --

No, you didn't have to worry too much. That was the way I got the name of Jonah, you know, from playing -- my name was Robert Elliott Jones, and so -- and the conductor would always call us by our last names, you know, he'd say, 'Hey, Jones --,' so and so, you know. So I went in one day, and I had just gotten in the band -- funny how things

stick with you -- and I was playing a march called, 'Our Director,' and it gets to the trio, and that's where it softens down, in the altos, (Singing), and I was playing that, and I didn't know -- I wasn't paying attention to my sharps and flats, and this thing went to E-Flat, and I kept playing E-Natural, (Singing), so he says, 'Somebody is hitting the wrong notes there. Watch it. Watch it.' You know, he rapped on his desk and stopped us and said, 'Watch it when you get down to the trio.' And he was very excitable, and he stammered all the time. And so we went down again, he said, 'Let's take it down again, from the top,' and we went down from the top and we got down there again, and I wasn't paying any attention, and, (Singing). He rapped again and said, 'Who is that?' You know. And sometimes you're wrong and you don't know it.
That's right.
You just keep going, you know. I knew better, but I just wasn't paying attention, you know.
Yeah.

And then he said, 'Watch it.' And finally he took it down again and we got down to the trio and he caught me. It excited him so bad, it made him so angry, he threw his baton at me, and he went to say, 'Jones, don't you see that's the wrong note?' And instead of Jones coming out he said, 'Jonah, don't you see that's wrong?' And all the guys laughed in the band, you know, and they all started calling me Jonah
after that and I've been Jonah ever since.
(Laughter)
My mother would say, 'Who are they talking about when they call you and ask for Jonah?'
(Laughter)
That's funny.

I've been Jonah ever since. But it was a great band. And it got to do little things like, you know, little mischief things, like the bass player, and I was having fun with him. I was telling him about it. We were reminiscing not too long ago, a very nice guy, he lives over in Jersey, but he's been in another business. He played with Louis Depps' band way back when Earl Hines was with him.
Really?
Yeah, years ago. He was one of the first out of the band, you know.
What's his name?
Louis Thompson.
Oh.

Yeah, played with Depp and somebody else. I can't think who the other -- somebody else's band, and probably a couple of others, but he was out in front of us, so we didn't know where he was. But he lives over in Jersey. He's been working for one of the distillers, Brown and Forman Distillers, out of Kentucky, but he lives in Jersey, has his
own home there. And he don't play anything now, but he was a wonderful bass horn player. Played the double-B, too, didn't play E-Flat.
What does that mean?
Well, that means what pitch the instrument is in.
Yeah.
See, some basses, it's double-B, you know.
Oh, I didn't know.
Double B-Flat. And some of them are E-Flat.
Oh. Why do they need the two pitches?

I don't know what that was. I know that the guys could get over the E-Flat better, because we had -- this guy I was telling you about, Mac, he could take that E-Flat tuba and he could play that introduction that Louis Armstrong played on, 'West End Blues.' (Singing). He could play that on that E-Flat. While the guys playing the double B-Flat, they couldn't make that.
Oh, yeah.
I don't know what it was.
The way it lay.
Yeah, the way it lay, and -- because we always used to wonder, you know, how they could get away with
that on that E-Flat bass. Before the bass fiddles had come into it, you know.
Yeah, right.
I think that's one reason why the Lloyd Scott took Mac, you know, because -- on the bass, because he was fast on it, you know, he could get over.
Yeah.

And he listened to those records, you know, Louis Armstrong's records, and we'd listen together when we'd go home, and we'd practice them. You had to forget it when you went back to Sunday school with the band, though.
Yeah.
We'd slow it down so we could hear what Louis was doing.
In your home?
Yes.
Did your mother say anything?
No. Didn't say a word. I guess she was happy we was in the house.
That you were doing it, yeah.

But sometimes she'd get a little peeved when I was there by myself, you know, and trying to practice things, you know, and they would give me a chair and set me out in the back yard. "Now sit back here and practice."
(Laughter)
Well, listen, we got off the track a little, because you said you got together with your friend.

Oh, yeah, I was telling you we got together and we were reminiscing about things we did and stuff, and we was afraid of him, because he was one of them great big guys. He was big, 'Cause we were smaller than him, and he was in his dormitory in Chicago, all of us were there together, sleeping there, and what happens is, all of were together, sleeping there, and what happened was he was laying up there, asleep, in the top bunk up in there, and he was sound asleep, so we got some candles and we lit the candles and we let that fall on his fingers, you know, and it kind of glued them together, you know. Glued them together, and then we run and jumped in bed, because we was afraid of him. We run and jumped into our bunks, and finally he woke up and he said, "Who did that? Who put this on me?" And nobody said a word.
(Laughter)
Was he mad?
I think he was a little bit angry, but we had nerve enough to do that to him, you know, because he knew that he had control over us, you know, that he could -- that we didn't bother him, you know.
Yeah.
We didn't bother him. He was like the leader of the thing, you know.
Yeah.
So we never bothered him, you know. We never bothered him, but we glued that stuff -- if he'd caught us at that he'd have probably killed us.
(Laughter)

Funny things like that, you know, come up in the band. With a lot of kids, they're always thinking up stuff. A guy went in once, on the road, one of them country towns in Kentucky we was playing, a lot of those fairs too, country fairs, and we would -- like Lawrenceburg and Mt. Sterling, they'd have a fair, maybe three days a week, on the weekend, and Lexington, Kentucky, they had a big fair there. We'd play that. And I remember once we were going, and so we stopped on the road to get a soda or something to drink, you know, and here comes the trombone out, come from a very good family, and this guy played wonderful trombone, and here he comes and the family, as I say, was very nice, you know, but some guys -- had a lot of kid stuff, you know. Now, you had them tin boxes that you'd keep them cakes in, penny cookies, or something, you know, penny cakes. Now, as soon as we reached there we was going to steal one, take one, you know, but he come out with about three boxes, come out to the bus with about three, and juggling them, too.
(Laughter)
When we get together we talk about him
Did they get after him? Did they spot him?
I think we left before the guy come out or something.
(Laughter)

And then we had enough sense to keep them hid from Mr. Allen, you know, and stuff like that. But everybody was eating cookes in there, you know. Oh, it was a crazy band. It was crazy. When you think of those little things you did back there, you know. So that was one reason we got this club together, was --
With Dickie.
Yeah, with Dickie. Well, it's called the Kentucky Club. We got that together because we was going to try to get some kind of monument or something for this lady, you know, Mrs. Allen.
Oh, that would have been nice.
But what happens is finally we brought in some other people that wasn't from Kentucky. See, some other musicians wanted to join.
Yeah.
Now the thing began to get big.
Yeah.
And also, when you bring the other guys
in, then you change the name of the club.
That's right. And they don't know about her or --
Yeah, they don't know from that, you know.
No.

So then they changed it, and finally they said it's got to stop at 50 members, no more than 50. First we had about 25, 20 or 25, 30 at the most. Then you got that, so then we said we're going to stop at 50, 50's enough, and then well change the name and call it the Friendly 50.
That was nice.
Yeah, it was pretty nice. But then the guys that we knew, you know, all the different musicians that we knew. But the other thing went out the window, the original idea, you know, for the monument.
That's right, yeah.
For the woman, you know.
Yeah. Well, what did everybody do, met once a week or something, the Friendly 50?
Oh, it meets once a month. It's still going, yeah.
Oh, it's still going.
Yeah, it's still going.
So up at the club, up there?
145th. It's called the --
Celebrity.
No, no, not there, no. See, the Celebrity Club was just to get the thing together.
Yeah.

The next time we met we met in a bar. A guy that was from Kentucky, but he wasn't a musician. Billy Coleman's bar, the Orchid Bar, they call it, at 125th Street. Then the next time we met, we met with Les Carr, he was a saxophone player, and we met at his house, and then Beeson came, as I told you. I only saw him that once, you know.
Yeah.

And we had a big laugh, and were talking, and I was so glad to see him. And I couldn't get out of him what he was doing or where he'd been. He wasn't around the guys anymore. And we had so much fun talking different things. I had an old goat down there. We used to call him George.
Where, at home?

Yeah, in Kentucky, in Louisville. So I could throw him, you know. I'd grab him by his horns, you know. I'd come up to him and pat him, 'Nice George. Nice George.' And all at once I'd grab him by his horns, and you'd twist his neck and he'd fall. Now when he falls over, you'd better be getting ready to run, you know, because when he gets up he's coming at you with them horns, you know.
(Laughter)

So Bill Beeson come by one day, after practice, you know, after band practice. So he come by and I was showing him how to do it, you know, because he wanted to do it. So I said, "Be nice to him now, because he'll get mean after you throw him down. And be ready to run," I said. So Bill got him by the horns, turned him over, and he didn't go down enough, and I said, "Turn him some more. Don't turn him loose now." So Bill finally got him down but he didn't run. You know, this goat was behind him, he was tearing after Bill. Well, he wasn't too reckless, you know. He was all right. Then we had a lot of fun reminiscing about that. But I didn't get into why he doesn't play anymore or what, you know, because some guys don't like you to be getting into their business, you know. So I didn't know what had happened. I knew I could have used him many a time, you know.
Is that right? You could have used him.

Yeah, I would have been glad to use Bill, you know. He used to come back and tell me a lot. He left way before I did, and he'd come back to Kentucky, and we'd walk a lot and he would tell me what it was like, you know, being in big bands, with Benny Carter. First it was Horace Henderson's band.
Well, was he older than you?
No, he just got out a little bit quicker, you know. He got out a little quicker, you see. And as I say,

I was up at some age when I was ruled with an iron hand, you know. When I left Sunday school I had to come straight home, you know. Sure. You'd come home and let them know you're there. You didn't hang around the corner or anything. This happened till I got up to around 16 years old.
No kidding.

Sure. Yeah, you tell them where you are, you know. And then they kind of let me loose and let me play with some of the adults around town, in the joints, you know, which is good for you. And another one that played in there was Bob Carroll. Do you remember him?
Yes.
He played with Teddy Hill.
Yeah.
He played with Teddy Hill. I remember quite a few of those guys, yeah.
Well, Louisville was really quite a place for a guy who was coming up.
Yeah, a lot of music around there.
Well, do you think that it had a lot to do with that, that so many guys got a foundation?

Well, them guys coming out of there, they would have never gotten out of there. They would never have gotten into music or nothing, unless you had a setup like that. As I say, this woman was so wonderful.
Yeah.

And it was a lot of older guys around there playing, you know. Winstead's Wonders, they called them, about seven or eight pieces, and Howard Jordan's band. He had about 7, or maybe about 10. And Tapp, this guy I was telling you, Furman Tapp, he' had about eight. That's who my brother-in-law played the trombone with. Because Dickie had gone, and he was playing with Tapp for awhile, and they come through and went with Lloyd Scott, and that was Dickie, and Bill Coleman.
Bill Coleman.
And Frankie Newton. Yeah. All them was in that band together, with Lloyd Scott.
Were they?
Yeah, they went there. And then my brother-in-law, my wife's brother, Russell Bowles, played with Lunsford in later years.
Yeah.
You might remember him. And he --
A trombone player.
Yeah. He took Dickie's place with Tapp. And finally he left.
Well, let's get to that, then. Well, who did you know first? Did you know Russell before you knew your wife?
Well --
She was in the band, wasn't she?

She did a little bit. She didn't stay long. She just come in, she fooled around with the clarinet, I think, for awhile, and I think she fooled with the baritone for awhile, and everybody who fooled around eventually didn't make it, you know.
No.
So she didn't have too much interest in it, so --
No.
But she only lived about two blocks from the place, and she'd just come by.
And her brother was in it.
And her brother got in there, later, after Dickie, see. He wasn't in there while --
Oh, I see.
See, Dickie -- I think he come in after Dickie left.
Was Dickie a bad boy in the band?

No, he was a nice guy. He was a nice kid. We used to laugh at him because he'd come out of -- we always used to call him Parkland, you know, because he was named for that section of town called Parkland, and it didn't have any sidewalks. It had mud, you know.
Parkland?

Parkland. P-a-r-k-l-a-n-d. And we used to laugh at him because he'd come out of there with mud on his shoes. We had two or three of them like that, you know. And we'd call him, "Hey, Parkland, how you doing?"
(Laughter)
But he was a wonderful player. Another trombone player out of there was Milt Robinson. Did you ever hear of him? He played with Andy Kirk for awhile.
Yeah. I think so, yeah.
Milton Robinson. Made records, and with Benny Carter.
Yeah.

Yeah, he was very good. But the way I got out of there was I got so I played around with them bands in town too, and I played with the adult bands, and one guy named Artie Jones, I played with him every Sunday. And --
What did he play?
He was a trombone player. He had just the trombone and one trumpet, and maybe two or three sax.
And what kind of gigs would you do?
Oh, we'd do dance gigs.
Yeah. And dance halls.
Yeah. He'd have his music there, so he gave me the book and I had no trouble with that at all.
Yeah.
No trouble reading it at all.
Yeah. All the guys that came out of your band could read.
Oh, yeah, they could read. They could read anything, you know.
Yeah.
And so while I was doing this a guy come through there, the boat come through, the Island Queen, and it stayed in Cincinnati. A beautiful boat, a big sidewheeler, you know.
Yeah.

And what it did, every -- around the summer, it would take excursions from Cincinnati to a park about 12 miles out of Cincinnati called Coney Island. And this boat would take excursions every day out there, and then around the middle of September, it would take a trip from Cincinnati all the way down the Ohio River into the Mississippi River and then to New Orleans.
All paddlewheel.

Yeah, paddlewheel. Playing excursions on each side. See, like Cincinnati, and then it would come down to New Albany, which is across the river, and then it would play on the other side, Louisville, Kentucky, then it would go all the way down and play the -- it would go all the way down and

stop at Paducah. Now, this band that I'm telling you about, that was playing the boat, they were from Paducah, Kentucky, and what happened, you'd get down to Memphis, and at Memphis the Ohio River pours right into the Mississippi.
Yeah.
Then you've got Memphis, play there, like a moonlight excursion. You'd go out at night about 8:00 o'clock and they'd get back at 12:00, the dance.
Well, all those excursions you talked about, they'd go out and come back, bring the people back to where they took them from.
Yeah, go out and bring them back.
And then start up --
And then start off for the next town. And you know --
What did the band do? Where did they sleep?
Sleep right on the boat and eat right on the boat. $40.00 a week, room and board. So the guys would come through there, and that was a lot of money at that time, you know.
Yeah.
About 1928, and the guy come through there and he says -- he was around the Musicians' Club there, and he was asking -- they need a trumpet player and a clarinet. They

only had one trumpet. And so they said, "Well, there's a kid around here who plays pretty good trumpet. Maybe he'll go, he'll take it." "His name is Jonah Jones. He'll be coming by here after awhile. Maybe --," so I went by, and the guy asked me about it, and I had a close friend in the band, sitting right next to me. His name was William Granger, and he played beautiful horn, beautiful trumpet, you know. I liked his playing. And we were buddies. And so the guy asked me would I go. Well, now, I didn't know how my people were going to feel about this, you know. I should be on my own, but they never felt like that, you know. So I was a little afraid to go by myself, so I told them that I'll go if you take my buddy, you know, my friend William Granger, you know. He said, "What do you play?" I said trumpet. He said, "Oh, we don't need two trumpets. All we need is one trumpet. We already have one. We're looking for a clarinet and a trumpet." I said, "Oh, no, if you can't take him I can't go." So then they went to talk to him, went to talk to Granger, and so I guess he asked the guys about Granger and they said yeah, he came out of that same band over there. He's pretty good. He can read anything you have. So they went to him. So he told them, "Well, I can't go unless you take Jonah." So finally the guy give up the idea of the clarinet, and he said, "Okay, I'll just take the two trumpets."
So he already had one?
He already had one, and that was three, and in those days you didn't use three. Parts weren't made for three trumpets, you know.
No. And people had to do a lot of solos.
Sure, yeah. So we went on there, and it worked out all right, worked out nice, and we met some older guys, you know, that was in the band.
You felt more comfortable because you were both younger.

And we were together. Now we don't have horns. But so what I did, I'll show you, when you're brought up right, what we done, we don't have any horns. We've got the Sunday school horns. They let you take them home, but not on the road, you know.
No. No.

So now we've got the Sunday school horns and we take these horns and go on the boat with them, and our first payday, we had it all planned. Our first payday, we was in Memphis, so we got our $40.00, and we went out and bought two horns, $20.00 apiece. Wasn't nothing brand new, $20.00 apiece, and we bought them and had them to crate our horns up and send them back to the Sunday school. Sure. You never thought of, you know, keeping them, like kids do today. They'd forget all about it, you know. So it was on our minds all the time, we've got to get these horns back.
Yeah, because she didn't know you'd taken them.
No, no. So --
But that must have been quite a thrill, to have bought your own horn.

Oh, yeah, we bought our own horns. Well, I think the main thing that made us do that was because we knew that we were doing wrong by taking them in the first place. We had to get them back as quick as possible.
That's right.
Or else you'd never come back home, because your family's going to come down on you and --
Sure, if you steal the horns.
Stealing the horns and things, you know.
Yeah.
So --
Well, what about your parents when you told them you were going on the boat? What did they think about that?
Well --
Or did you go first and then let them know?
Yeah, I let them know later. Let them know later. I don't think I would have got out of there.
Were you living at home?
They wouldn't have went for it, because
they wasn't for me -- after I got up, they wasn't for me playing music. They were for me going to college. Wanted me to go to school, you know.
Yeah.

Go to college and then this woman had great connections, Mrs. Bessie Allen, the woman who had the band. If you showed any kind of promise, you know, not only music, but character or something, and you wanted to go to school, she had connections where she could send you to Tuskegee, one of the -- you know, the black universities Tuskegee or Fisk, something like that.
Yeah.
Because some of them did go, you know, some of them didn't play music after they got up to a size where they could go to college. Instead of staying with music they went to college, you know.
And got into something else.
Yeah, and got into something else, you know.
That's right.
Wonderful woman. I'll never forget her. And so now we sent our horns back. Now we feel safe.
Yeah.
But now we were getting a touch of the world. We were playing Memphis on this side.
And you'd never seen Memphis before.

And on the other side is Helena, Arkansas. I'll never forget it. It's just like today, you know. I remember it just like today. And then you'd go down a little further and you'd run into Vicksburg, Mississippi on one side, and you'd take the excursion. If you're coming in in the day, the calliope plays, you know (Singing).
Oh, yeah. Yeah.
You know, with the steam coming out?
Yeah.
That's to let everybody know you're there.
That's right. And then everybody comes down to the --
They come down and look, you know. Then they go back home for dinner and get dressed, and then they come on the boat, you know.
Yeah.
For the moonlight ride.
How much would they have to pay for those excursions, can you remember?
I don't know, now.
A couple dollars, I suppose, huh?
Maybe. Maybe a dollar and a half.
Yeah.
Something like that, you know.
Yeah.
Because they'd draw a crowd wherever they went.
Oh, yeah, sure they would.

Then you'd go down further, then you're in Louisiana and Mississippi. Then you get to New Orleans. A big thing, because all the other boats from St. Louis, like the Streckfuss company they'd all start to salute you when you're coming in. All kinds of whistles and things. Exciting, you know.
Well, how many boats would be in there like that?

Oh, it'd be about -- I imagine about four or five boats, you know, because Streckfuss had two or three, and I imagine there was a couple out of New Orleans, and you're coming into the Gulf now, you know.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
All six of you working together all that time?
Yeah, uh-huh. Never went anyplace. So a guy sent for me to come down here, named Jimmy Smith.
Yeah?

He had a band, the Missourians, and it was all with Cab, and Cab -- so half of them decided to go out, because they put Cab in front of this band, and I think some of them didn't like it so well, because they was already organized. Then they were -- they was organizing their own band, so I come down in about 1932, to play -- they sent for me to come down and play at the Savoy. They were in the Savoy. Danny ______ Dixon was on trumpet, and Ted, and we played the Savoy for about two weeks.
Well, wait a minute. You're going too fast. Wait a minute. We'll just finish this off, so we can get started on the other one right.
T251V
Well, I wanted to -- I just want to -- we mustn't forget where we were, but --
One, two, three. I think we were there with the band and --
Yeah. But listen, before you do that, before we get too far away from the fact that you worked in that first band when that was the first band that Roy was in
too --
Oh, yeah, with Horace Henderson, yeah.
No, it wasn't Horace, was it?
Yeah, it was Horace's band.
Oh, it was?
Yeah, that's the one I said they had Red Harlan on trumpet and Bernice Morton on trumpet.
Oh, yeah. I'm sorry, you're absolutely right.
And then when Roy left we got Granger.
Well, listen, when you were blowing there with Roy, you told Stan* at one time that you found that very beneficial, you enjoyed it.

Oh, yeah. I'd never heard a guy blow that much trumpet before, you know, and unless it was Louis, and I didn't know a guy existed like Roy. He was blowing -- I'll say he was blowing as much or more than he did in the later years, you know.
Was he really.
And he was only about 17.
Where did he come from?
Out of Pittsburgh.
Yeah, that's right.
I know Horace -- I knew when I went there, we went up to the house to practice, and this guy was blowing
* Stanley Dance, jazz critic-historian-author.
Yeah, because he hadn't had any experience.

I remember once he was playing -- he had to read for me at that time, you know, just coming out of that band. If you couldn't read, there was no excuse. Anything -- I can go back as far as I can go in music, reading, that was supposed to be the foundation of everything, you know, and if a guy didn't read, I didn't have no respect for him. But Roy kind of changed all of that. He played so much. You know, I told Horace one time, I said, "Hey, he's not playing the right part on that sax part there, you know." I said, "Roy's not playing the right part there." So he says, "That's all right, Fathead." He used to call me Fathead. He says, "That's all right Fathead. Leave him alone. Sometimes he puts his own sax part to it." I said, "What do you mean, puts his own sax part?" He said, "Yeah, sometimes he puts his own sax part to it. Would you believe it, his own part sounds better than the one that's on the paper sometimes."
(Laughter)

I was a little angry, too, because this guy was blowing all this horn out here, you know, and wasn't reading. But it was a great thing and I was glad I got in at that time, because I played jazz at that time, I got it from him, listening to him so much, and from admiring him so much, you know. A little of it had to rub off there, you know.
Well, how long was that, several months?
Yeah, I imagine. I imagine. Yeah, I'd say several months. It wasn't quite a year.
Where did he go on to from there?

Well, see, he went with Speed Webb in another band, a big band, that was touring. So many bands in them days was touring, you know. So he went with a big band called Speed Webb, which has Ronald Jones in it. And -- but let's see, we went to a place -- I was getting a little ahead of my story -- we went to play a battle of music while he was with the band, with Horace, in Detroit, and we was playing a battle of music with a band called Earl Walton, and they were on one stand and we were on the other, and the first time I seen Roy's brother Joe, he was playing with Earl Walton.
Oh, was he.
Yeah.
Alto?
Yeah, playing alto, yeah. And he got after Roy and he gave him the devil, you know. I don't think
they'd seen each other for a long time, you know. So he told him that to stay around here and let me help you out with your reading, you know.
Gee, is that right.
Yeah.
He was older?

Yeah, I think he was a little older. But anyway, the -- this guy played so much with him, until some of it had to rub off, you know. He could just play anything, "Boo Hoo Jack," note for note, like Louis Armstrong, and there was a hard solo in there. I know, because I tried to play it myself and couldn't. And he could play that thing note for note and make it swing too, you know.
Well, did he have quite that much -- he didn't have all that much range at that time, did he? I don't think.
Not as he had in later years.
Because I think he changed his embrochure a little.
Yeah, he could have. Because when I hear him now he's hitting those high B-Flats and things. At that time if he hit a good F -- if he hit a good F back in them days that was a high note, you know.
Yeah, that's right. Yeah. Was he easy to get along with in those days, Roy?
Yeah, we used to go around together, you know, and he was the same way, just as crazy as always, you know.
Yeah.

And go around and jump on everybody's bandstand and blow them out, you know. He was always -- he always did that, you know. And sometimes he couldn't -- they knew, when he come in, the trumpet players would get off the stand or something, and stop playing. And he'd say, 'You go up and get them started.'
(Laughter)

And I'd go up and get them started, and here he comes, you know. As soon as we get them going good, then here he comes. And he was real little, you know, and he'd sit right on the edge of his chair, and he'd be stomping his feet and playing, you know. That's when they started to call him Little Jazz, you know.
That's right. Had they started to call him Little Jazz then?
Yeah, well, right after that, you know, because everywhere he went in all different towns, he --
He always had to go blow.
Oh, he'd have to go at you, you know.
So he was making a name for himself, then.
Yeah, all over. People liked him, you
know. But I think it was more or less musicians appreciated him.
Oh, yeah.
Because the public wasn't too hip, you know, to --
Did he get that buzz in his tone then, that early?
I don't remember him having it then.
No, I don't -- he was sort of more like Louis then, he played like --
Yeah.
Only more open.
He says, 'I never heard Louis.' See, I'd never heard Louis. But you'd never had to hear Louis.
No.
You were just influenced by him automatically.
That's right. Everybody was blowing Louis, anyway, weren't they.
Sure. Everybody, you know.
Yeah, sure.
You didn't have to meet him, or --
I mean you hear Roy play Louis now.
Sure. Not only him, but a lot of other guys.
Sure. Sure.
A lot of these boppers play Louis and they don't know where it come from, because they got it from another one and they play it twice as fast, you know, double up on it, you know.
That's right. Yeah. Well, that's good, Jonah. Well, I didn't want to miss that, you know.
Oh, yeah, that was a wonderful time.
Well, listen, let's go back now.
Then when he left --
Yeah?
Then I took over some of his solos, you know.
Oh, yeah, I see.
See, and I could play them almost like he played them, from listening at him all the time, you know. Sure.
Like Johnny Hodges says, get out of the kitchen.
Yeah, sure. So when I had a good lip then I could play the first parts and play the solos, you know. Sure. Didn't bother me at all.
No. Fancy that.
Yeah, and --
Well, you always had the good tone, Jonah.
Yeah, and a pretty good first tone, I'd
say. I used to like to play first trumpet, you know.
Yeah.

Because sometimes -- you see, things had changed a little bit from then, you didn't have a special man to play first. You had a man -- I know Horace sometimes would give -- if he was humming an arrangement, a head arrangement, he'd give Roy the first, because he was swinging. See, he'd play the first part and swing it, you know.
Yeah.
He'd really swing the whole thing, you know. So I learned something by that, you know, that you can in brass sections put it on top there, so it'll have some feeling to it, you know.
Yeah. Cootie was like that.
Oh, yeah, sure. Cootie would swing anything.
Yeah.
Power, too.
Power and sound, that beautiful tone he had.
Oh, what a sound. So then after that then he went with Chick Webb during them times.
Oh, did he?
Yeah, things was changing. Not Chick, no.
Speed Webb.
Speed Webb.
Yeah.
Sorry. Speed Webb. And Speed had with him at that time Renald Jones and Vic Dickenson.
Oh, did he.
Yeah, Vic was there. And I don't remember the -- oh, a guy from out of Milwaukee was playing the alto. He was very good, had a very good sound. Leonard Gay was his name.
Oh, yeah?

Yeah, Leonard Gay was very good, and they had a wonderful band, and we'd follow each other around, you know, and you'd see somebody out of Speed Webb's band one night, they put it on a wall, 'If you hear a scream in the night, it's the mighty Speed Webb.' And they used to scream all the time (Singing). So they'd leave all these different towns and leave all these little sayings backstage, on the shell, you know, of the bandstand.
Yeah.
You'd come in there and you'd read all that, you know. And he had a good band, you know. There were some nice bands out there in the west, you know, around Indiana.
Well, they built a lot of people, didn't they?
Oh, yes.
Well, listen, now let me take you back to where we were. Luke sent for you.
Yeah, then Luke got them to --
And Joe Thomas came in too.
And I worked there for awhile. We were five pieces in there. They had four rhythm and myself, and then in come John L. Henderson on alto, and Joe Thomas on the tenor.
Yeah, so then you had seven.
Then we had seven, and we got to swinging in there pretty good, and we had a little battle of music, where Stuff had a band which was about three blocks away.
This was Buffalo.
Yeah, in Buffalo.
Yeah.
Called Little Harlem.
Oh, yeah.

This club was owned by a woman by the name of Ann Montgomery. And he had a band in there, and we used to get there and they had this Round the Town broadcast, and whatever -- and we'd get to battling on that, you know. We had a half hour, so we'd stretch out.
Oh, on the air, a battle on the air?
Yeah, to make it hard. We'd study up things to play, arrangements, so we could sound better than

Stuff. And then sometimes Stuff would be listening to us, when we'd play, and then he'd change his whole radio program. He'd say, "Those guys feel good tonight. We're going to change the whole program and open up with 'Ring Them Bells', or something like that." You know. And once we caught them. They come over in the daytime, and was copying our arrangements, you know, and they would play them in front of us. If they would go on first, they would play them, and we'd have to change our whole thing around, you know. Oh, it was fun in music then, you know, it was great fun.
Yeah.
And in the meantime, during this time, in '31, I left -- I left and went with Lunceford then.
Now, wait a minute. Now, wait a minute. How can this be? You were telling me a little while ago that somebody sent for you and you went to the Savoy.

Yeah, well this is '32. '32 was when I went there. But around about '31, when the band -- when we went out of the Vendome, and what they did they brought in -- the guy decided to bring in a band like Willy Bryant. Willy had Teddy Wilson, Benny Carter, you know, and they decided to bring in this band, a big band from out of town.
I see, yeah.
You know. So we went out, after about a year there.
Well, now, wait, one thing I wanted to ask you was who did Stuff have in the band?
Stuff had Peanuts Ho[lan]d on trumpet and a guy named Buster Nash on drums. He was a great drummer. And Fran Sherrill --
What did he play?
-- on the alto and clarinet.
Oh.
Yeah, later he got into the mortuary business out in Toledo. Had him. Now, they had -- didn't have too big a band. That was about it. Maybe they had --
Four. Five.
Yeah, about five or six pieces. Six at the most.
Well, had Stuff got a little name for himself by then?

Well, around Buffalo. Of course he had been around before, because he had played with Alphonso Trent before that, you know. Maybe that was '28 or -- '28. And he had been here once to record with Jelly Roll Morton. He had made some stuff with either Jelly Roll or King Oliver. I forget.
Oh, I see.
Either one of them. He used to talk about it, he had made a couple of record dates around here.
Yeah, I see.
Either with Jelly Roll or King Oliver, I forget which one.
Yeah, I see.
And then he comes back to Buffalo, comes to Buffalo -- because that band, [Alphonse] Trent, he come in there with him and Peanuts together, and they stayed around Buffalo quite awhile.
Oh, I see.
So he finally got him a band in Little Harlem. Now, we --
So what happened to you? You left them.
We left the Vendome.
Yes.
After about a year, and Lunceford come in town, and the music sounded so good, so I went right away. He wanted a trumpet player and --
Who all was in the band at that time? That was in '33?
Around about --
Around about '31.
Oh, yeah.
About '31, early. Because then what happened was he only had Paul Webster was there, and a guy named Doug Clay, three trumpet, and these two guys he had brought
up from Memphis, and he had schooled them himself.
Paul wanted to hit all those high notes.
Yeah, but he wasn't playing no high notes like that then.
Oh, he wasn't.
He was playing nice horn and he could hit a nice F. But not too much over that.
No.

But you see what happened, see, he left, and when he left, then Lunceford put me in and he sent for another guy named Eddie Tompkins and put him in. He just kept one of his regular trumpet players, Clay. So we got in. So we worked there awhile, and --
Who was in the reeds?

In the reeds was Willy Smith, a guy named Fats, who he had brought up in the school where he had taught, and -- let's see, Fats and Willy Smith and George Clark. George Clark played tenor with Cootie's band.
Yes, that's right. That's right.
And he was -- that was the three of them, Willy Smith, George Clark --
So what kind of arrangements did they have?
Nice stuff. Willy would write one every now and them, and [Edwin] Wilcox would make them mostly all the time.
See, Wilcox would make a lot of them. See, this was before Cy or Tommy Stevenson.
It was. I see.
And Henry Wells sometimes would make one.
Oh.
Had one trombone.
And was Jimmy on drums?
Crawford was playing drums.
Crawford. [Moses Allen]
Mose was on the bass.
So you must have got a kick out of playing with Crawford, didn't you?
Oh, yeah, I enjoyed it. That whole band. I liked the band.
Yeah.

And then he made it even still better, because I had to quit. I had to quit after -- I didn't stay a year. Well, we was quitting all the time anyhow, going to different things. And I liked being with them because I liked the way they played, but they didn't work all the time. Sometimes you got Friday at Rochester University and Saturday at Cornell. So they'd give you $10.00 a night for that. And when you'd get back to the hotel, then you'd have a meeting and you'd have to take $5.00 out for the gasoline, and the tires, so that left you 15, so now you've got to take out $5.00 to
have the instrument truck overhauled, apiece, and then you'd go home with $10.00, you know. So --
It was a cooperative band.

Well, no. That's what he promised. That's what was promised when I was there. He said if we ever make it, we're all going to share and share alike. But I got out before I had a chance to see it, to see if we'd ever get a break. But some of the guys, you know, told me, it never happened like that. So I didn't know, because I wasn't there, but I imagine that's the reason it feel apart, you know, because so much was expected and so many guys put so much in there, you know, for nothing.
Yeah, that background, they'd come together and --
Willy Smith was making this stuff, and he got nothing extra for that. Wilcox got nothing extra for that, you know.
Yeah, that's right.
And Henry Wells got nothing extra.
Yeah.

So I remember once when he needed a trombone player, he was going to try a trombone player, so right away I said Dickie Wells. So he said, "No, I don't want no New York musicians. I have to get somebody else, you know." You know, it was funny about that, he'd always send somewhere
else, you know, like we brought in Jock Carruthers, you know, sent to Kansas City and brought him in.
Well, maybe he thought they'd be a little too hip to work like that.
Yeah, I think that was it.
Yeah.

But anyhow, I said, 'Well, what about my brother-in-law, Russell?' You know, so he said, 'Have him to come down. I've got a gig New Years Eve, and have him to come down and sit in.' So he come down and sat in, so he kept him, you know.
Oh. How long did Russell stay with the band?
Until it broke up.
He did.
Yeah. When it broke up he went down to Macy's and got him a job.
He was happy in the band, huh?
Yeah, he must have been, yeah. But he never was the type of guy -- he's the type of guy that just liked whatever happened, you know.
But I mean he didn't play a lot of get-off, did he?
No, he didn't play too much. But he knew a little bit, because he followed Dicky and his band back in

Kentucky before he left, and he was playing things like, "What You Call Them Blues," and, "Stampede," and all that stuff. You know, they'd take them off of records, you know. So I imagine he must have took the solos off too.
Right, yeah.

So he'd played a little. But anyhow, he didn't have too much of that to do, when Trummy come in and tried to put on a third trombone, and they put Trummy in there, you know, Trummy and Wells. And then when I left the band, he brought in Steve, and Steve, that was a great thing. He'd never heard nobody hit no high note like that. Tommy Stevenson?
Oh, really?
He's the one who made, "Rhythm is our Business."
Oh, yeah.
That was before Paul come back again.
Oh. So he started it.
Yeah. Steve was the first one I ever heard to make notes way up there like that, yeah.
Could he blow good as well?
Well --
Or was that more --
Mostly high notes. That was his thing, the high note man, you know.
Yeah.

Then Eddie Tompkins -- because we left the band and Eddie Tompkins left the same time I did, and then he come back. Because he come after me again, too. He said, 'I think I've got a chance to go in the Cotton Club. I would like you guys, you and Eddie, to come back.' And so I'm playing now -- by that time I was with Stuff, but I'd been playing around with Stuff too a little bit, because I had to quit his band to pay rent. So now, in the meantime, we go back, after Willy Bryant and them leave, back into the Vendome, but Stuff has got the band.
Oh.
See, Stuff's got the band when we go back. Stuff takes the band over.
And he hires you.
And he hired me, yeah.
Who else was in it?
In that band --
Luke is not in it, then.
I don't think Luke was in that band. I think they had Jimmy Sherman, who used to be with the Charioteers, on the piano.
Oh, yeah. Yeah.
And bass was a guy named Turpin, Sylvester Turpin. Drums was Buster Nash. Trumpet was me. Trombone was Teddy Wilson's brother, Gus.
Oh, really?
Gus, yeah.
He could blow, couldn't he?
Gus could blow a beautiful horn and write beautiful arrangements, but --
Well, what happened there?
