It was something -- something with Gus, because see what Gus would do, he would make a nice arrangement, sit up all night, you know, and we'd be talking, and he'd sit up all night making arrangements, you know, and he'd bring it in and pass it out and we'd run it down, you know, play it, and we'd say, "Wow, that sure is great, man." And he'd say, "Oh, don't do me like that, you know. Don't bring me down like that. Don't put me on." He thought we was putting him on. "No, this is beautiful. It's great." And you'd say let's play it again, and we'd play it again, and we'd say, "It's beautiful." And he'd say, "Pass it in. I want to change the introduction," and you'd pass it in and he'd tear it up. So it got so around there for awhile, when he'd arrange we wouldn't say nothing. We'd be quiet as a mouse, because it would be great, you know?
Isn't that extraordinary.

And then one night him and Stuff got to arguing over something small. I forget what it was now. Something that didn't mean nothing, you know. Don't be late next time. You know, or come on the stand. When you see me up here

be up here, you know. Something like that, you know. And he walked out, left his trombone in the chair and walked out, never seen him again. Never seen him again. I run into some band once, and they told me that they saw him on his way to Boston, hitchhiking, with his bag, you know. Sometimes I'll ask Teddy. When I saw Teddy, I'd ask him, and he'd say, "I dont' know where he's at." Because Teddy had him here doing something. I think he wrote a couple of things with Benny Goodman.
Isn't that a shame?
Yeah.
Isn't that funny?
Sure was.
A pity.

Now I got away from Stuff -- oh, yeah, now I've got to go back to when about '32, in the middle of that, things are happening in there, you know, with Stuff awhile and Lunceford awhile, and they sent for me to come down to -- Jimmy Smith was his name, a bass player, out of the Missourians. He wanted me to come to the Savoy and go to work.
Well, hold it one minute, now. Just one second. I keep stopping you at that same place. But tell me -- I mean you and Stuff became so very close.
Yeah.
Well, so you got along good right away, when you went to work with him. I mean you got along good
Oh, yeah, we got along good, but the only thing about this is things change, you know. I'm working in the Vendome again.
I know.
With Stuff with a bigger band, and he's in charge of it.
Yeah.
He's got it. And so --
How does that go down?
Well, that goes down beautiful because you're right there on a steady job, you know.
Yeah.
And everything is all right.
Yeah.
But this guy sends for me -- I always wanted to come to New York -- so this guy sends for me, I'll go down here, you know.
So you quit to go down.

Yeah, I quit to go down to work with him, you know, and I come down to find out the money wasn't as much as I was getting in Buffalo, and we also played at the Harlem Opera House, that first week at the Harlem Opera House, and the --
Savoy?
Savoy, we doubled. So that was great. That was pretty good bread.
That was good money, yeah.
For two jobs, but then the next week I didn't get but $22.50, so I didn't like that.
Well, who was in that band?

I can't think of all the guys. One of them was R. Q. Dixon, because he was sitting right next to me; a trumpet player. And another one was a guy named Ted Colon. He was in it. And naturally Jimmy Smith on the bass.
Were you playing opposite Chick?
I think it was Chick, yeah.
Yeah.
I think it was Chick's band.
Yeah.
Because that's when I first seen that little trumpet player named Hunt. Remember a trumpet player with Chick named Hunt? [Louis Hunt]
No.
I can't think of his first name.
No, no, I don't remember him.

And we did that, and then after that two weeks was up, I said I've got to go back to Buffalo and straighten my business out around there, and they said, 'Well, you don't have to take your horn.' I said, 'No, no, I take my
horn everywhere I go." I never come back. I went on back with Stuff.
Yeah.
Went on back there, and Stuff got -- enlarged the band some more.
Had Stuff put anybody in your place?
No. He had nobody in there, but there was another trumpet player already there when I left. I can't think who he was. Anyhow, we had Dick Vance and myself.
Oh, you did?
Yeah, and a guy named Sleepy, out of St. Louis. William Tomlin was his name. Good trumpet player. Different style from anybody I ever heard.
Really?
Yeah.
What happened to him?
Well, he went back to St. Louis and somebody raped his daughter and put her in an ashcan, and he never got straight no more. He was --
Killed her?
Then he went crazy and died.
Oh, what a horrible story. Killed the little girl?
Yeah, his daughter, you know. Well, things happen, you know. So, now with this band, Stuff comes to New

York, we had George Clark and two altos, George on tenor and two alto players. Good altos, and clarinet. And we go to -- into the Lafayette. See the Apollo wasn't open in '32, and then we go from there to the Lincoln Theater in Philadelphia, and things didn't work out too good, we're stranded again. So we all get back to Buffalo, and MacRae --
Teddy?

Teddy MacRae, was playing the pit band when we was playing at the Lafayette, and Teddy wanted to join the band, so he did. We didn't have no fourth part, you know, saxophone, we only had three sax, so Teddy joined the band, and just took him a job and bought him a uniform and everything. He said, 'I like this band.' It was a good band. And so we went on back to Buffalo, and we come back in one by one, and Stuff kept this band going pretty good around there, you know. And as big as it was. And here comes Lil Armstrong, and she took over the whole band. She was looking for a band, so we all decided to go with Lil.
Stuff and everybody.
No, all but Stuff.
Oh, I see.
All but Stuff.
Oh, well, that was kind of heartbreaking for Stuff, huh?
No, he knew he could get another one
together. So we all went with Lil, and then she was featuring me as Louis the Second and all that, you know, and it was good.
She must be nice to work with, Jonah, huh?
She was great. She was great. And we used to play out at Graystone Ballroom in Detroit, and everywhere.
Did Lil play nice piano?
Yeah, I liked her piano playing, you know, for that --
Yeah.
For the band, you know. In that time, you know, it was great. And she was a nice entertainer, you know, out there with her high hat on and things.
Yeah.
She tried to be a Blanch e [Calloway] type.
Yeah.
And she knew her music, because she wrote some pretty nice things there and we enjoyed it, you know.
Some arrangements?
Yeah. Sure.
No kidding.
Yeah. And we did some things there. I don't think there was too much on it, you know. I don't think the agents and things was too much in favor of going out.
Yeah.
Like that Little Bitty Missus and the great big Louis Armstrong, and they didn't like that. Like they used to put that little bitty Blanche and the big Calloway.
Yeah.
I don't think they enjoyed that too much.
No.
So we played there for awhile. There was Milt on trombone, Milt Robinson, who went out with us with Horace. And Luke was in there. I remember Luke come in on guitar.
Oh, yeah.

Because she wanted four rhythm and four sax with MacRae, and Dick Vance and myself, and Sleepy. So then we travelled around with her. Now, after I get to Detroit, I found out I don't like this, because we're not working regular enough and they're paying you pro rata. So we're not working regular enough, and so we get into the -- I go into John McKinney's Cotton Pickers in Detroit.
Oh.

And here comes Mac. He says, 'Look, you guys -- I heard somebody wasn't going on further.' I said yeah, 'I ain't going no further with the band. I'm going back to Buffalo.' So he said, 'Well, I've got some things here you can do. You can work with me, you know.'
Who, MacRae?
No, McKinney's.
Yeah.
McKinney's Cotton Pickers.
Right. Right.
So McKinney was around and the band, he wasn't working to regular, you know.
Yeah.
So, I went about two months with him.
Who all was in that band, Jonah?
You know, I can't remember them guys.
Don was still in it?
No, Don -- all that had gone.
They'd all gone.
Yeah, they were all of them gone.
Cuba was gone?
Yeah, Cuba was gone. I forget who they had on drums.
Yeah. It wasn't much, really.
No, it wasn't much then. It wasn't much. Wasn't anything but the arrangements, you know.
Yeah.
You got a kick out of playing them.
Joe Thomas, he'd died, I guess. You know, the singer that --
Oh, yeah, he was killed, long before that.
Fathead, we used to call him.
Yeah, Fathead, yeah, right.

Was gone, and I can't remember nobody out of that band, to tell you -- one guy named Wallace on tenor, [Benny] and he wasn't much of a -- you know, there weren't any names there. It was gone, you know.
Yeah. So you just stayed like a couple of months.

Stayed a couple of months and went back to Buffalo, and when I get back to Buffalo, here's Stuff, and he calls me and says, "Hear you just got in." And I said yeah. He said, "Okay, if you ain't doing anything I'd like for you to come out here. I've got a little group out here. I've got myself and -- I've got four rhythm and myself."
Where?
A place called the Silver Grill in --
The what grill?
Silver --
Yeah, right.
-- Grill, in Buffalo.
Yeah.

And so I went on out there and worked with him there for, oh, a few months, until Ben Bernie and Dixie Beal, I think, come through there, and so Dixie listened to the group and said, "How'd you guys like to go to New York?" "Yeah." So he said, "Okay, I'll talk to the fellow in the

Onyx Club and tell him," because, because they knew that a group called Farley and Raleigh are coming out, they're going to California, and he said, "He's looking for a group to go in there." So, in the meantime he come down to hear the band, and we opened up there on February the 4th, 1936, and stayed there about 18 months, you know. And then Stuff had this little number, "Eyes of Mud," == "I'll Be A Moppin""
I remember.
And it was a big hit for him.
Yeah.

And then we went to California. We went to California to work -- went to California to work, at the Famous Door out there, and we stayed there, I think about -- well, we had a little trouble there because nobody liked California. Everybody wanted to go back to New York, you know, so Stuff told me he was putting in the notice, and the guy said, "You can't put in no notice," the manager says. "You've got a six month contract where we can't fire you and you can't leave, you can't quit." So then we said, well, we'd never seen no contract where you couldn't put in a two weeks notice, so Stuff put in a two weeks notice anyway, we come on back, and Joe Helbart (PHONETIC), who owned the Onyx, he said, "Well, just lay around awhile and see what's happening." Because he had carried this band, but it hadn't gotten together right yet, see. Because when we first went in there they followed us
but they didn't do too good. They had Leo Watson and Pete Brown and Frankie Newton, and then got Charlie and Buster and Procope. , you know.
Yeah.
And little by little they weaved in, and they brought in to set it off, Claude Thornhill found this girl out there, and he called and said he had a girl out there and sing Scottish songs.
Yeah, Maxine. [Sullivan]
Maxine. And he brought her in to sing, and then the band took off then, you know.
Yeah. We'll put it down, Jonah, shall we?
Yeah.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

October 26, 1978

rfm
P R O C E E D I N G S
All right, Jonah.
One, two, three, yes.
Yes, you were saying that they all blew their whistles.

Yeah, saluting us, coming in. They do that, all the boats, and I guess they had about two or three boats with the Strekress (PHONETIC) Company, all the old guys had worked on, back in St. Louis, you know.
What was the first company you said?
Capitol Boat. That was from --
Oh, yeah. Was it a shipping company?
Yeah, well Strekress Company, out of St. Louis.
Oh, I see.
That's who had a lot of boats, the pleasure boats, you know.
Yeah, I see.
And a lot of the St. Louis musicians played on them, and Red Allen and all them guys played when they'd come up to -- left New Orleans, some of them would come up to St. Louis, you know.
Yeah.
Some from Chicago and some from St. Louis. A lot of them guys played on them boats out of -- excursions
running out of St. Louis, going up the river a piece and back, you know.
Yeah.

But they were doing that in a lot of places, because they did the same thing in Louisville. They'd play on them boats, and there were a couple of boats around Louisville there, they'd go up and back , you know, different clubs would give a dance or something like that.
Yeah.

Then sometimes they just have it open, anybody that's got a dollar, a dollar and a half, would -- could ride. And so that was quite a thing for them to salute us, and then the next thing that was great, what I enjoyed, is that this would be -- we'd be passing each other, because when you're in New Orleans you take this out every night, so the rest of the boats are going out too.
Oh, yeah.
And you could hear the guys blowing from the other boats, you know. And then at night when you got off, then you went out and started a jam session, you know, be jamming.
What time would you get off, about midnight?
We'd get off about 12:00 or 1:00, yes, something like that. Then we would go out and find places to

blow. And that's when I found out I couldn't play nothing. I said, good God, everybody that could pick up a horn around there was playing like Louis Armstrong, and they had that tone, that great big wide tone that Louis had, had the feeling of him, you know. I never seen so many, you know, so many guys around there at that time. Well, we finally found a place where Granger and myself would go and blow, and this guy wasn't -- see, he wasn't too good, so we could blow with him. We felt a little comfortable there, you know. A little comfortable there. Then we would -- we were sitting there one night, playing. I'll never forget it. We were in a place called Ramona's down there, and we were blowing, and people weren't paying no attention to you, you know. They were dancing and drinking and we were in there, we were battling with this little buy in there, and he wasn't bad, but we figured we had a little bit over him, you know, so it's something to do, anyhow, after we got off from work.

So all at once I heard the prettiest sounds in my life coming through the crowd, and I looked up and there's this guy, tall, light skinned fellow, and I often wondered who he was. And he had on overalls, with a camel hair cap. And he took his horn out, back by the other side of -- in the back of the room, and just started walking through the crowd, blowing it, you know. And this guy was playing everything that Louis Armstrong was playing, you know. All his numbers and all the

same passages, you know, and things, and I said, "Good God, who is that?" The guys said, "Oh, man, there are a lot of guys around here. That could be one of many guys. Many guys sound just like Louis down here, you know. But the trouble about them, their reading is a little bit off, you know."
Yeah.
But we got -- yeah, he come up on the stand, and the first chance we got we put our horns in the bag and got out of there.
(Laughter)

And stood back there and listened to him, because this guy was something else. I've often wondered, you know, could he be some guy, that come up later you know, and I might have met, you know, in later years.
Yeah.
Because I didn't know what was going on at that time, you know.
That's what I wanted to ask you. Well, first of all, could Granger improvise too?
Yeah, sure.
Oh, he could.
Better than I could, yeah, sure.
Really?
Sure, yeah, he was better.
Well, what happened to him?
Well, you see, some guys don't have that initiative, you know, to pursue something, you know.
The push, yeah.
To go out there and go ahead, you know. You know, go ahead and get it.
Yeah.
Or take a chance, you know.
Yeah.

See, I remembered what happened. Now, these guys are talking. After we played down in New Orleans -- we'd play down there till I think around the 1st of November, and then she heads back up the Mississippi River, and then the band gets off at Paducah, when it gets to Paducah, Kentucky, and then it goes on to Cincinnati and goes in, you know, for the winter.
Yeah.

So now I'm thinking about getting back home, but they keep telling us, no, we'll go to Paducah. We've got a lot of work there. You know, I believe it, and so we get there and we find out we're doing about one job a month, you know. So there's nothing happening. This is the biggest thing these guys have got is that boat every year. But so now they're doing about one job a month. So I'd got to get out of here.
You're hungry. They've got their home.

Yeah, they've got their home there. So me and Granger, we got together -- because every time we'd talk about it they'd try to talk us out of it. And so one time we said, well, we'll get a train and go on back home. So we did, we went back to Louisville. And then I'm there only about a week, and here comes a telegram from Horace Henderson, and Horace has all these guys in the band now. He has -- Russel's in there, trombone, and the trumpet player was -- Spratt, we called him, Bernice Morton, he was a trumpet player, out of the kid band, you know.
Yeah.
He was playing second.
How do you spell his name, B-e-r-n-i-c-e?
Yeah.
Yeah.

And he was -- well, he's deceased now, but he was a nice little trumpet player. He was out of the band. There was a whole trumpet section, all but Roy -- they had Red Holland on trumpet. I spoke about him before. Matthew Holland was his name. And he left --
Wasn't he the one that played the baritone?
No, that was Duncan.
Oh, yeah.
Matthew was a trumpet player that played around here with Charlie Johnson and different bands, you know.

And then he finally dropped out of sight. I don't know what happened to him. I used to see him years ago. He left Horace, and then let's see, had him, and this guy I told you, Bernice Morton, and Roy. And that was the trumpet section of Horace Henderson's band. And so he left, Red left, Red Holland left, and then they sent for me. So I come into the band and then there was me and Bernice Morton and Roy.
Well, that was your second professional job.
Yeah.
Well, that was a pretty good break, wasn't it?

Well, the only thing that was different on this job, the job on the boat you made money. See, with Horace you could play and he'd give you 25 cents and you'd split it up. You've got to take it. See he was playing on percentage. See, I got a good taste of it when I was on that boat. You got your $40.00 every week, no excuse.
Yeah, you got your money.
And your room and board, you know.
Yeah.
So I'm out here now, I'm glad to play with these guys, you know. Because Roy, it was about the first band he played in too.
Was it?

Yes, so he was there. And he was the man with the solos, and Red played first and Bernice played first. Well then I went in, after Red left, there was me and Bernice and Roy, and then finally Roy, I think Roy left, and they asked me was there another trumpet player down there, and I said yes, Granger. So then he sent for Granger. So Granger come in, and then we had another guy from Louisville played the guitar, beautiful guitar, a guy named Luke Stewart. Did you ever hear of him?
No, I haven't.
Played with Stuff in the later days with Stuff's band. Around about '38. And he was pretty good, because he and Charlie Christian tied up in Kelly's Stable one night, you know.
No, kidding.
He was a great guy, a great guitar. Yeah, he's in Buffalo now.
No kidding.

So what happens is there's about four of us now in that band, and of course Luke was not in the band. He was out of Kentucky. So then we started playing these one nighters on percentage, and sometimes you'd have a few people and sometimes you didn't, you know, and that's the way it was. And we were booked out of Cleveland, you know. So we'd play different towns, like through Pennsylvania and little

towns, Oil City and Scranton and Wilkes Barre and things like that, and in Ohio, you know, and then somebody booked us on a date, the agent booked us on a date to go to Celeron Park (PHONETIC). I think that's in Jamestown. And between Buffalo and Cleveland. So we were on a one nighter there, then into Buffalo for a week at the Rainbow Gardens. Well, we got -- I don't know why this happened, I don't know how it happened, but we got there. There wasn't any Rainbow Gardens. So now here we are, stuck in Buffalo. So we stayed around there a couple of days, then Horace is gone, you know. Horace disappears. Now we don't know where Horace is. So here's the band. So a guy named Tom Amagon, an Italian guy, he had a club called the Zilla (PHONETIC). It was a dance hall, you know.
What's his name?
Tommy Amagon.
Amagon.
Yeah.
Okay.
It was a pretty well known family in Buffalo.
Yeah.
And he had a place called the Villa, out by the old railroad station in Buffalo, and he liked jazz musicians. In those days you ran into a lot of people that

just liked jazz musicians. They'd sit and listen all night, and they couldn't play nothing but they'd be right there, you know. Every time there was a jam session they'd stay there as long as the musicians would.

So he had a place, he said, "Well, come on and play. Play for me on --," so he saw us jamming. We didn't worry about it. We had no place to stay, had nothing, you know, and no way to get no food, but we'd be at a jam session that night, you know. So what happened, he said, "I tell you what you do. You come on out there on Saturday and Sunday and play for me," you know, and he said, "Whatever I take in just split it up between you, you know." So we said good. So we went out there and we did that, and he said, "Look, I'll tell you what I'm going to do for you guys. I'm going to put some beds in here." He had a place on the side of the hall. Said, "I'll put some beds in here for you guys."
Where you worked?
Yeah.
Really?

Said, "I'm going to put some beds in here for you, and I'm going to --," said, "Now, you can get your food, if you can hustle up enough money to buy some food, then you can cook it right here on the grill." He had the grill where he cooked his hamburgers and hot dogs, you know?
Well I'll be darned. Fancy that. He was
really a good guy, then.

Never forgot him for that either. But it was great. Now we had a guitar player. This guitar player I'm telling you about, Luke Stewart, he would go out, he had a little more experience than we did, because he didn't come up in that band. He come up with the other guys. So he knew a little bit more about getting around. So he would go to a hotel called the Vendome Hotel, which was in the black neighborhood, in the Harlem part of Buffalo, and he'd go in there and play for tips. And he would come back and he would get the tips, and the tips was good there, and he'd buy a whole lot of groceries and stuff, and he'd bring them out there and we'd cook them, you know, and things like that. So we made it like that for a couple of weeks. Then Granger said, "Oh, I can't do this. I've got to get away from here, you know." I said, "Well, heck, let's don't be in a hurry. Let's try and see if we can get something. Don't run right back home. Let's see what can happen out here, you know."

So nothing happened for us in Buffalo, because in the first place he was in a big hurry to get away. He wanted to go back home. He didn't have no eyes for that. So I said, "Well, we'll go back to Cleveland." See the only reason I wanted to go back to Cleveland was because my wife's aunt had a home there, and out of Horace's band, me and Granger and Elizabeth's brother-in-law, who was -- her nephew, you know.
Yeah, right.
So we didn't have no trouble, you know.
And --
So you could stay there.
We stayed there, yeah. She didn't even want you to eat. You know, you were brought up different. You wouldn't sponge off her. It was enough sleeping there, you know.
Yeah.

So sometimes she used to make us eat by saying -- leaving a note that said, 'Jonah, I had to go downtown, so I'd appreciate it very much if you fellows would clean out the pots and pans and wash the dishes for me, because I might be late getting home and I want to cook.' We would jump in there, man, and eat them greens and barbecued ribs, throwing that stuff out. So it's funny how things happen to you, if you try.

Now, a lot of people will come to your rescue if you try, you know. I've always had a belief they'll help you along. So -- of course I didn't want to wear it out, you know, and I didn't blame Granger, because -- but he said, 'Well, it's all right for you and Russell, but for me, I can't make it. I won't do it.' And I don't want to stay out here unless he -- unless he's with me, you know, because we're buddies, you know. We've gone everywhere together, we've come up as kids

together. So now he sends home for money. So I have to send home for money, the fare back. So they sent me my fare, so we went on back. But I wasn't satisfied. I was very unhappy, and then they said, "See, why didn't you go to school like we told you? See what happens?" I knew I was going to get that, you know, because if it had been left to me I'd have stayed in Cleveland or Buffalo and made it --
Made it somehow.
-- some kind of way, you know.
Yeah.
So now this is --
Now you had the problem of how to get away again.

October of '30, when we come back. October of 1930. Now, about the latter part, say about the end of December of '30, here's old Horace again. Here he comes again. He's telling me, "Now, I've got a band over here in Indianapolis." He was playing in a place called the Walker Theater there, and he says, "I've got a band in here, but I only have one trumpet and I need a trumpet and trombone," and he says, "Can you find a good trombone," and stuff, you know, and I'm so crazy about the music I'll go back with him again, you know. I want to play so. After he went off and left us in Buffalo and he comes back, drove over from Indianapolis, which is only a little over 100 miles, about 110 miles or something. So he drives over from Indianapolis, and that's
when I said, 'Yeah, I can get you a man.' Because he had the band -- I don't know if you've heard of this band or not. It was called Coris Davis (PHONETIC). Coris Davis, yeah. It was --
How do you spell Coris?
Coleridge.
Oh, Coleridge.
Yeah. And he had a band and it was really the Hardy Brothers Band. Did you ever hear of them?
Yes, I did.

The Hardy Brothers. It was their band. One played sax and the other one plays -- I forget. I think he -- one played saxophone and one played trumpet, yeah, that's right. So there was about seven of them playing in the pit band over there. That's the first time I seen the Ink Spots, you know, on the stage there, in a show. So he took us over there and -- he wanted to know if I could find a trombone player. So I told him yeah. Well, see, I liked the bands because I just liked to play the arrangements they had, you know.
Yeah. You wanted to go on.

Yeah, there were good arrangements back then in them days, too. These guys play arrangements for me, you don't have to talk no money. I'm ready to go and live the best I can, you know. And Horace always played Fletcher's
arrangements, you know. That was it in them days.
He had those arrangements, huh?

Yeah, sure. And sometimes he'd go in the book and take them. Sure, he'd go in the book and take them sometimes, you know. Horace, he had a lot [say] And you could tell that they'd been used already, you know. He'd bring them in, and we were so happy to get them, you know.
Well, Jonah, what has Horace got to do with the Hardy Brothers Band?
Well, he went in there with the Hardy Brothers and --
To front it or something?
Yeah. Well, Coleridge Davis was the piano player, so he went in there to front it, you know, and direct it, you know.
Yeah.
And then he come and got me, and asked me to get a trombone player. So I got this fellow, Milton Robinson, so he comes into it. You were asking about him before. Played with Andy Kirk, and Benny.
Yeah, that's right.
So I told Milt. We were good friends too, so I told Milt, 'Come on man,' I said, 'Go over here and try this.' I said, 'We're not that far from home, you know.'
Yeah. Was he eager like you?

Yeah, he wanted to go, too, see. So he -- see, he played the baritone in the kids' band for a while, and after Dunc, you know, and then he went on trombone for awhile, and when you're playing the baritone you're not too far from the trombone. It's about the same mouthpiece. You might have to get your ear used to the sound, you know. But he did that. He always did play a little trombone along with it. So we went over and we had a wonderful engagement there. You got paid every week, about $30.00 a week. Of course you had to pay your room out of that, and your food. It wasn't like the boat, still. You had to pay your room out of that, but that was all right, you know. And now --
What town was this?
Indianapolis, Indiana.
Oh, yeah. Yeah.
This lady was named Madame C. J. Walker. There was the Walker Building there.
The hairdressers?
The hairdressers, yeah.
Yeah, Duke used to talk about that.
Yeah, Madame Walker. She had a big building there that was built off of that, you know.
Yeah, off the proceeds from the --
Off of her stuff to grow hair or make hair look better, or control it or something, for women.
Or for treatments.

Treatments, yeah. And she must have made a lot of money because she had a big building. That thing was about eight stories high, you know. It wasn't a skyscraper like around here, but for Indianapolis. And it had a theater in there, and so that's why we went.

So we went in there, and we stayed I guess about two months. Now, coming on back home, well I wasn't too particular coming back home. So they get to talking about -- they were out of Richmond. Said, "If we go back to Richmond you'll love it. We've got it locked up around there. We have the -- gigs all the time, you know." And they'd be talking and I'd be listening, you know, and so -- but I'm a little smarter now, see, because Horace said, "Well, don't worry about it. When we leave here we're going into Cincinnati, a colored theater there, and I think it was the Roosevelt or something like that, for a week, and the next week we're going to the Globe Theater in Cleveland, and then when we leave there we're going to Detroit, there's another theater in the black neighborhood." So that's three weeks, so we said we'll stick it out, we'll try this, you know.

So they got the chorus girls, the whole show and everything, you know, and all we had to do was to play for it. We did this, but while in Cincinnati, I contacted Wesley Helvey (PHONETIC) and Zack White. These guys had the two best
bands in town.
Was Zack White a piano player?

Zack White, he was the leader of the band. That's with Sy Oliver, and all of them guys played with you know, a lot of those guys come up with that band, Zack White. Then you had another one called Wesley Helvey's Troubadors. That was -- Vic played with that, Vic Dickenson, , Frankie Newton, Bill Coleman. And --
They'd come up with the kid band and gone on to them?
No, see they weren't in the kid -- Vic wasn't in the kid band.
But Bill Coleman was?
No, Bill Coleman wasn't either. None of these guys in Helvey's band. They wasn't. See, they -- I'm just telling you about these two bands.
Yeah.
Being in town. And what I'm doing, I'm contacting them and telling them, you know, I may not be with this band long, you know, so if you've got an opening or something, you know.
Yeah, sure. Making your contacts.
Yeah, making contacts. So now we go into Cleveland and I do the same thing there, where I'd been before, so I knew some of the guys around there. And I went
on to Detroit.
Well, did you go and jam in those towns so they could hear you blow?
Yeah, sometimes you'd go out and jam, but they very seldom asked you about it, you know, because you -- even if the leader wasn't there, some of the guys would tell him, you know.
Yeah. That's right.
They can read, and they can play too, you know. You always wanted -- you were looking in them days for somebody to read, make sure they could read, you know.
Yeah.
Because you found a lot of trumpets, found a lot of any kind of musicians around but they wasn't -- they were self-taught, you know.
Well, that's why the kid band was so important.

Yeah, that's why it was such a background, sure. It was everything to me. I never could have did it without that. Because with a private teacher you don't get what you get from that. With a private teacher he takes you and you never know how you sound and you get disgusted, you know.
Yes.
But with that band, with all these kids
in there, you're having fun, and also playing the music. And you're learning, you're showing each other things, you know.
Yeah.

So that was the greatest thing that ever happened, you know, I think. And so now we go on and we finish these theater dates, then these guys tell us about going into Virginia, Richmond, Virginia. So we get into Richmond, Virginia, well, they seem to be pretty popular around there, but the way I gathered it, it wasn't the greatest band in town. I thought that the other band was much better. It was called Johnson's Happy Pals. Did you ever hear of them?
No.
They played the Savoy, back, long years ago.
Oh, really.?

Yeah, Johnson't Happy Pals. And I got to know, through Tyree. [Glenn] See, we heard a guy practicing upstairs. Me and Milton Robinson was walking around one day, and we heard a guy practicing, so we went up there in the hall, you know, and it was Tyree, you know.
Well, Tyree's from Texas.
Yeah, but he was down there with the Happy Pals when I first met him.
Was he?
Yeah, with Johnson's Happy Pals. I guess
he left Texas by that time, you know. Oh, he did.

Yeah, it was about 1930 or '31. So anyhow, we get down there and nothing happened. Every now and then we'd go out, everybody'd go out and get $3.50, and go out and make $3.50, so it wasn't nothing happening you know, to keep us really going. So then I sent a telegram to Helvey and asked him if he had an opening for trumpet and trombone. So he says we'll send you a ticket tomorrow, you know, and we got a ticket and went and joined Helvey.
How come he had an opening? That was fortunate, wasn't it?
Yeah, I guess so. Well, I think what happened, that he'd been playing around with a smaller band and he wanted to --
And wanted to expand.

Yeah, he was bigger before, and I think he probably cut it down, and then he wanted to -- because when I got there, another one of the fellows out of the band was playing the trumpet. His name was Jeff Cass, and he had come out of Louisville, out of that band. We had played together, and he was on trumpet and I'm on a trumpet, and Milt Robinson's on trombone, so the whole brass section's out of there, you know.
Yeah. That's nice, isn't it?

Well, in the reed section was a guy named John L. Henderson. He was a good first, beautiful tone. He had been in that band. Another guy named George Loving played alto, he was out of the band also, out of the same band.
Is that right?
So there you got three bass and two of the reeds, and the drummer, this Charles Bloomer who I told you about. He was in that band. So we was right at home, you know.
Fancy that.

So now we get in this band and we start travelling around again, and the guy is getting a little more work than Horace got, you know, than Horace Henderson did, and he's paying off, a little better businessman, you know. And it wasn't bad at all. So then we -- now we go back to Buffalo on a steady job, work a steady job then. I see some of the guys that I left there, like Russell and Luke that was with the band.
They had stayed on there?

Yeah, they'd stayed around. They hung around. And oh, Al Gibson, another one, he hung around. He stayed there. Oh, quite a few of them. So we got back, we got back to see them all and they was doing pretty good. Luke was at the -- had a regular job now, a steady job, in the Vendome, you know. He was working there for tips, then he went in and they gave him a job. So they had four pieces. They were working with a piano, bass, drum and guitar. And the entertainers was
I remember that.
You know, and they would give her money, you know.
Yeah, uh-huh.
And she'd go around and she'd come back, and after she went around to all the tables, and she'd dance some more, you know, and go out.
Yeah, that's right. Would she split that?
And she'd split the tips with the band, you know.
Yeah.
And on top of that, the guy's paying $35.00 a week.
And the guys are getting to blow, back of her.

Yeah, and the guys are blowing, and these chicks would come in with different keys. 'I want so and so in B-Natural.' And, 'I want In Dreams I Kiss Your Hand, Madam, in F-Sharp, you know.' So that taught you to play in them keys, you know.
Yes, that's right.

And if you had a good piano man. Because I used to tell them, oh, what's the difference between F-Sharp and a G. But I'd play it right the way she wanted it. So that made you learn your keys, you know. It was good for you there.
Yeah.

But this was before I got there. This was when Luke was there. So I got back and it was nice to seem him and talk to him, and we stayed around there for awhile and then we left. We stayed down there about, oh, two months, working a steady job, and then we left and went out to tour some more, through Pennsylvania and Ohio and all around. And then we went back home to play a battle of music with a band in Louisville called Purdue's Pirates, and they had the two bands playing, and Helver's Troubadors, in a battle of music, you know. And so we got into that. And while playing that, I get a telegram out there from Luke Stewart the guitar playing, and saying, 'Have opening for trumpet. Let me know if you'd like to take it.' 35 weeks. So, I wired him back and told him yes, you know. I hated --
So by now you're ready to go out all by yourself.

I hated to leave this band, you know. I hated to leave all the guys, you know, I'd been with. But I found out then, I says, no, you just can't go and have a buddy all the time, you know. You've got to go by yourself sometimes.
Yeah.
So I went on in Buffalo.
How old were you by then? Would you say nineteen?

I imagine about nineteen, yeah, about eighteen or nineteen. About nineteen, nineteen or twenty, I guess. And then -- well, let's see, this was 19 -- I think this was 1930, this was around August of 1930, and I went into the Vendome, and this was something else. This was $35.00 a week, and it was like Harlem, you know. All the white people would come down, you know, and people in different rackets and things, and they liked you, and they would give you big tips, and it was the depression time, and we never walked in -- and I went back, so this made five of us, four rhythm and a trumpet.
Oh, yeah.
And we used to pick the tips up every night. The girls would go around and make tips, they'd give us half, and then people would come in and ask for different numbers and give you money.
Yes.
We had some guy come in there, he'd give you a fifty dollar bill. And so we split up -- I don't remember a night walking out of there with under $50.00.
No kidding.
Under $50.00 each, we had, tips.
Really?
Uh-huh, under $50.00, and you blew it. You blew it.
Yeah, because you figured --
You were going to get it again tomorrow night, so why not?
Yeah.

You blew it shooting pool. They had a poolroom that stayed open all night. We were playing nine ball for $10.00 a game. And then finally we enlarged the band. We brought in this guy I was telling you about, John L. Henderson, on alto sax, and Joe Thomas, that used to play sax with Jimmy Lunceford.
Yeah.
Because he was in that band too, of Horace Henderson's. So he got stranded there in Buffalo, too.
Oh, was he?
Yeah. That's why he was around there. See, Joe was a waiter.
Does Joe come from Louisville? He lives in Louisville now, doesn't he?
No, he's out in Kansas City now.
Oh, yes, so he is.
But he was from around Ohio somewhere, around Cleveland, because I saw him, oh, about three or four

months ago in Cleveland. He come in town to see his family. And Horace was looking for a saxophone player, alto sax man, and somebody told him about this guy that played a little sax in Columbus, Ohio. Well, we were in Cleveland, but he told him about this guy in Columbus, said he's a waiter there, at some hotel, but he said he plays pretty good alto, you know. So on our way to West Virginia, Huntington, West Virginia, we stopped and picked up Joe, you know. And Horace could talk you into anything, you know. He was talking about giving up his job and come with the band. So he come. He had a car and everything. We'd shoot firecrackers in the car and we tore it up something awful, you know. Kids, you know.
Finally, when he got stranded he stayed in Buffalo, and then later on this guy started playing tenor, and he turned out to be a great tenor man, you know.
Yeah.

So then we had that band of six pieces, and we had a good band there, with Joe and John and myself, and had a good drummer and everything. We swung very good, and that's all you could think about in those days, was swing, make it move, you know.
I know.
And I made that, and I said, well, I'm going to stay right here. So I stayed there, I guess, about two years, and then till things --
