Well, okay, will you talk a minute?
Yes. Everything's cool now. We've got it made.
Okay, Jonah. I think where we finished off you'd just said that the job had been offered at the Onyx, through Dick Stabile, that's right, wasn't it?
Yeah. He come back there. He come to Buffalo and we happened to be playing a place in Buffalo called the Silver Grill. Money was bad, but the people were nice and we --
Was that Joe Helwell (PHONETIC)?
No, not at the Silver Grill. This was before we got to New York.
Oh, I see. Right.

Then Dick Stabile come to hear us and we Farley and Raleigh, who were in the Onyx at this time, they were getting ready to leave to go to California to make a picture, a moving picture, since they had just made a hit record called, 'You Blow Through Here,' 'The Music Goes Down and Around and Comes out There.' So they were leaving, so Dick Stabile told Stuff, 'This would be the very group to follow Farley and Raleigh in the Onyx Club.' So he said, 'We're going to have them come down and take a listen to you.' He said, 'Oh, good.' We didn't think it was going to happen, you

know. You have so many promises down through life. You get so it just goes in one ear and out the other. So, sure enough, they set it up. The guy come down to listen to us, and they said all right, on the 4th of February you open. Well, this is about December, or November, it could have been, the last part of November, the first part of December, and they were setting this up. So when we got ready to go to the Onyx, but then we kind of backed out, because the manager of the Onyx -- I mean the manager of the Silver Grill in Buffalo said, "Look, Jonah, let Stuff go ahead and get a band down there in New York and you all stay here and I'll raise you. I'll double your salaries if you all stay. You take the band and I'll double your salary. And when Stuff decides to come back, he's still got the job." So I said, yeah, it was a good idea, because you know, you're settled in and you're not particular about moving. And he did a lot of travelling about them different bands I told you about.

So now Stuff says, "Okay, that's a good idea." Everything was all right with Stuff. You know how he was. And so he come on down and he got a band together. He had Frankie Newton and Manzie Johnson and some of the guys. So about -- and he started rehearsing them. And about two weeks before opening, why Joe talked to him and says, "Is all the fellows in town?" So he says, "No, they're not coming. I'm going to use another group." So Joe Helbluth (PHONETIC) says, "Oh,

no." He says, "I want that same group I heard. I don't want no other group." Now, we had already signed a contract with this guy. His name was Toppey, in Buffalo, you know. And so Stuff says, "They're not coming, but I've got a better group." So Joe Helbluth said, "I don't want no better group. I want the same group I heard and the same guys." So he said, "Well, they won't come." So he said, "Well, we'll get them down here." "So forget about what you're rehearsing now."

So now a fellow come up to talk to us. I don't know who he was. To talk to us, and we said, well, we didn't know, we'd signed a contract. And he said, "Oh, forget about that. You open on the 4th of February in the Onyx." So I went on by and checked it out and everything with the authorities, so they said, "Okay, we think this is the best thing for you to do."
Well, how about the contract with someone else?
Didn't mean nothing. It didn't mean nothing. We went on down to the Onyx and went to work.
Do you think they put some pressure on them?
It must have been.
Yeah.
See, we never -- they'd never tell us nothing
Yeah. Yeah.
The only thing they do with musicians, they give you orders.
That's right.
So they said, 'Now, you be there. You open up on the 4th.' So there was, on the 4th.
And little did you know that this was going to be like a turning point in your career.
No, I thought what could it be, you know.
Yeah.

So we come down and did that. Now, while we're here, we get to go into the Roxy, we double in the Roxy Theater, and then one time we was tripling. We was playing the Roxy Theater and the Onyx and doing the Lucidin Show.
Did stuff have -- what office -- did an office have him?
That was Consolidated Radio Artists.
Oh, I don't know them.
Which was Charlie Green.
Oh.
Yeah, he used to have -- you know, Ryan. Remember Babs and her brothers?
Yes.
Well, he used to handle all of that, you know, and -- well, he was in the Brill Building at that time,
and then later on they moved into the RCA Building. It was a pretty good office. He had some pretty good things. He booked Lil, too.
Oh, did he?

Yeah, be booked Lil when I was with her. It was a pretty big office at one time. I don't know what they're doing now. I haven't heard of them lately. But we went in there, and now we're working there, and at this time you didn't get Sunday off. There was no such thing as a day off. You worked seven days.
Is that right?
Sure. Back in them days nobody got a day off.
They didn't, huh?
You worked seven days, not unless you was in maybe radio or studio musicians or something.
Is that right.
And that's what the Onyx Club was then, it was a hangout for the -- mostly the musicians that worked in the studios.
Yeah.
Manny Klein and --
Well, did -- was there no substitute band there?
No, just us and the piano, Frankie Froeba
Oh, yeah.
A guy named Frankie Froeba played the piano and for a while they had the Spirits of Rhythm alternating with us. That was Leo Watson and Doug and all of them --
Oh, yeah, right.

-- the Spirits of Rhythm. They alternated with us once. And then pretty soon -- they wouldn't change us but they'd change the other group sometimes. And once they had Billie Holiday working in there with us for a while. Not long, but for a while. Because we was recording mostly with her at that time.
Oh, were you?
Yeah, we were doing a lot of stuff. 'I Cried For You,'
Who, with Stuff too?
Not Stuff, no. Me and Cozy -- [Cole]
And Clyde?
No, it would be Teddy's band, so Teddy would be playing the piano. [Wilson]
Oh, yeah, I see.
Cozy and myself and --
Right. For Brunswick Records.
Yeah.
Was it?
Yeah, it might have been Brunswick. I think it was. It was either Brunswick or Vocalion . 1776

Broadway. And we'd have -- sometimes Benny Goodman would be on the date and sometimes Allen Reuss And we'd change around. Sometimes we'd have Johnny Hodges, Harry Carney, sometimes they'd have Ben Webster.
And Lester, I think. Oh, no, that was later.
Then later come Lester. Later come Lester and Buck in there.
Yeah, right.
See, when we come in, Basie hadn't come to town yet, because John was coming in the place and he was telling us about this great band out in Kansas City, you know, that he'd heard.
Yeah.

Count Basie, you know, with Lester Young and Hershel Evans and Buck and all of them. And finally, when they come in, they opened them at the Roseland, and we went over as a greeter. We played a couple of numbers with the band, you know, with our group, you know.
Did you?
At Roseland, yes. It's so long ago, now.
No kidding.
Yeah, it was wonderful.
That was about 1936, I think.
Had to be about '36, yeah, had to be
about that.
Yeah. Well, so that was Joe Helvuth (PHONETIC), wasn't it. Well, did he own that club or did --
I think he owned it and I think Carl Kress, if you remember, had something to do with it.
Oh, did he?
I don't know how much. Maybe he put in some money there, too. Because Carl Kress was a great guitar player, you know.
Yeah, I remember, yeah.
And he'd be there practically all the time, and he was a studio man, so all the rest of the guys would come over. I imagine that helped to draw them, you know.
Yeah.
Over there, with Carl being one of them, you know.
Yeah.

So we got to know all the guys through that. The Casa Loma Band and all of them. They'd come there every night. They'd come into the Onyx, and sometimes me and Pee Wee Hunt, the trombone player, would do a little number together, you know, a little jive number, just spontaneously, you know.
Well, I was going to ask you, when you started putting the derbies on your head, remember?
Yeah, I'd wear the derby and Stuff would wear the high hat.
Yeah.
And we'd work up front together.
Yeah.
We had a little sketch.
Well, that's when you began 'I-se a-Muggin,' wasn't it?
Yeah, 'I-se a-Muggin', and all those things. So --
Well, that was really Stuff's first exposure in New York, wasn't it?
Yeah, really, yeah. Yes. Yes.
And it was yours in a way, too.
And mine, too, sure. Sure.
And yet, Jonah, I thought I knew you before then. I knew Cozy.
Yeah, well, Cozy was -- see, Cozy wasn't with the band when we first went into the Onyx.
No.
No. We had a little guy named Johnnie Washington. He stayed with us for about, oh, three or four months, in the Onyx. And then we brought in Cozy.
Oh. From where, can you remember?
Well, let's see, I don't know who he was
Yeah.
And so we rushed to get back, and so we got to know Cozy pretty good.
Yeah.
Through hanging out, you know.
Yeah, right.
And going different places and different houses.
And on the record sessions, because he was on Billie's record sessions, wasn't he?

Oh, yeah, sure. Sure, definitely, he was on there before I was. And we used to go up to different places and listen to Billie before we recorded with her. When Red Allen was with her, you know, and Red would do a lot of stuff. But Teddy --
I don't remember when Red Allen was with her.
Oh, yeah, on a number called, 'Paintin' the Town Red.'
Oh, yeah.
Yeah, I'll never forget that. I don't think I have it, either.
Listen, I'll tell you one thing that I
think we might do as we go along. Stanley mentioned it. He said, 'Get Jonah to talk about different guys.' So while we pass trumpet players, speak about them. You know, what did you feel about Red?
I thought he was a good trumpet player. I thought he had good feeling.
So did I. I loved the way he sang, too.
Good soul. Yeah, and he had a little soul in his singing.
Yeah, he did. He had an absolutely unique sound. Nobody sounded like Red Allen.
Nobody sounded like that.
He had a plaintive kind of a -- oh, complaint in his style, didn't he?

Yeah, he was like -- he didn't have to play strong and he didn't have to play a lot of chords, because he could play eight bars and take down and take up and play another eight bars, you know, and play it.
Yeah.
Oh, he was so beautiful. I followed him all through my life, as I did other guys.
I was going to ask you, I mean the thing was by the time Red got on 52nd Street he had slipped off a little bit from his peak, I think, don't you?
Yeah. Yeah.
It was when he was with Fletcher that he sounded good.
When he was with Fletcher was when he was great.
Just beautiful.
He also played some good stuff with Luis Russell.
Yes.

He played good there. But when I really started to listen to him, he was playing in a band -- playing in a group, and I think it was a group -- I can't think what they called them now, but it was Horace Henderson. It could have been his Stompers or something, Horace Henderson's Stompers.
Yeah.
But he would have Red and Hilton Jefferson.
Yeah.
And I don't know who was on -- oh, and Benny Morton on trombone.
Really?
Yeah. I have a few of the old 78s of that.
Have you?
I brought them with me from Buffalo.
Is that right.
Yeah, so we used to sit in Buffalo and listen to this all the time. Thought how great he was you
know, and oh, there were some good things made with that little group. Not to be popular, you know, but --
Yeah, I know what you mean. Good, swinging music.
Yeah, good, swinging music.
Yeah.
And they had -- they must have had maybe a half a dozen sessions.
Well, I was going to say, you see, Red made some under his own name.
Yeah.
Which were very good.
Yes, he did.
Which he sang the vocals on, because I guess in those days they thought it was commercial for him to do it.
Then they had someone called Allen [Coleman Hawkins] Hawkins, when Hawk played with him.
That's right, yes.
I've got all that stuff.
That's good.
Yeah, I have it on records.
Listen, Jonah, do you mean that you collected these and you've still got all the records you were buying in those days?
Yeah, back in Buffalo.
You kept them with you. You never --
I'm so sorry that I missed those in Kentucky, because after I left, you know, I guess my mother must have just thrown them away, or they got broke or something.
That you first had, you mean?

Yeah, that I first had, with Louis Armstrong and Red Nichols playing "Indiana," "Back Home in Indiana," and Adrian Rollini and all them guys, you know. A pretty nice thing. And Teagarden playing things like, "Dinah," and all that stuff. I had all that stuff back there in Louisville you know. But -- and I left, and naturally I had forgotten all about them myself. Other things were happening. And living from room to room, you know.
Yeah, going from place to place.

Yeah, place to place. And I guess my mother figured -- it was a long time before I went back. I guess she kind of figured -- and when I did go back I never thought about the records, you know. They had moved and I never thought about that. So when it did finally come around to it, then she said, "Oh, God, I don't know where the records are." Those things must have been lost years ago. Probably threw them out or something. But I listened to all them trumpet players, like Red Allen. He was great. He had his own -- what I liked about those days, every trumpt player had
his own style. You knew who he was.
Yeah.
When you heard Lips Page play you knew that was lips.
Yeah.
When you heard Red Allen play you knew that was Red. When you heard Rex play, altogether different.
Yes.
Joe Smith.
You wouldn't confuse one with another, no, you wouldn't.
Never confuse them. You could hear them on records and tell just who. Where today, you don't know.
No.
You don't know who they are. Everybody looks like they're trying to play like Diz or something. And --
No, all that variety of style is gone.
Yeah. That's what I liked the best about it, because really it looked like good or bad, that guy's expressing himself, whether you liked it or not.
That's right. Remember Frankie Newton? [Coleman]
Yeah, Frankie and Bill. All them guys back there.
Or you can go way back and think about Bubber Miley.
Yeah, Bubber, sure.
A guy like that that had a --
And we were talking about Freddie Jenkins. He played with Duke. He had his own way. We listened to a record in France on him. It knocked me out when it come on there one night.
Really?
Uh-huh. (Singing) Oh, he killed me, yeah.
(unintelligible).
Yeah. He was something else. The thing about it, we always thought of Duke as a sister band, you know, to Cab.
Yeah.

And so -- because we was booked out of the same office, and in fact once there was only the two bands out of the office. My agent now is Sam Burke. He was booking with Duke and Cab and left Mills by that time, you know. And Mitlow was the head man to keep the stuff together.
Yes.

And so Freddie got sick, and to show you the kinds of hearts guys had back in those days, we would get together every year, around about Christmas time, and put in a little money apiece, you know, everybody --
Both bands.
Well, our band did. I don't know about Duke, but we did.
No, I never heard of it before.
No, but we did it. Our band did it. Cab's band did it, and we'd send -- get a War Bond -- see, it was during wartime.
Yeah.
And we'd send Freddie Jenkins a War Bond every year.
Wasn't that nice. That was very nice.
It wasn't much, but it was something. He was in the hospital, you know.
Well, it was very nice, and it must have moved him, you know.
Sure, to let him know that somebody was out here thinking about him.
That's right.
Because he stayed there quite awhile, I think, with that TB he had, I think.
Yeah. He was sick a long while.

And I was so glad to hear that he's back, because I missed him. I heard at one time that he was a disc jockey in Dallas, and we played there last year, in '77, so I figured maybe we'd get to see him, but I inquired about him and nobody knew, and we didn't have long to inquire, you know.
Well, you know, I think he was in Ft. Worth, which is what, like half an hour away, 40 minutes away or something like that?
Yeah, about that.
And I suppose maybe he hadn't come around.
Yeah, I always like his style. That was strictly him, you know, it was him. And [Artie] Whetsol -- even Whetsol, in the band. Who could sound like Whetsol playing "Mood Indigo."
That's right.
When they'd bring them three down front.
That's a beautiful sound.
Yeah. I mean a lot of guys have played it, but I mean for some reason unknown, I don't know --
You know, I think the only guy that would recall Whetsol at any time would have been Ray Nance sometimes.
Yes.
You know, because Whetsol had that very soulful and delicate thing.
That's right.
Which Ray would -- I suppose maybe because he was a violinist.
Yeah. Yeah, that could have something to do with it, yeah.
Then he would come up with that. Duke
loved Whetsol.
Oh, that guy was something else.
Yeah.

Something else. I'll never forget the three of them, you know. At one time when I was in Buffalo, two of the bands come into town, like they always used to come into Shea's Buffalo on the circuit, and they stayed at the Vendome Hotel, so Sonny would come in and sit in with us sometimes and so Sonny said, "Hey, you want a job in the band?" I said yeah, you know.
I was just going to ask you. Did you --

I don't know whether he was going to put on a fourth trumpet or what, but that was when Whetsol and Cootie and Ray was in it. So I said sure, you know. So he said, "Okay, come on down to rehearsal tomorrow. We're going to have a rehearsal. And come on down and sit in on rehearsal with us." I said okay. So -- we were so crazy in those days. As I said, we were a bit on the young side. And sometimes we didn't get to bed. Sometimes we didn't stop playing till 11:00 o'clock in the morning. That's in the club, and nobody said nothing. Nobody bothered us. And we didn't mind it, because we were getting tips. You know, every time we stayed there, the place was loaded, 10:00 or 11:00 it was still loaded, you know. So you'd get home about 12:00. I'd get home then about 11:00 or 12:00 o'clock. I know it was late, because I had told

my wife that I might go by and rehearse with Duke, and I was tired when I got off. I said, "Oh, I can't make it. I can't make that thing, that rehearsal today." And I was a little leery about it, too. I didn't know if I could make the band or not, you know.
All that fine music.
Because I had heard that some of the stuff wasn't written down.
That's right.
And that, you know, you had to pick it up by ear.
Yeah.
At that time, you know. I don't know about later years.
That's right.

And I said, "I don't feel like going through all that, you know, playing by ear." But I'd have like to play with the band because it was a great band. They'd just made that picture Check And Double Check.
Yeah.
And it was just getting so I was listening to somebody else outside of Fletcher. Because I used to listen to nobody but Fletcher, you know.
Yeah.
Because he had such great cats in that
Yeah.

So I didn't go, and you know, I always thought of Sonny, because they left there the next day and went to the theater in -- Shea's in Toronto, and he called me up, you know. "Hey, man, what happened?" You know, so I told him I thought I'd better not do it. I said I'd better lay dead around here a little longer, you know. I'm pretty well set here, you know. So he said, "Okay. Maybe next time. Because Duke heard you and he'd like to have you. He asked for you to come down and rehearse, you know."
Funny, isn't it? You don't know what might have happened.
No, I don't know. It might have gone off to another thing.
Yeah.
Well, you look down life's road in the back, and you say you had so many roads that you might have went down, and you didn't do it, you know.
And especially with you, because what he did, he made a different person out of every person that came in the band.
Every man that come in that band.
Look at Ben Webster.
Look at Al Sears.
Yeah.

Al Sears sounded good there. He played a thing in there, "Happy Go Lucky," or something, and the music that he put behind him fit him, fit that tone. Al sounded better with that band than I ever heard him in my life. And he was around Buffalo at the time, you know, when we were around there.
I wasn't here then, I don't think, when he -- in fact I think Stanley and I had married and I was in England.
Oh, I see.
But I never could understand how that happened or who brought him into that band.
I can't understand it. I didn't know what was going to happen when Barney brought in a tenor, because I can remember way back there they didn't use a tenor, not for solos.
That's right.
Maybe Barney might have played some parts with it.
That's right.
So I didn't know how a tenor was going to go into that band, whether it was going to make it sound like all the other bands or not.
That's right.
See, because all the other bands featured tenor and he never featured tenor.
That's right.
Because like Barney, you know, "Lightning" on a clarinet.
Yeah.
I never heard anybody play that much clarinet now, since, you know, not like that lightening.
No. An extraordinary style.
Yeah, the style. Good God, individual. But that's what I was speaking about, individual styles, you know.
That's right.
You knew who they were, you know.
That's right.
You could take Barney and put him in Fletcher's band and you could tell that was Barney.
Sure.
Yeah, sure.
But then the thing was, like take Ben Webster. Now, since Ben played like Hall, you know, you might have figured that it would come out that way.
Yeah.
But going into Duke's band it came out differently, didn't it?
It was something else. Yeah. Yeah. It was something you never expected.
That's right.
You'd sit down and listen to it and listen again, and you'd say, wow.
And when Ben wrote those saxophone choruses, like for, 'Perdido,' and --
Yeah, 'Perdido,' and stuff, oh, boy.
And so the whole section sounded like Ben.
Yeah, they did, sure.
Yeah.

And then you'd hear a little of Johnny Hodges into Ben sometimes. You'd hear a little Johnny influence there, when he was playing a pretty number sometimes. I could hear, and I'd say, 'Johnnie's having a little influence on Ben, too.'
Yeah. And Ben said so, didn't he?
Sure, he said so. He said so.
Oh, yeah, that's true.
But a great band. It was a great band. It was the greatest.
Well, that's interesting, Jonah. It's a pity you didn't, you know. But I mean you don't know what all might come of it.
No, I don't know what it would have been.
But it would have been interesting.
I think that maybe it would have been a thing like -- because you know how he would do, he would put things behind you, like this guy --
That's it.
Make this guy sound good.
Look what he did for Rex Stewart.
Sure. Who would ever have thought Rex would fit in there.
The trumpets and all that. Extraordinary. What was that --
They had, 'Tooting Through the Roof.'
Yeah.
Yeah, 'Tooting Through the Roof.' Oh, goodness, that's -- him and Cootie. And then you had them playing 'Trumpet No End', which was, 'Blue Skies.' Had about five trumpets in there.
Yeah.
Francis Williams and Cat [Anderson]
That's right.
And Tap Jordan.
How about 'Boy Meets Horn'?
'Boy Meets Horn,' yeah.
I mean who but Ellington could have brought
Yeah, 'Boy Meets Horn.'
Yeah.
It was a beautiful thing. Well, that's the way it goes. You see --
You don't know.
You never know.
But it's a pity in a way, if you'd just even spent two or three years with him --
Oh, yeah, I'd have loved that. I'd have loved it till today, you know, but that day, to tell you the truth, I had cold feet, you know.
Yeah.
Because these was guys that I didn't know how good -- I was just getting to know them, since I was playing Buffalo, that they were coming in there every year, to play the theater.
Yeah.
You know.
And they were funny guys, too.
Oh, yeah, they were different types of cats, different types of cats.
I mean they weren't outgoing guys and they all had their own little worlds going.
Yeah. Yeah.
You got left on the outside for quite a little while.

And it was a funny thing about the difference between them and Fletcher. When Fletcher would come to town it would be mostly -- after they'd finished, I don't care what they were playing, there would be a jam session. So that would mean me and Peanuts Ho|land which was about the only two trumpet players that was playing all the spots. We had practically all the work, you know. And they would come and wake you up, Fletcher and he's in town, blowing. There was Rex and some of the guys, you know, and Hawk. And we'd get up and you'd put your clothes on and go down there and start blowing, you know.
But with Duke it never happened much.
No.
They never took the horns out to blow when it come the time.
Ben would.
Yeah, well, Ben, but he'd been doing that for a long time, see.
But he was about the only one, I think.
Yeah.
Well, I guess Rex would, or --
Rex could. I know he did when he was with Fletcher. I don't know how much he did with Duke.
No, not so much.
It seems it calmed him down a little bit, when he got with Duke, or something.
Yeah.
I don't know why, but it seemed to.
Yeah. Well, I established him, I think, Jonah. You know, before I think he was fighting for himself. Don't you?

Could have been, yeah. He could have been. I never really knew what it was, because it looked like he was getting -- one thing Duke would do, he wouldn't let you sit in there and not play. He would find something for you to do after he'd listened to you. He'd sit there and listen to you, and after he'd listened to you, he'd come out with something for you to play.
Yeah, right, just right for you.
Yeah, sure. I think he would have did that for Red Allen.
Yes, I believe he did.
I think Duke would have did it for just about anybody.
Yeah, but see, he had that jungle in him, you know, that suited Duke very much.
Oh, that guy was --
He had a lot of Louis in him too, didn't
Sure. Sure. You could hear that New Orleans sound there.
Yeah.

But all that Louis influence, and so many beautiful guys I knew around here, even guys that didn't play with the biggest of bands, you know. There was a guy around here named Mason once. He used to play with Blanche Calloway. He was a great trumpet player. And Peanuts was a great trumpet player too.
Was he?
Yeah, Peanuts played very good.
Did he.
Sure.
What was Mason's first name?
[Henry Mason]
I was trying to think of it. Now, I think we might have called him Gus Mason, something like that.
Oh, yeah.
I can't think of his first name.
I never heard about him.

And Shad played a good horn. Shad played good. He played with Cab, Shad Collins. And so everybody was so beautiful in them days. Everybody played his own style. Everybody had his own style of playing. That was his own self-expression, like it or not.
Yeah, even in Basie's band there was Buck.
Yeah. Buck, and then Harry.
And there was Sweets. [Harry "Sweets" Edison]
Yeah, Buck and Sweets.
But it was the beginning of the change, though, Jonah, because they didn't stand out quite the same.
No.

In other words, they -- as a matter of fact they were, none of them, quite -- I dont' know, powerful isn't quite the word, but they weren't quite as dominant personalities on the trumpet as the guys that had preceded them.
No, they couldn't be. Because these guys were so powerful. Rex Stewart.
That's right.
Satchmo. And you were talking to me about Red. And you're talking about Cootie.
And you know the one guy we haven't talked about, and I know you loved him, because I can remember you both sitting in together, Bunny.
Oh, yeah, sure. Sure.
He was such a remarkable -- such a remarkable fact that there should have been a guy like Bunny Berigan.
That's right.
Because he was a fiery --
He kind of puzzled me, you know?
Yeah.

He puzzled me when I first met him. Of course that's many years ago. It's a different thing now. But I had asked him was he white, when -- so I said, 'Are you white?' He was sitting there playing one night, we were jamming uptown, on Lenox. We had got off from work. He was working up the street from us, in a place called the Swingland, with Red McKenzie, and he was working up there. So we had intermission about the same time, so we walked around. So at this time we'd go uptown and blow, and we went up to an old place on Lenox there, and there wasn't nothing there but a piano. And we'd sit in there and blow all night.
You and Bunny?
Yeah. Because for some reason he always liked me.
I know.

I'll tell you one thing was that they were going to have a thing at the Paramount at one time, and Stuff's band was supposed to be at this side, and Bunny was supposed to be on the other side of the stage, you know, with Red McKenzie's band.
Yeah.

Bunny was with them. And we had rehearsals there. I don't think the job ever come off. And during intermission, Bunny said come on, we'll go over and have a little taste. So we went over and had a little taste, because he liked a taste, you know, all the time.
Yeah.

So finally we had a Saturday swing session and we become friends, and he began to tell me about playing the Saturday swing session. He said, 'That's all right,' trying to tell me how beautiful it was, you know. He says, 'That's all right, but you must remember, in order for me to do that I have to play through the week, and they call me in to do these little minuet things and all that kind of stuff.' He hated that, you know, like little light classic things, like a studio musician.
Yeah.

And see he didn't like this. He liked to play his things. He liked to play that, and he hated to go in for that, because I know some nights he used to say, 'I'm due there at 1:00 o'clock. I ain't going there no more. I'm not going to do that thing tomorrow.' He got one of them -- I don't know what that is. So he hated to do it, but I hated to see him get to the place where he couldn't or he didn't stop drinking. Yeah, he couldn't stop drinking. He would say -- I told you like when I was sick -- did I say that, when I
Well, we haven't put it on here, but we'll get to that.

I used to drink quite a lot. And so -- back in 1940 I had a heart tremor, so I went to the doctor, and to tell you the truth, he said, "You'll have to stop drinking and smoking pot", which we was in them days.
Yeah.

To tell you the truth. So he says, "You've been drinking that 100 proof whiskey. That speeds your heart up. And you smoked the pot, that slows it down. The two have been pulling against each other so many years," he said, "Your heart is tired." He said, "You don't have a murmur, or it's not damaged in any way, but it's just tired, you know, just barely beating." But he said, "If you'd quit, you'd be like new, since you're young." So I said okay. So he brought me out of it and I began to feel a little better after a week or two, and then I got back in and working with the type of guy, Stuff Smith who, if you come on the bandstand and you're sober, why he got very upset about it. I remember once he -- me and Cozy was fooling around in the daytime, and we was having some drinks in the day, and so Cozy said, "I'll tell you what we'll do. Let's just calm down. Let's just stop drinking for awhile, you know, two or three days, and look around and see what's happening. We've been out now for about a year. Let's come

down now and see what's happening." So we said, yeah, we'll start now, do it now. So we stopped. We didn't drink that night at all. Stuff gets on the bandstand and starts off, here, now, let's play so and so. Okay. He starts off and --
Now record.
One, two, three, four five.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

You Please Come Home," and work up front together, me with the derby on and he with the high hat. Or he'd start singing something and then he'd say, "Come on, fill in," and I'd get up there and fill in with him, and it would wind up being something, you know, more times than it wasn't, than it was nothing, it would fall. Because you had a lot of musicians in there, all them studio musicians, pulling for you know.
Yeah.
So I'd say he did the best, but Cab -- I think I said something about why I left him.
Yeah.
I left him by --
Where did you leave him?

Well, I left him, I think the last job was the Sherman Hotel. Well, now we started doing the hotels. I said the La Salle, and then from the La Salle we did the Three Deuces first in Chicago, and then to the La Salle Hotel, and then into the Sherman. They had both bands on the stand, Eddie Condon's with Bud Freeman in it, and our band. And there the two bands played together on the stand. Then, from there, into Cincinnati, the Netherlands Plaza, downstairs. People were trying to book us on good jobs then. And now he gets here to the Green Lantern Room in the Edison Hotel, and he --
All right, Jonah, just talk right there.
T45N
One, two, three, four.
Yeah, that's about right. All right.
And then you worked the Sherman?
At the Sherman. We were in there with Condon and his band, and it was a great engagement, playing together, and then from there --
Was this about '35?
No, this is -- no, because this was after the Onyx.
Oh, yeah.
We went to the Onyx in '36 and '37. We went out there about June of '37, I think we went out to --
To California.

To California. So this must have been about '40. This was '40, and a lot of things was happening in that year. And -- no, what happened is that the last job we played was Blatt's Beer Garden, because we was having so much trouble with Stuff. We was working the Sherman Hotel and things like that. He would take the money and buy an automobile, see. Now, when we couldn't pay the hotel bill, why the manager just said, 'Look, you guys have got to pay sometimes. You all haven't paid anything in two weeks, you know.' So now he don't want to hear about what happened with Stuff, you know, that Stuff's not paying off. Stuff went somewhere and bought a car, with the

payroll, the whole payroll. So now we go to the union in Chicago, so the union had him to give all the money to them, and they would pay us off. You know, they would pay us off until he got caught up again, paid up for two weeks, you know, two weeks behind. So then the union -- so then we had all this trouble, so then we said from now on, we told the booking agent, send out individual checks. That's the only way we can make it. We can't make it, because Stuff is subject to take the money and do this anytime, you know. So Stuff said, "That's a good idea. That's a good idea, yeah."
Now, he said it was a good idea, but he didn't really like it. After we started getting paid, after they started sending us out separate checks, then he didn't like it.
It's like he's not the leader.
Yeah. He began to say, "Send me the checks." See, they sent me all the checks and they sent Stuff his, and they sent me the checks for the other boys, you know.
Yeah.

So then I'd give a man his check and Stuff would say, "Now, who's running the band, me?" I said, "Well, you said it was all right, you know, because I'm not going to stay here while you buy automobiles and things, you know. I can't afford this, Stuff." "And the other guys feel the same way. They'll tell you." And see, he probably wanted to do something with the money then, and he couldn't get his hands

on it, you know. So then he went back to Buffalo, so that was all. We finished at Blatt's Beer Garden. That was it. And that's when I come into New York and we waited around. I went down to the booking office, and they said, "Well, it looks like he's going to stay there, because he'll get himself in trouble if he ever comes here to work, because he's got a contract with us." I said, well, I don't have time to wait for him, you know. So they said, "Well, Jonah, what are you going to do?" So I said, "I'm going to work with Benny Carter," because Benny Carter had a band, and we went to work with Benny. This was '40. Went to work with Benny Carter. There was Pop Smith, Bobby Williams and myself. So we went into Roseland and stayed there awhile with Fletcher, you know. No, what we did, it was with Benny Carter, but we left Benny, the whole band, the whole band in that same year. We made some records with Benny, then everybody left Benny because Benny was going out of town. Every now and then he'd have a gig, you know, maybe two or three gigs, sometimes one a week, and so Fletcher's going into Roseland, so the entire band left Fletcher and went into Roseland with Fletcher.
Left Benny and went into Roseland with Fletcher.
Yeah, went into Roseland with Fletcher.
Now --
Well, how did Benny take that?
I don't know, I didn't ask him . We just

all quite. You didn't have to give no notice, see, when you're not working steady. You just leave, you know. So we all went with Fletcher. And I never heard Benny say anything about it, because I went to his house after that and everything. You know, he lived close to me uptown, and so I'd go by during the day and he never said nothing.

So everybody went over with Smack, so now, while we're over with Smack, we're having a ball, you know, because it's nice and the money was short, and now, in the meantime, and this was the third time, Cab -- I get a call from Cab, you know.
Is this the first time you'd ever heard from Cab?
No, it was the third time, because he was calling me and Cozy all the time with Stuff. when he was
Oh, he was.

He wanted us to come to the Cotton Club, and we was working in the Green Lantern Room at the Edison Hotel with Stuff. The Cotton Club had moved downtown and he had come backstage there and talked about joining the band. You know, he was trying out trumpet players. That's when I sent Diz down. I said, "Look he's trying out trumpet players down there, Diz, why don't you go down there and see about that?" You know, so he went down and he got the job. So I stayed with Stuff, because I wasn't particular about leaving until I really got sick, you know. So then, after we worked with Fletcher, now all the time working with Fletcher, Cab, he says, "I want
you to come with the band," you know. So I said all right. So I had to put in a notice. So he said okay. So then I tell Fletcher.
Yeah, I just -- yeah, I want to ask you --

I said, "Fletcher, I think I'm going with Cab, because he offered a little more bread, you know, and I think I'll go over there for a while, you know." He says, "No, stay here. I'm doing some things with Benny Goodman and you can be in on some of the recordings and stuff," and he says, "What the heck, you've got all the solos and things. You can sing them little things there." I said, "Yeah, but I promised him before that, when I left Stuff, that I was going with him, and I do need a little more bread." The bread was real short there. It was back there in the '40s, so -- it was about 1940, about the end of '40, because then Fletcher was such a nice guy, I called Cab back and told him, "I can't make it, Cab. Again I have to let you down, because he owes me --," I said, "I borrowed $200.00 from Smack and I've got to pay it back." He said, "Don't worry about that. I'll send you enough to pay him off and enough for your pocket, too." What are you going to do? I had never had anyone say this, you know. And he sent me about $300.00, and I really didn't owe him that. I just told him that, to stay with Smack, because Smack got so he really wanted me to stay. So I went back and told Smack I can't do it. I told him what I did. He said, "Whenever you want a job, I want you to know you're always welcome back here."
That's nice. So you got on nicely with Smack.
Yeah, sure, no trouble at all.
Did everybody?
Everybody I know around. I never heard nobody say -- and Pops had been with him for years and Pops never said nothing against him.
No.
You know, Pops was with him back with Rex and all that.
Yeah, I know it.
Well, Pops was a wonderful guy, anyway, Pops Smith.
I mean nothing like Horace.
Oh, no, a completely different thing, the way I found it, you know. The way I found it, he was a completely different guy, you know.
Yeah. Really a very nice guy for a leader.
Yeah. Yeah, I thought so. That was a big thrill just for me to be in for that a little while, in Roseland, you know.
So then I went on out and joined -- February 21st, I remember, I joined Cab, you know, and he was playing the Stanley Theater out there in Pittsburgh. So I walked in and

there's Dizzy [Wright] on the stand, so I walk up there and he just said, "I didn't think you was coming, because you ain't gonna get nothing to play. What we do over here, we set up a show, and that show goes through for the whole year."
Cab be telling you that?
No, Dizzy was telling me.
Oh, Dizzy.
Said, "We set it up for a whole year, and that same show goes, the same numbers, and if you don't have a solo --,"
You don't get one.

You don't have one for a year, you know. So he said, "That's the reason I was surprised to see you come." So I said, "Well, I had to come anyway. I had to get out of town. I'm tired of playing with Stuff." I want to take it easy. I ain't drinking no more, and I So I go over there and I'm waiting to see when -- because I heard a lot of things about Cab, how rough he was and everything. But he never did me like that, and the only thing was, he said, "Now, Jonah, I don't care what you hear, nothing you hear on the outside, there's only three things I want you to do, and if you do these three things we'll get along beautifully." He said, "I want you to be on time, play my music and have on the uniforms I give to you." He said, "If you do those three things we'll get along fine." So I decided to do that, and I stayed
there 11 years.
Well, Jonah, were you there when Diz hit him with the chair, or whatever?

When he -- when he was supposed to be cutting him with a knife. Yeah, well, this was a silly thing, too. Musicians are always kidding around. We was at the State Theater up there, in Hartford, and all the time me and Dizzy have been rolling up paper wads all during the show, you know, spitballs they call them. And so when Cab would go off the stand to change, three or four times, you know, during one show. He'd come on with a tux, and you'd see him again, he's got on a white tux. Next time he's got on all blue, blue shoes. And the next time, tan shoes. So he changed. So now, when the Cab Drivers went out there, that was Tyree, Danny Parker, Benny Payne, Cozy and Milt Hinton. No, that's the little band out of the big band. The Palmer Brothers you're [Addressing Stanley Dance] thinking about. These are the Cab Drivers.
The Cab Drivers. How cute. The Cab Drivers.

Yeah, the Cab Jivers. And what we'd do, now when they come out, then he'd go off to change clothes. Now, me and Diz got all these paper wads or spitballs, and we'd be shooting -- and Ch Berry was in on this -- so we'd be shooting and grabbing our heads, Cozy would be playing and grabbing his head, and Cab come back out there. It was a big

stage. We used to play in some big houses. We used to play some better houses than Duke. See, we'd play in Chicago, we'd play the Chicago Theater and Duke would be around at the Oriental, you know. Because they'd all be at the same office, you know. We were all out of the same office. He would get some of the lesser ones, and I couldn't figure that out for nothing. As much as them guys play over there and we don't have that kind of music, but I guess it takes you a long time to figure some things that are right before you. But Cab was visual. Duke was sound.
Yeah.
It takes a little -- to listen, you know, it's a little harder to listen, than if you can just sit there and look, you know.
Yeah.

So that was it, you know, and I'd notice when we'd go out there to play, we'd leave together, all be hooked up the same way. We'd have our own pullman cars. Duke would have his own pullman. And we'd have our own baggage cars. And we'd be going to Chicago, and every time Duke would be going to Stevens and we'd be going to Sherman. Used to do it every New Year's Eve night, you know. And I used to wonder sometimes why, and I seen him outdrawing back in them days, you know. Cab would outdraw him. It was just because it was visual. People could see.
That's right.
They wanted to see him sing hi-de, hi-de, ho, you know.
Yeah.
Which is good, you know. He did something with it and give a lot of musicians work, you know. But that was funny about that, now.
So what happened?

See, this was done all over the country. This wasn't the first place we started. Cab come out there and seen this stuff all over the floor of the stage and never said a word. It was in Chicago, maybe in Philadelphia, at the Earl. Anyway, just that day, in the theater, he come to the wings, and he swore he saw Dizzy's hand up in the air. He come out there and he's mad. He's cursing. Now the finale's coming on. The girls and boys are dancing, you know. And they're arguing, back and forth, at each. "You little simple so-and-so, why are you throwing that? When you going to grow up?" You know. "You lyin'! It wasn't me! And Cab, you another lie! It was!" Now the curtain goes closed, you know, and Cab starts around the [wagon] after Diz, and Diz jumps down, so we, the brass section, we grabbed Diz, and Chew and them they grabbed Cab, you know. We said, well, we were just kidding, and just say don't do it no more, and we won't do it. So Cab -- they turned Cab loose and he started walking that way to his dressing room. We were supposed to go this way.

We turned Diz loose, and Diz run up behind him and scratched him on the hand. Wasn't nothing bad. Downbeat had a whole, great big thing about it, how Diz was hanging onto his tails or something, slicing him. But scratched him on the hand, and there was trunks in the hallway where he was going, and he turned around fast. It kind of scared him, you know, and he hit his thigh on one of the locks on a trunk, you know.
Yeah.
That was worse than the scratch he had on the hand. But you know, they made a big thing out of it. Now, Mittler's there, the guy that manages the whole thing.
I know.

Duke and Cab. They were supposed to be incorporated, or something, you know. So I went in to talk to him, but I've got a job waiting, you know. I've got a job waiting, in case I don't like what's going on with Cab. You know, you heard so much stuff, about how he hollers at you and you know, stuff.
Uses language?
Huh?
Uses language?
That's what they said. They said he's a hard man, he's a hard man to work for.
Yeah.
I didn't find him that way. I didn't find

him that way. So -- but anyhow, I'm a little skeptical. So when I get out here, Charlie Barnet is already ready, already called me from Chicago to join the band. Now, so I've got a job. I know I've got a job, so I didn't mind if we got fired. So I went into the office, into Cab's dressing room. So I said, "Look, I think you're mistaken about Dizzy." I said, "I was throwing paper wads out there myself." I said, "We've been doing it all the time, you know, and you never said anything about it." He said, "Maybe you was doing it, but I saw Dizzy's hand up in the air." See, Diz had done so much different things in the band, you know.
Yeah.
Because at that time he was really a big kid then, you know.
Yeah.

And he just come down on him that day. And I said, "Well, I don't think it was him. I think it was me and I wouldn't want to see him get fired unless it was really, you know, for something he didn't do."

So then Mittlek spoke up and said, "What do you expect the man to do? Do you expect him to keep him after he cut him on his hand and all that, you know?" So that was Mittlek, so then I backed out of it, because I'm not about to talk to Mittlek.
No.

He looked like a mole, anyhow, so I didn't want to talk to him. I talked to Cab. So then I let it go. So then I told Diz, "Well, when we get back to New York I'll call Charlie," and I said, "Maybe he can give you that job, you know." So the next day I called Charlie Barnet and I said, "Well, I can't come, but I've got a good man for you." He said, "Who?" And I says, "His name is Dizzy Gillespie." He wasn't too known then. But he said -- right away he said, "That's that guy that cut Cab, ain't it?" He said, "Hell, I don't want him in here. I don't him in my band." You know, that fast. Just about a day or two, how the news travels, you know. Charlie said, "That's that guy that cut Cab. I don't want him in my band." But I really missed him, you know, because we had a lot of fun.
Well, what did happen to Diz? Where did he go?
Well, that's when he went into the woodshed. That's when he went in to practice, and he was already getting together with bebop.
Yeah.
[Parker]

He'd already heard Charlie and he was raving and everything about this guy that runs the G-minor 7th against a C 7th, and that gives you your flatted fifth, your flatted seventh, your flatted ninth, and all that, you know. Because he was there telling me all of this, you know? He

was telling me this when he come back raving. And we were pretty good pals, you know, in the band. And he was raving about this, and we said, "What can it be?" We'd never heard of the thing. "Yeah, but this guy is playing something else." So now he's telling me all about it. He was trying to show me how it goes, and I said, "Yeah, but like two and two is four, you know." And he said, "No, not exactly." So now he gets enough nerve to get up on the stand, and he had a chorus of "Some of These Days," and so he gets up there and he makes the thing, and it sounded real funny in those days on the trumpet, because it wasn't being played. (Singing). And Cab said, "What the hell is that?" He said, "Don't make that in my band. Don't play that, whatever it is. I don't want to hear that." He said, "Give that part to Jonah," you know. So now he's down there and he says okay, and so he gives it to me, you know. There wasn't no hard feelings. So he gives it to me and I started playing it, and all at the same time Dizzy's showing me this thing. He's so insistent about this, you know. He's down there and he's got Milt [Hinton] playing the bass between shows, and because the bass and everything's got to go along with it, you know, and the rhythm, you know. And Danny, he wasn't practicing between shows, and Benny Payne, he wasn't going to practice between shows. But Milt would practice with him between shows, you know. And he's getting this thing together. He didn't care, because -- but I was there and I

wanted to see what he was doing, you know. Anyhow, we always walked around together between shows. So now he's showing it to me, and he says, "Jonah, you see this? And if you get here and you've got this chord going too long, just sit there playing the straight F chord. Play that chord one bar. You've got four bars after it, then go to F-sharp and come back to F again, you know." And I said, "Yeah, it's interesting." So I get on the stand with "Some of These Days," and I made one of these things, and Cab said, "You too?" He said, "I'm going to fire both of you." He said, "I'm going to fire both of you, playing that. I won't have that in my band." So I said, "I better stay away from this." Because you began to think about it, you know. You began to think, well, maybe this is something, you know what I mean? And sure enough, here comes a guy, bebop records, and here comes the opening of the Bebop Club, you know, on 49th Street. So, well, maybe this is a thing here. But I said, no, I've always been pretty sensible about where I'm going. I've been commercially thinking. I think I've been a little bit commercially thinking all along, you know. And one reason I had to do it was because I had a family, you know. So I went on back to playing my old way, you know. And you had to do that in Cab's band, because he kept you in that mold, you know. Now, like you couldn't do with Stuff, you know, start out taking all them choruses and things. Many a night I sat up there and played 25 choruses,

you know, and he's just hollering for more. Stuff's hollering for more. And over there you played just what you were supposed to play, you know, with Cab. So I said, well, that's it. I'm not going to kill myself with the whiskey over there with Stuff, drinking every night, you know. And had had a couple of attacks then. So I was able to come out of it. So I -- this is going to be it. So one morning (Unintelligible). We're on the Strand Theater, and he comes out in his zoot suit and his chain, and he walks around, and we make an introduction and go into I think two choruses of the blues in E-flat. And at the end of it I'd always end up on F, high F, you know. And I didn't know that he was directing my solo until one day I'd been fooling around all night, you know. Instead of going to half hour, about 10:30 in the morning, at the Strand Theater. And I didn't feel like making no F there that morning. So I played something else, you know. And when I got ready to end up I just ended up maybe (Singing), something like that, and so he called me after the finale, you know, and he said, "You messed me up this morning." And I said, "How?" He said, "Well, you always made that F up there on Geechee Joe'." I said, "Oh, yeah." And he said, "Well, you didn't make it this morning." I said, "No, I didn't feel like making it this morning because I was fooling around out there all night, you know, and I wasn't together. I didn't get to warm up good." He said, "Yeah, but don't do that, because you can't see me, but

when you're playing I'm directing all your notes." And he said, "I direct all that stuff right pointing to you, and you're supposed to go up on that F and I threw my stick up, and I threw my stick up this morning and you made something else down here." So these are the little things in life, you know, that you learn as you go along, you know. Now, it tells you from now on don't be so smart, trying to end up on F, you know, unless you intend to do it all the time, under any conditions.
Yeah. Don't take off anything.

Under any condition. I don't care if you've been up all night and you've had no sleep, don't. I don't want to hear that, uh-uh. Because he'd tell you in a minute, you know. And he was right if you look into it. You go out and hang out with him. Sometimes he'd take Tyree or me or somebody to go along with him, and you're hanging out, you know, and up all night and fooling around, and then you get in bed and maybe get a couple of hours sleep, and then you might do this on a stage, you know, on a big stage, it looks bad, you know, in the Chicago Theater or something.
Yeah.

And he catches you. "Oh, no, wake up there. Don't do that. Don't do that." So Tyree say, "I was with you." He said, "Look, Thatain't had nothing to do with it. Today is another day. Play my music now." Which is right.
Yeah.

But you see, what he had, see we had three valets. Now, one was just to take care of him, see, and this valet, see, he'd be hanging, drunk, and that valet, Rudolph, he'd take him in there and put him in the shower, cold shower, And then, he'd go out there and shake his head on "Minnie the Moocher" And every now and then he'd feel dizzy and he'd run to the wing, and Rudolph would stick that ammonia on a stick, stick it under his nose, you know, and that would straighten him up again.
Really.
Oh, yeah, a stick filled with ammonia.
You mean after Cab had been out late that night?
Yeah, all night. And maybe he'd feel a little -- you know, his head might be swimming a little from drinking.
Well, I wouldn't have thought he was as regular as that, to go out with you and Tyree.
Well, he'd do that at times. He'd pick who he'd want to take out, you know.
Is that right.
And Tyree, him and Tyree, he'd take Tyree quite a bit, you know. Like he'd hang out with the Jones brothers in Chicago. They were the guys that were the big number men, you know.
Oh, yeah.
On the South Side.
Yeah.
And then with the Sewell Brothers. They're the ones whose parents had those oil wells in Oklahoma.
Yeah.
Yeah, Johnny Sewell and --
How do you spell that, do you think?
I guess S-e-w --
S-e-w-e-l-l?
I really don't know.
No.
But Johnny Sewell and his brother, you know, and they used to sit around. And they had a place out there they called the Bath House. They used to sit around and talk all morning in Chicago, you know.
Where abouts was that?
About 35th and Indiana, somewhere around there.
That wasn't called the Vienna.
It could have been. It could have been.
No kidding.
The Vienna Baths, or something.
No kidding.
Yeah. All the guys used to hang in there.
You know, they'd hang in there. All of them would meet around there, with Joe Louis and all that gang, you know.
Yeah, that'd be it, I think.

Yeah. Joe Louis would come in there and they'd talk about money and things like that, you know, and they would tell Cab, "Oh, you ain't got no money. You don't know what you're talking about." You know, these guys have got oil wells. "You don't belong in this argument," you know. And finally they'd say, "Look, these guys --," these Jones brothers, when they got up their income tax, I think it was about -- it was in the paper that they had to pay about $4 million income tax, when they first --
Numbers...?
Uh-huh. It was in the papers.
How about that.

So they would all be arguing about money. They'd tell Cab, "Now, you go -- when you leave New York you borrow all the money you can get, and you come to Pittsburgh and borrow all you can get," and they'd set a marker like that. "You go to Detroit and --," and they'd tell him different places to go, and they said, "And we'll come out and we'll cover it for you four times." They'd say, "You ain't got nothing. You can't talk --," and they'd be just kidding, you know. I don't know, they got a kick out of this with them, and Joe Louis and all of them. At that time, at that particular time. Certain things happen at a certain time, you know.
Yeah.
But that was -- I enjoyed the band. I enjoyed it. Chu was there for awhile, you know, or Jeff, you know, all the guys.
Hilton, you mean?
Yeah, Hilton Jefferson. It was a nice --
Everybody got -- yeah.
No getting drunk and stuff like that.
Yeah. Everybody got their money.
And no smoking no pot. That was clean out of the question.
Oh.

Because you've got the dressing rooms back there and Cab's always passing by, and smelling, to see if he could smell any pot coming out of anyplace. And if he -- I'll tell you one thing he did. They call this hard, but I think he was right. I asked him about it once. I said, 'How come you're so hard on the guys?' Because singing all them songs, like, 'Cokie Joe,' or, 'Going Down to Chinatown,' --
Yeah.

He says, 'Everybody thinks I use something anyhow, so I don't want you guys to be caught because if one of you is caught, there goes my name in the headlines, 'So and So with Cab Calloway.' He said people would say I told you, you know. He says, 'You're going to connect me up with it.'
Yeah.
"So if you want to do that, you're gone."

And he wouldn't give you like two weeks notice. He'd give you two weeks salary and your fare back to New York. He didn't care who you were. You didn't work there no more. I remember once he come to me and he says, "Now, don't worry about no clique because I will fire the clique." (Laughter). He said, "Don't worry about no clique, you hear, because I will fire the clique."
(Laughter)
So in a way he was a tough cat, you know.
But you had to be to run all them guys.
Yeah.
You had to be tough to run all them guys.
Well, they were a complete opposite, Ellington and Calloway.
Oh, yes. Altogether different.
Do you think they were friends at all?
I can't see where they were too close.
No, I don't think they were too close.
They just come up together with this guy, with Irving Mills, you know.
Yeah.
And would --
And there was probably even a little bit
of jealousy there, you know.
It could have been, yeah. Sure, it's always there, you know, with people.
Yeah.
It's a little bit everywhere in this business, you know, a little jealousy going on.
Who did the arrangements mostly for the band at that time?

At the time I come there it was Andy Gibson was doing mostly everything, in '41. Then pretty soon he got Buster Harding, and Buster stayed with him all through the things, and every now and then he'd have somebody else to make an arrangement, like Chappie Willett would make something sometimes, or Benny Carter had some things in the book, but it was made before I got there, you know. Or he'd find somebody. But he always liked to have an arranger, because like you're doing that picture, "Stormy Weather," that was around '42 or '43, and we did the -- a little after, "The Sensations of 1944," with Eleanor Powell and Woody Herman. So he wanted to have an arranger always on hand that he could -- if something come up in the picture he'd write it out right away and get it out, you know. He always kept an arranger on hand, but he would buy a few things outside sometimes, you know. Then after the other trumpet player come in, Eddie Mullins, he made a couple of things. Not much, you know.
Well, I always thought Andy Gibson was really very talented. I don't think he ever got the credit he should have gotten.
No, he didn't. He could play nice trumpet.
Could he.

Yeah, played very nice trumpet. I liked him playing trumpet. But he never did get the credit. I don't know why. I think he went over with Barnet for awhile and did something, yeah, but he never got the credit that was due him. But he was a good man, a very good musician, and -- but you see now, you've got to finish it out. See, Cab would always say they may be taking advantage of him. See, he'd come in with a nice arrangement and it'd be swinging, you know, and then you'd die out. (Singing). And he would walk up to us and say, "Now, try to end it just down and riff, just go so and so." And Cab would say, "Oh, no. I don't want that. Give me an ending. I'm paying you. You gave me an introduction and I want an ending, too."
(Laughter)
"Every time I come in it always dies out, I hear you, up there die out."

And Andy always kind of figured he was going to say that, you know, because Andy would get up close to the band while Cab was sitting back out here, you know, and say, "And you all die out right down here."
(Laughter)
And Cab heard him, you know. Yeah, that was a funny thing.
Did Cab pay better money than everybody else?
I think so. I think he did. In fact Rex told me, so I have to go by that.
Yeah.

But I know one thing he did better. He would give you the full month of August off with full pay, for your vacation, every year, four weeks salary. But you was working from one year to the other, you know, right straight through, January to December, but he would give you four weeks off in August and your fare back to New York, and he would tell you, 'Now, come back here the 1st of September rested up and ready to play. Don't be going out there jamming and come back here tired, you know.' And then he'd do that. Then, Christmas is his birthday, so he'd give you two weeks off. I don't care where you were, he'd give you two weeks off with full pay for Christmas, and your fare back home.
Well, nobody did that.
I never had it in my life. Never had it in my life. So I said this is it. I'll just set here and don't play, that's all, just set here.
How old were you by then?
Oh, I don't know, I was 37. I had to be.
Oh, you were into your middle 30s.
Yeah, had to be. Going into the 1940s, yeah.
Because you couldn't have done that 10 years before.

Oh, no. When he called me up the first time, I said, 'Oh, no, no.' I was playing with Stuff then, you know. I even turned Tommy Dorsey down, see. Once Tommy was there, about '38 there, when things was going. Bunny Berrigan was drunk, as we were talking, and he didn't show up, which he did sometimes. And so Bud Freeman and Davey Tough said, 'Well, get Jonah.'
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with Jonah Jones
Sides 7-8
October 26, 1978
