PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395

rfm
PROCEEDINGS
T452
And some of the bands, maybe I can think of them. Wasn't too prominent.
You can lean back if you like, if you're more comfortable.
One, two --
Yeah, we did.
Oh, you did.
Stanley checked it. So you go right ahead now, and you lean back and I'll turn the volume up. I'll turn the volume up. You speak a little bit and then we'll check it out and see how it is.
One, two, three, four, five, six.

Off we go. So where we finished, well, we were talking about Stuff and everything, but I think in a way we ought to figure out how long you were with Stuff and how come you left. Tell about your heart thing.

Well, I'm very happy, and we come in here, it was like the Union said. When we went off to California and left the Famous Door, we wasn't supposed to put in no notice. We said we was going to put in a two weeks notice because we didn't like California.
Why didn't you like California?
I don't know. Me and Cozy, we couldn't find the places we liked to go, you know, and the things that we liked to do, you know, that we did in New York. So California

was a little spread out, and we wound up going to the same place every night, especially when you get off late from work, see. California at that time was like a country town. There was no place to go. All the clubs was closed. Your club is closed so you know everybody else is closed. Well, around here, you hang around all night then, you know.
Yeah.

Walk the streets and stuff. So then we said, well, we're going back to New York. We told Red Colonna, who was Jerry Colonna's brother, he owned the place, he and a guy named Parker, they owned the Famous Door, and so we told them we were going to put in a notice. We'd been there about two months and a half. We were going to put in a notice. He said, "You can't put in no notice. We have a contract on you with Consolidated Radio Artists that you have to stay here six months. We can't fire you and you can't quit." So we got to arguing with him. We said we never heard of a job where you can't quit, you know, you can't quite if you want to. Two weeks notice, that is a union law. So they said no, not the kind of contract we have. So, you know, we figured they were putting a thing on trying to make us stay here. And Cozy kept saying -- and we'd be riding out there together, so we were -- if we put in a notice, we were supposed to leave on the Saturday after that, you know, two weeks. So then Cozy would keep saying, "Don't forget Saturday. Don't forget Saturday." That's it, you know.

So, Saturday come and so they called up -- somebody calls up from New York, long distance on the phone, and says, "We want to speak to Stuff Smith." So Stuff says okay, so he answered the phone. So he come back to the bandstand and I said who was that. He said some guy said he was Bern Back. And Bern Back was a big man, official, in the national union, not 802, in the national. Bern Back was his name. So he said it was some guy said it was Bern Back, said not to leave. He said, "Stay on your job." So we said we didn't care if it was Bern Back or who, we're going in the morning, we're catching the train out of here.

So that morning, we got on the train and we come on back home. And we laid around awhile. So Joe Helbarth had been telling us come on back, because they wasn't doing too good in there, you know. Business was bad, because Kirby hadn't got the band set. In fact I don't know if it was Kirby's band or not, because they had Leo Watson they were trying to take out of the Spirits of Rhythm. They took Leo out of there, and they had Pete Brown. They had Frankie Newton and some other guys. So maybe he had -- yeah, he did, he had a band was supposed to be his band, but it hadn't settled down. He hadn't got Buster Bailey and Procop and Charlie yet, you know, so he wasn't doing too good, and he didn't start to do good until he brought in Maxine. Claude Thornhill brought her in, heard her in Pittsburgh and recommended her. So then they -- with her singing these
Scottish songs, they had brought the band up with her, you see.
Yeah.
And it was a nice -- things happened, you know. Like other people had sang Scottish songs, but it was just the time for her, you know.
Yeah. She had that very pretty voice.
Yeah, and she had that little voice to go along with it.
Yeah.

So they started to roll, but meantime we were laying dead, because Joe Helback, he'd been calling Stuff every night almost and, 'Come on back. They can't keep you out there.' You know, and by him saying that that helped, you know, but after we got back here, now he says, 'Take it easy. Take it easy.'
The union had probably got to him, too.

Oh, yeah, sure. Now he says, 'Okay, we'll sign contracts,' after we've been around here about a month. And the minute we signed the contract, about two days later we get a letter from the union saying, 'You are expelled from the Federation of Musicians.' You know, for leaving that job out there. Wow. Now, here we are, Stuff, here's these guys got these big cars and Cozy's got this big La Salle, and here's Stuff got a big La Salle, you know, and I had took Stuff's Ford, his 1936 Ford, I took it over. That was all right for me. I
just used it in the morning when I would get off from work — ^ with the three bars in front of it. And all these guys had cars and stuff. Now we're expelled.

So now we don't know what to do, so we go to Joe Helbarth and show him the letter. Joe said, "Well, I don't know what I can do, because this comes from the National. If it was 802 maybe I could do a little something, you know." So now we go to the agent and we tell him.
What agent? Consolidated?

Consolidated Radio Artists. Charlie Green. He's the one that handled us, you know, he booked it. So he said, "Well, Jonah --," because Stuff, he never talked no sense. Nobody never knew what to talk with him, you know. So they'd always tell me. So he said, "Well, Jonah, you know you guys wouldn't listen to what you were told. You wanted to do everything you wanted to do. I don't know what you're going to do about it now. You'll have to go up to the National."

We went up to 802, and they said, "No, we don't want to be bothered. We don't have anything to do with you all. We don't have anything to do with what you guys do." Then Rosenberg (Cherman) was the President. He was over on 6th then. And so now they said, "You guys have to go to the National."
So we went up there where Weber was, you know, and later become the guy from Chicago --
Petrillo.
Petrillo, yeah. And so it was Weber then x International

and we talked right to him. "Look, Mr. Weber, we come up to see what we have to do to be reinstated or whatever, and why, when we put in our two weeks notice." And he began to tell us, "Well, you guys had a contract out there to stay six months where you couldn't break it." Well, what did we know? So we said, "Well, we don't know how we're going to get back to work. When will we get back to work?" So he says, "Well, whenever you're ready to go out there and finish out that contract. Go back out there and finish out that contract, you know." So now we're fooling around here and everybody's getting broker and broker, and everything, the car payments them guys have got, them big car payments are coming up on them. And it goes so far till they start taking the cars, and a guy named Rosenberg, they had some kind of contract with him where Stuff had signed to get -- and Rosenberg was supposed to get 15 percent, and they took us to court. And Rosenberg's got us. What did we know about law. He's got us down there.

And so Rosenberg had already followed us. See, where Rosenberg come in, he got to us before we went to California. He says, "Now, you're going to need somebody to represent you out there. You're going to be doing pictures and all that kind of stuff, you know." And then Stuff signed up with him. "You will need protection out there for 15 percent." Stuff signs up with him. Now, while we're off, Rosenberg is taking us to court while we're trying to figure out how we're going to get

back to work. He takes -- he goes in court and he tells them, "That fellow there has three or four sets of automobile drums," talking about Cozy. And this one over here, Stuff, has got four violins and drums, and they go through all that, what each one of us had. Well, I didn't have anything, outside of I had kids, you know. And then it was over and we had to go back again. Over, go back. So the Judge said, "I don't want you bringing that man back here no more." So I was lucky, you know. "Don't bring him back up here no more. What are you going to do, are you going to put him on welfare? We've got enough people on welfare now." That's what saved me. But the rest of the guys had their cars taken away and some of them their instruments, you know.
But, Jonah --
And this is on the b.s. kick. Because this was the guy on the outside that Stuff had signed with, you know?
And I mean what way was he out of money? Just because you hadn't filled the contract?

Yeah, sure. And what they did to him, the way they treated him at the Famous Door in California, he'd come by there at night. See, he was supposed to represent us and he said we were going to get pictures and all that stuff out there.
A white guy?
Yeah, Rosenberg. He was Jewish fellow.
And he said we're going to get pictures and stuff, and we needed him there to see that everything was all right, contracts and things.
Yeah.

So he knew us and he rode out there with us on the train. We was youngsters and crazy, so he tried to collect the money from the first week in the Famous Door. So Stuff said, "No, no, don't give him no 15 percent. He's supposed to get 15 percent if we do pictures or something extra, that's the way I understand it." So they said, "Well, the man said he's got a thing here, you signed it, where he's supposed to get 15 percent." So Stuff said, "You give him 15 percent and we ain't going to play." So then Red Parker, who owned the place, told Rosenberg, "Don't you come in here no more. Leave them alone as long as they're here. And if you come in here again I'm going to throw you out." So he didn't come back. The only thing, he would drive and park outside, you know, and he'd call me, "Jonah, ask Stuff going to do about the 15 percent?" I said, "You ask him. You know what they be doing in there. He said, "You're going to be in trouble when you get back to New York." I said, "Well, to hell with it."
So that was the kind of trouble that Stuff would get you into all the time, you know, but still you liked it because you liked to play. At that time I think I played the best in my life.
But how did that end up, Jonah?

Well, it ended up by them saying now -- see the subway fare was a nickel, and we couldn't get a nickel to get out of town, after we'd laid off so long, you know. We was laying off a long time. We had apartments, you know, and stuff like that, and we didn't think much about saving money and so then we was just about down to our last nickel. We went down to the American Federation and we told them we were ready to go back with -- to finish out the contract. So he says okay, and when are you leaving, so I can notify them? We said, well, whenever we get the money, the fare out there. So he said, "Well, you had fare to come back here didn't you?" He said, "Okay, find a way to get back there." So we said, "Look, there's no way in the world we can get that much money to go out there, you know." So he set up a thing where we went back to Buffalo, to the Silver Grill, where I told you we started. He set up a thing. Peanuts was working in there now. So they set up a thing where Peanuts would come out for two weeks and we'd go in.
And make some money.
And make enough money for fare out to California.
Well, then, he didn't do too badly, that guy, Weber, then, huh?
No, he just made us --
He made it possible somehow.

Yeah, to get back. So now we go back and then the guys now figure they can do anything and get away with it. I mean they've got us now. You were so smart before leaving, so now we go out and we worked about -- I think we had, oh, maybe three months and a half to go, so we worked about two months and they closed down. See, they didn't even finish it up. They closed down then, and we're stuck out there, and without paying the money or anything. All these things -- well, of course we got our money at the end of the week, but when they closed down we didn't know it.
No, and you found yourself and you didn't have anything ready.
And we're way out here in California, you know. We were just lucky that we had a little money saved, you know, in case something happens, you know.
Was business not good, Jonah?
Business wasn't as good as it was at first. See, when we left they brought in Fats Waller, and for some reason it didn't go good. Who knows what these things are.
No.

They went for us all the way. I don't know why. We had people, Kay Francis and Jack Oakie, and Georgie Stone and all these big producers and music directors and stars, Bette Davis and all of them come in here, you know, and it was the place to go, you know.
Yeah.
And then when we left, the business fell off.
Yeah.
Because the cook told us. "You guys left it was pretty dull in here." And they brought in Fats Waller.
Yeah.
They brought him in with a small group, you know, and it just didn't go. Then when we got back in it still didn't go.
No.
We had it then, we should have kept it rolling.
They moved on somewhere else.
Yeah, should have kept it rolling, you know.
Yeah.
See, things change in life.
Yeah.

Everything changes. So when I look back on them things, you know, it was a great experience. I mean I tell you, I didn't know what road, you know. You wanted to know what happened when Sonny Greer -- wanted me to come with Duke in 1930 and I got cold feet. Ain't no telling what will happen, what would have happened to me if I'd made the -- built up a bigger name faster, you know.
Yeah.
Because even if I had sat behind him and put things there, you know, but I was afraid, you know.
Yeah.

And then I was pretty happy there anyway, and making about $50.00 a night tips. In the Vendome Hotel. But now we get back here and then we start to act halfway decent. It was mostly Stuff. I say it was mostly Stuff, because he was the one who had signed everything, you know. Once in California, before we left the first time, he left by himself, and you know what we did? We got Eddie Barefield. Yeah, I'm glad we leaned on it awhile, because I remember. Now, he was out there about a month and a half and he said, "Let's go back to New York, you know?" And I said, "No, you've got to put in a notice and you've got to go to and ask the agent about this." They had the representative there in California. So he must have went and they said, "No, you can't do that, Stuff. You've got to stay there." So we come to work one night and Stuff wasn't there, and they told us -- we called the hotel and they told us Stuff left this morning for New York. And I called up Eddie Barefield. So I got in front of the group and the Bear played. He was out there. I forget now how Eddie Barefield was out there, but he was there, and I brought him in there, because he wasn't working, so I brought him in and I got in front of the band. And we played and the guys said, "That's
all right, I hope he stays in New York and we'll keep the band just like this."

But then they sent him back. The union sent him back to California and then he comes back and we started laughing at him because they sent him back, so he tells us now, if we all had left together they couldn't have done it. "But they made me come back because you all stayed. If we all had left together, it couldn't have happened."

Now, Cozy goes for this hook, line and sinker, because he wants to get away, you know. He wants to get away from California too. And he goes and says, "You know, Jonah, he might have something there." I said, "Well, maybe." I said, "I don't know. I don't know." He said, "Do you realize we've got three months and a half more to go out here? They can have all that sunshine." He wanted to get back, because you see, New York was a different place then. You know, it was a lot of fun. So then, okay, not it comes up again. Stuff sat back there and said, "Well, if you all want to go, I'll put in a notice. I'll put in a notice. We can go together. We'll go right back to the Onyx." And that was before we all left.
Yeah.

Then that works up to where we all left together and they made us go to Buffalo and pay our way on back out there and then we come on back. But we didn't go back into the Onyx. We went -- because by this time John
Kirby's cooking in there. Yeah, with Maxine. They don't need us now.
Yeah.

See, John Kirby is cooking in that place. So then we started to playing around, like Chicago, the La Salle Hotel, I told you they shot the tear gas gun in the back. It was a class hotel, you know, and the man's got all the signs up there, you know, and Stuff brings this chick in and we play "Stompin' at the Savoy" and he's playing (sings "I love you") to this chick, because - they had been drinking all day. And Mr. Smith wouldn't talk to him at all, the manager. So — He only talked to me, you know. Because the sign's up there as big as can be. "Musicians. No drinking. No sitting with the customers. No standing at the bar. No bottles brought into the hotel at all." Not into the lockers or no way. We had those lockers full within a week. We had all kinds of bottles in there. The first night we were standing at the bar and Stuff was sitting at a table, and the next night we were all sitting at the tables, you know. And so the thing about that was -- another thing about that was we had to play that hour for dinner, as I said, when we first went in there the man said, "Keep it down, soft, during dinner," and we didn't. We went in there and played loud, all the numbers we used to play, and long numbers, you know, and building all the time. And people got so they liked it. The place had been a graveyard. The waiters and everything said, "This place has been a graveyard before you all come in here." And we got people used to listening to that stuff, and we packed that place, you know.

They'd come in at dinner and everything, you know. So now Smith, the manager, said, "You can't play loud, Jonah, because it gives them indigestion. It's too loud." So we'd play soft, and people would say, "No, come on, play loud. Play loud." They wanted it, you know. We were supposed to be in there for four weeks. We stayed five months.
Now we come to the Netherlands Plaza in Cincinnati.
No, wait a minute. What about the shotgun?

Oh, yeah. In there we did everything. As I say, we went in there, we went to the bar. People started asking us to sit at the tables, and so Smith couldn't say no because these are the big customers, and they're going to say what is this, they can't sit over here, you know. Can't sit at a table? We'd like to talk to him, you know. And then Stuff was hanging out all day and bought him a tear gas gun. He comes in at night and our dressing room's right off the kitchen, and he goes out in the kitchen, and the waiters are running through there, you know. A lot of dinners are being served and they're running back and forth. And he shoots off his tear gas gun, and everybody's crying. The waiters is crying, the cooks is crying, and Mr. Smith starts back there and says, "What's going on back there?" They said, "Don't go in there. Don't go in there." He said, "Why?" They said, "Stuff just shot a tear gas gun back there." He said, "Oh, God, what next?" He said, "What next?" So the man called me, he said, "Look, if

there was any way I could get you all out of here," he said, "You wouldn't spend another day in here." But he said, "You've been doing such great business. The place has been packed every night." He says, "I don't understand it, you guys do everything in here." I said, "Don't say you guys. Tell it to Stuff." He said, "I can't talk to him. He always runs by me all the time, you know." So now, to set it off good, now Petrillo's a tough man out there, so Petrillo's got a thing somebody's supposed to be elected there, some Mayor's running and he's Petrillo's man. Gene Krupa's out there at the Sherman and we're in the La Salle, so he called all of us down and says, "Now, look, once a night I want you to stop in the middle of a number when you've got everybody on the floor, stop in the middle of a number and say we are dedicating this number to Mayor So-and so," and he says, "If you're broadcasting, I want you to dedicate a number out of your broadcast to Mayor So-and-so," you know. So we got in there. What do we know who the Mayor is? We don't know one Mayor from the other, you know. We just come to Chicago to work. So now we stop in the middle of the number and he says, "We are dedicating this number to Mayor So-and-so," you know. So when we got off the stand, Smith says, "Jonah, Jonah, come here." He won't call Stuff. He says, "What are you doing?" I said, "What?" He said, "That's the Democrat. We're Republicans in here. What's happening now? Dedicating numbers to people and all that stuff? Who told you

to do that?" I said, "Petrillo said do it." He said, "Well, you better go ahead and do it then, if he told you." He said, "You'd better do it, then," you know. After it happened the man must have wanted something but he come in there one night and about 10:00 o'clock and we wasn't supposed to get off till 1:00, and he come in there about 10:00 o'clock and said, "You all come up in Room 1432, I'm having a little party up there."
(laughter)
Who said that?

Petrillo. Said, "Bring your instruments and things up there, you know." And we walked right on by Smith and went on upstairs, and we played, oh, two or three or four numbers while we were up there, you know. It was about 10:00 o'clock, you know, so I guess we must have sat around and had a few drinks, playing socializing, and it's about 11:00 now. The place was packed. So he said, "Now, you all can go home. You don't have to go on the stand no more tonight. You can go home." And says, "There'll be a bottle of whiskey waiting for you on your way out." So he had called them up and said, "Give each one of them a bottle of that 21-year-old Grandad, you know," and they gave each one of us one. We took it home. Sure. Tell you the truth, I had so much real life experience, especially with Stuff, it mostly happened with him. As great as he was, there's nothing -- I don't know, we used to say he was crazy like a fox. But everybody loved him, and if you said anything to him the people would get angry, because they'd say

you're dogging him, you know? Even I couldn't say nothing. I used to call him names. He'd get up on the stand and he'd make you mad. Here we are on the bandstand at 6:00 o'clock. We were supposed to play from 6:00 to 7:00 for the dinner hour, and come back from 9:00 to 1:00. Now, it happens that a certain night in the week, when you go on at 6:00 o'clock, you're on the air, too, NBC, coast to coast. Now, we get in there and get ready to hit, and everybody'd say, "Where's Stuff and John," [Brown] the bass player, "and Stuff." Don't know, you know. So the the announcer, he don't know from nothing, so we just go into it. It was lucky we had George Clark on tenor at this time, you know, we had added a tenor. And so the man gets up there and says, "And Stuff Smith and his Onyx Club boys, coming from the La Salle Hotel, the Blue Fountain Room." So we'd get up there (Singing) -- played on the trumpet. And then we'd start playing the numbers we've got and I'd keep telling the man I can't play the arrangements we've got, so I have to tell the man, I whisper to him while the tenor playing is playing I tell him what the next number is, you know. Because they liked for you to write it down so they can have it in front of them. But by him not being there. And finally, just about five minutes before we'd go off, here comes Stuff. And I'd say, "Where in the hell have you been," you know, "Man, we're on the air and everything, coast to coast." He'd say, "We got hung up in that traffic. We was at the ball game. And John got stuck too."

And I said, 'Why did you take John?' He said, 'Well, John was with me. I didn't think we were going to stay that long. I didn't think the game was going to run that long. So we stayed there and saw the game and I thought I could make it,' because he always drove fast, you know, but that traffic had him, you know, he couldn't move. And he come in there just like nothing had happened. Okay. Let's take it. After the broadcast we all got it now. Said, 'you all let him take it out.' And they wasn't even dressed or had their uniform on or nothing. He had on a riding habit, you know, and a green shirt and khaki riding pants and boots on, back in them days. It's all right today, but back in them days, he had boots on. He was way ahead of everybody. Now it'd make you so mad, but it didn't do you any good, so you just threw it out of your mind, you know, and you went on. And you know, you took it as it come, you know.
He never worried.
No, he never worried, you know.
Like when he was thrown out of the union, that didn't worry him?

No, it didn't worry him at all. He'd always call and say, 'Well, what did you all do? Did you all go down to the union today?' I'd say, 'Yeah, man. There's the man giving me the devil and you were the one supposed to be catching it.' He said, 'What'd he say?' I said, 'Who the hell do you think you all are? You all are coming from the country
Oh, yeah.

Because he really gave us the devil, you know. "Who do you think you are," you know. And now Stuff won't come to the meeting. He won't come down there. So we have to go. So he's laying around cooling it, so finally, when the last thing come up where we're supposed to go to Buffalo, why then -- and to work and get the money to go back, then he came up there, you know. And it didn't matter what you'd tell him. It didn't make no difference. He would do the same thing. And he would do such little things, you know, some time. Sometimes he'd do such little things. Great as he was -- and I must say he's the greatest guy I ever worked with in my life that I can remember, you know. He'd have one number, he'd know it right away. He don't need to practice. He'd know it now. He's got it, one time. But I remember in Milwaukee, we played at Blatt's Beer Garden, and Fats used to be out there in a small group, and we were staying at some people's house. We had a saxophone player, George Clark , he was living upstairs. Stuff was living downstairs in the next place. And I hear the people talking about -- me and George was laying up there, and listening, and people were saying, "And that little man, I

don't know how he got out of there with that trunk on his back. I don't know how he did that." And George said, "I wonder if they're talking about Stuff." So we got dressed and we went over next door, and we said, "What happened?" They said, "Your leader, you know." This is the last day, see, and rent wasn't nothing, about $15.00 for the week or something like that, you know, but Stuff done went in there at night and took his trunk out, and I guess he took it to the station, you know.
Carried it out?

Yeah, but he must have had someone with him, and somebody probably had a car. He had to have a car. Couldn't carry it down the street. But I just heard them saying, "That little man, how he took that trunk out by himself Out in Milwaukee I'll never know." In them days they didn't look for you to do nothing like that, you know what I mean. Kind of settled people, like, you know, didn't look for you to go out and not pay a $15.00 rent, you know. And what happened, we went on the bandstand that night and these people called up the manager, and the guy that owned the place, he took the money out, you know. But it was so small a thing to do, you know, it made us feel so bad, you know.
Yeah. Yeah. Poor.
Yeah, such a small thing. He could do these things like that, and then when it come to playing it was altogether a different thing. It was whole new bag then,
when he picked up the violin. He was a genius. He was a genius when he picked up his violin. Perfect pitch and all that stuff, and played more than anybody up there.
Never got tired.

Right, never got tired. Always pushing, pushing. We both played better than we ever played in our lives, right there -- me and Cozy, because he kept pulling you "Come on. Come on. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah." You know, in his spine, you know. And I think we both swung more in those days. Maybe you know more about your horn today. You have to know more about it, technically, but I mean just down swinging it was better with him because he inspired you to do it.
I don't think he was ever as happy with anyone else, do you?

No, I think that was the best for him of all the different things he had, his trio and all of that. All that stuff never really moved him like we did. He could come down -- and all those little things we used to play with him, had no music with him. He'd get in there and think them things up himself, you know, "Crescendo (n Drums" (Singing). And he'd just be humming all that stuff to us at rehearsal, you know, and you've got to remember that night, because he's going to remember his. He's going to remember his part, sure. And you know, all that kind of stuff. And then, as I say, we did a lot of spontaneous things, like you was talking about, "Baby, Won't
