She was crazy there for awhile.
Just talk to me.
One, two, three, four, five. I think we've got it again.
Okay.

So we were talking -- I think we were playing in a place in Newark called the Merry-go-Round, with Stuff, and Tommy was getting ready to -- this was way before Charlie, now, you understand, before Charlie Shavers, and so Bunny, he can't make it this night. He gets a little tipsy and he can't make it, and so then Bud Freeman and Davey Tough was speaking to me and they said, "Well, get Jonah. Get Jonah. He can read the book." So Tommy turned around and said, "Oh, Jonah?" They said yeah. So he took me and then we went up to the Savoy to play this battle of music with Chick, and Chick walks around in front of the bandstand and looks up there, and says, "I don't know what you brought him up here for. We're going to blow him out just like we're going to do the rest of you." And we all laughed about it.
Now, I went on for years, still with Stuff. This is back with Stuff again, around '38, and we went on, then again we were playing -- no -- he called me up.
Tommy.
Yeah, he called me from -- and we're in

Los Angeles now, and he wants me to join the band. And he says, "We've got some arrangements for you. We've got 'Hallelujah' and different things, and we'd like you to come over and we'll see." "Oh, wonderful." So I says, "Well, how much will you pay?" So he said, "Don't worry about the money. The money's all right." Well, I was getting a hundred and twenty-five with Stuff then and enjoying it, having fun, you know.
Yeah.

And so Tommy says -- so I didn't know. Then one day I get a call from the airline, says there's a ticket here for you from a Mr. Tommy Dorsey. You're supposed to meet him in Indianapolis on such and such a date. So I said, "Well, you send it back to Mr. Dorsey, because we have some more talking to do." You know, he hadn't told me how much I was going to make. And on top of that he hadn't paid me for the gig I did at the Savoy, which was almost a year, you know. So I didn't worry about it, because I figured a man like this I ain't got nothing to worry about with him. So now I says, "Send it back." So I guess he got it, because I got a call again, a couple of hours from then, and he said, "Jonah, what's the matter, what's wrong?" I said, "We never did get the money part straight, you know." So he says, "You're going to make more money than you're making. I'm going to have you take a little band out of the big band and record with that. Then you'll be recording with the big band." And I said, "Yeah, but
I'd like to have something, a bottom, where I know what I'm going to get every week, you know." He said, "Don't worry." I said, "Yeah, but I am."
That's a nerve, to tell you don't worry.

I said, "Write me a letter." And I've still got the letter. I still have it. I got a letter that says -- did some talking and he says, "And we'll pay you $3,750.00 a year." I've got the letter. "We'll pay you $3,750.00 a year." Now, I don't know if he thought I couldn't figure that out, you know. It was about $75.00 a week. Or what, you know. But --
How about that.

But I was getting a hundred and twenty-five with him. So, well, these are the little things that went on. You know. But now -- so I never even answered the letter. I didn't even bother about answering the letter. So now we leave California. My wife is with me. The second time I was out there. So we come on back. She had some people in Cleveland, and we stopped by there, and we see that Tommy's in town. So I go down, backstage at the Palace Theater, just to say hello to the guys, you know. So the kids was all back there, and the valet saw me, "Hey, Jonah. Open up here, let him through." So I went on in. "Does Tommy know you're out here?" "No, I just caught the show and thought I'd come back and say hello to everybody." So I went in all the rooms and talked to the guys

and said hello to them. Then I went in Tommy's room, you know. "Hey, Jonah, how you doing?" You know. So I said, "All right." But the reason I didn't do that, I told him, I was getting more with Stuff. I was getting a hundred and twenty-five. So I said, "There wasn't no use in me keeping you hanging, you know, so I didn't want to go through it too much, so that's why I didn't answer you, you know." So he said, "That's all right. I didn't know what you were getting. You never said. That was just what you were going to get, but you could make way more than that, you know, with recordings and broadcasts and things like that, you know." So I said, well, no I kind of like it over there, you know. And we sat and talked awhile, and the wife was there, and finally he said, "Where you going? You on your way back to New York?" I said, "Yeah, we're going to stay around a couple of days. I'm going to take my wife out tonight for dinner. We're going to a couple of clubs on Cedar Street there, the Cedar Gardens and stuff." So he said, "Okay, have a nice time. I'll see you when we get in New York." And he gave me a hundred dollar bill, you know. So that's almost a year later since I played with him, so I guess he was paying off then. Because I never asked him for it.
No.
I never asked him. I never asked him for any money.
It's funny how these -- I mean, you know,
we all know that Benny was tight. I didn't know that Tommy was too.
Well, I don't know, but I couldn't see what -- he couldn't forget. I suppose he can't forget that I played there, you know.
Yeah.
But maybe he thought it wasn't worth nothing or something, you know. Well, what the heck, to say thanks for coming by, you know.
Well, how did Charlie Shavers and Sy Oliver make out with him, did you ever find out?

No, I never knew too much about it. I know that Sy had made some stuff in there, called -- Charlie told me, "Those arrangements have still got your name on them, when you were supposed to come over there. Why didn't you come?" I said, "Well, we couldn't get together. We never got together, we didn't get into it very seriously, you know." I wasn't too particular about leaving Stuff anyway at the time. So he said, "Yeah, they've got about --," because Tommy told me, "Sy's already making some arrangements for you, you know." And he ain't talking no money or nothing, and I'm trying to think will I be happy, because at that time I thought happiness was Stuff, you know. With Stuff you could play all you wanted to play, you know.
Yeah.

Anything, you know. So -- and I said, "I don't know about playing in a band of that type, you know." But I figure now I could have did it, you know, because I could have read anything he had in that book.
Yeah, I'm sure of that.
Because Cab had some mysterious numbers in that book, and you had to know what you were doing to read it. And that band wound up being a good band, if you listened to it. It wasn't a swinging band.
No, I know it was a good band.
But it had good sound. Everybody had big tones in there.
Yeah, Jeff and --
Yeah, Jeff and Tyree. Tyree Glenn, Quentin Jackson, Keg Johnson, Claude Jones.
Yeah, they were all good musicians.
And four trombones. Man, they would get to playing sometimes and it would be so beautiful.
A pity that he wouldn't do like some bands do, like he's on a date, why wouldn't he let the band swing out at times, you know?

Well, I think he wanted to be the show. I think he figured another thing. I think he might have been watching Duke. Now, I'm surmising this. He might have been watching Duke and the trouble that he was having out of soloists.
He made a lot of group instrumental records.
Who was that?
A lot of those instrumentals were --
That Cab made?
-- good records.
Oh, yeah, he made some of them, but he was going to let too many of them go.
No, not too many. I mean --
See, he'd -- now he had "Ghost of A Chance," with Chu Berry, which was nice.
Yeah.
That was Andy Gibson, wasn't it?
Yeah.
Then he had "Ebony Silhouette."
Well, that was a beautiful thing.
That was a nice thing.
Yeah.
And then he had this thing -- let's see, what else he had -- oh, Milt. Oh, that was "Ebony Silhouette." Then he had me doing -- he had Jeff doing "Willow Weep for Me."
Yeah.
Then he had Buster write "Jonah Jones and Cab," and that caused a lot of commotion, in the band.
(Unintelligible) Crescendo in DRUMS

Yeah, the crescendo. Well, that was Stuff's number. Show you how things get mixed up, that was Stuff's head number, and he hummed it to us in the Onyx Club, and we played it all the time, you know. Then, when Stuff went over with Cozy, somehow or another it become somebody else's number, you know. That was the same number we'd been playing with Stuff all the time. And I never said nothing, but I just sat there and looked, you know. But he would get numbers for you. Now, when you first come into the band, to make you feel at home, welcome, you played this thing about six months. You're running down in front, you know, and playing the trumpet thing, and then all at once number 89 is out and we're putting in "Willow Weep for Me." But you can't say nothing. What the heck, Jeff's been sitting here for six months playing nothing, and you've been running down here, you know, and then pretty soon Jeff goes, and then Jeff plays about six months, and then pretty soon Chu Berry, putting in "Ghost of a Chance," today. Changed the number again, let you have it. And then where the argument came was on the weekend, Saturday and Sunday, you've got to cut the shows short, because you start to doing five shows, you know. Instead of the four, you're doing five. Or some places might hire you for six. At the Apollo the shows goes on every half hour, all day, on Sunday, yeah.
So now he'd say, when you'd walk on the stage, he'd say, "The drum number's out." He wouldn't tell Cozy that in front.

He would tell him, "Drum number's out." And we'd watch Cozy all during the show, and he'd be sweating and he'd be so mad, he'd be sweating and sweating, it rolled off of him. And he didn't cool off for the whole hour, and when he come off, and if the curtain closed, he'd say, "Hey, Cab, come here. I want to talk to you. I want to talk to you just a minute." And he'd get Cab in there and he'd say, "Don't take my number." And Cab said, "Yeah, but I have to cut the show down." "Yeah, but don't cut me out. Cut some of those acts out out there." You know. So Cab would say, "No, can't cut the acts out, because they're getting paid to stay out there, you know. But don't take my number out all the time." He'd argue about it, but Cab would still take it out. But he'd wait till he hit that stage, you know. He wouldn't tell him in front. He'd wait till he hit the stage and say, "The drum number is out." And you'd see Cozy swelling up and everything.
Would anybody else argue, other than Cozy?

Oh, a few guys did. Of course the original guys didn't say much, guys like me. I guess we expected it, you know. I had to talk to him once and I was sorry I did, because it didn't call for that, you know.
Why? What happened?
Well, it was a little thing, he had an arrangement made for me, you know, that -- "Can't Give You

Anything But Love." He had two or three things for me. (Singing) --"It's a good day for singing a song, it's a good day for moving along." He had that made for me. And then the guys would say -- some of the guys would say, "Damn. He ain't never let nobody come down and sing by himself like that."

He had a (unintelligible) back there. Like he had a number made, on his trumpet." (Singing) Here comes Jonah blowin' And I heard somebody say, "He ain't never called nobody's name before. How did he rate that," you know? I don't know, the man just did it. But you hear all of these little jealous things, you know, which don't mean nothing. If you listen to them things it'd run you crazy. And you can't blame them, because they're setting back there doing nothing.
Yeah.

And here are you, going. So he would do that with me, and I guess maybe I didn't jump at the first time or something. Now he had an arrangement made of "I Can't Give You Anything but Love," where I'd come down and sing and play. When I'd get to the end I'd say, da, da, da, da, with the F. And so we were rehearsing at the Sherman Hotel, and I says -- so we play it, and I sing it and we play it, and I wouldn't -- to save myself for that night, I wouldn't make it up high. You know, I'd make it down. Da, da, da, da, you know, and he says, "Let's take it down again." He's still waiting for me to make it up, you know. So I made it down again. So he says,

"Damn, Jonah, make it up like it's supposed to be." He said, "Play it like it is, like you're supposed to play it tonight." You know. So I said, in an undertone, "Oh, kiss my so and so." So he said, "What did you say?" So I can't back down now. I said, I guess "Kiss so-and-so." So he said, "You guys are -- I don't understand you guys. I spend money to have arrangements made for you and then I have to take that. Now, these things cost me money, and I only asked you to play the thing like it's supposed to be." So I listened to that and then I went on and played it. But he never bothered me no more, you know. He never bothered with me any more, in that way, you know. In fact, he was perfect. He was perfect in every way afterwards. Maybe -- I had to do that. But I don't think so, I had to do that. Not intentionally, not for -- especially for him to hear it, but I just said it under my breath, you know, and he heard me, setting out on the floor, and he heard me. Well, I can't back down, you know, when he said that, so, "What did you say," you know. Wait a minute. Don't pull me down front like that, you know, because I'd starve first.

But we -- after that he'd ask me, he'd say, "Now, if you want to buy a horn, don't go to no bank and get the money." He says, "If you want to buy a horn I'll let you have the money to pay down on it and you can pay it back like you want to. You can give it back to Mr. Wright, you know, as you want to, out of your salary, every week, if you have it, or if you don't

have it, you know, just tell me you don't have it this week, you know." And I got to thinking about it, I don't want to buy no horn, because this guy will get me stuck in here and I can't get out, and I owe him all this money, you know. (Unintelligible).

So then, another time, he saw me looking at a trumpet, backstage in the Regal Theater in Chicago. So it was an Olds, so I was looking at this Olds, and the guy brought down about three of them from the shop, and I was looking at them and he passed by and saw it, and he says, "You going to buy a horn?" I says, "I'm thinking about it." If I could pick out the one which I liked the best. So he says, "Now, if you're going to buy that, tell Mr. Wright." He was the manager, the road manager. He said, "Tell Mr. Wright to buy it. Tell him to buy it and he'll pay cash for you. That'll save you your credit charges, carrying charges. He'll pay cash for it and you'll pay it back, $5.00 a week, or whatever you want to pay." Well, I didn't work for nobody like that. Then I told this one night on the -- they were working at the Stevens and we were working at the Sherman, and we were on the subway. We'd get the subway together every night, you know, coming to the South side. And I was telling him about that. He said, "What, you'd do things like that?" I said, oh, yeah. I'm telling him about the horn. I said, "Can you do that where you are?" He said, "Uh-uh. I've been trying to get $200.00 for six months,

borrow 200 for six months," and he said, "I can't get it." He said, "I can't get it. I've been trying." I said, "That ain't nothing over here." I said, "The guys don't do it over here because they don't want to get stuck. They're scared that they might be stuck and they'll want to leave, but they'll be in debt, then, you know." I said, "The cats won't do it, but they can get it."
Did he do that to many guys? Did many guys take him up on those things?
Very few. I think I took him upon the horn.
Yeah.
I think I took him up on the horn, because I really needed a horn then.
How long was Jeff with him?

Oh, he was with him when I joined and he was with him when I left, so he had to be with him over 11 years. I was there 11 years. Never had no idea I would stay that long. No idea in the world. And Fletcher had sent me this letter too. "If you ever get tired of where you're at, come on back here." And I liked that music of Fletcher's, but I had to have a job where you'd get paid every week.
Yeah.
And he was paying -- like way back then when the other bands was paying $70.00, you know, $70.00 for

seven days, $10.00 a night, he was paying like 90. Then when I went in the band, in '41, I was getting 110, and I guess about a year or two later I was raised to 125, and when I finished up in '52, I was getting 250. You know, so I don't know what the other salaries --
Yeah, every week.
Every week. See, we were working every week.
And then you made record sessions.
But then they was cutting -- they cut the band down then.
Oh.
See, we cut it down to seven.
Oh, I see.
Had Jeff, Keg and myself, Sam Taylor and three rhythm.
Was that a little more fun?
I liked it better, because it looked like I was getting back to Stuff.
Yeah.
Then he cut it down to four, Panama, drums, Dave Rivera, piano, Milt Hinton, bass, and myself. One horn. And he had to have the trumpet to growl on 'Minnie the Moocher.'
Yeah.
But I was glad that I was the one that he
picked.
Yeah.

Because we went all down to Cuba and everywhere, you know, and it was nice. I enjoyed it, you know, and I got to do little things to break -- to break up the monotony. He'd let me come down and sing a number too, you know.
Yeah.
But he would still direct it, you know, he would direct cadenzas and things. And what the heck, you say, what are you going to make a big thing out of that.
That's his act, sort of.
Yeah, you know, it's an act.
Jonah, didn't J. C. Heard come in that band?
Yeah, he come in after Cozy left.
Oh, he did.
Yeah, Jay come in. It was when Buster Hardin wrote that drum solo for him called, 'Wild Man's Dream.' And then Buster stayed in for quite a while.
Buster played piano in the band?
Yeah. Buster only played when we used two pianos.
Oh, I see.
See, in a picture or something like that. If another piano around was on the stage, Buster would be around
with the band, you know.
He played sort of an arranger's piano, didn't he? I mean he didn't play --

Yeah, not too much of a soloist, you know. Just arranger's piano. Maybe you'll see him in that picture, "Sensations of '44," where they've got one piano over there, another one over there. One's Dave Rivera and one is Buster. That's when Illinois Jacquet was in the band. See, when Chu died, we tried to get a tenor player, so we got Mac Rae, who was going to Canada, and when Chu got killed coming out of Youngstown. He was going to the Peace Bridge, going to Canada. I'll never forget that night. See, and they used to -- there was Lamarr and Brownie [Andrew Brown] He was the third alto player. He'd been one of the originals. And Chu, playing a little town like Youngstown, they wouldn't get in the bus. They had to use a bus to get there, so they would go into Cleveland and stay around, fool around all day, you know, say hello to the guys there, and they'd come in and play the job, in time for the job, you know. Well, there were three of them, and so they were driving. I think it was Lamarr's car. So this night, the last night, there were two of them over here, getting ready to put up the car, put the car away. We're going to -- we're going into Peace Bridge and then into Toronto. So they start out in front. And we get about a few miles down the road, and there's been light rain, you know, and then we see an automobile turned over,

and Cab said, "Man, there was an accident up there. Now I guess we'll be held up here for who can tell how long," not thinking it was them, you know. And the closer we got up on them -- because Cab always rode up front, and he said, "Man, that looks like Chu laying out there," you know. And he says it is. We stopped the bus and all of us jumped out, and we got him, you know, picked him up. He was laying there. His head was bashed in back here on the side. And his pipe was broken in about three places. And Brownie was setting up on the bridge, one of those bridges you go into like that, and you go around like that, you know. Well, when he went to make that turn he started to skid and hit against the side, you know, and turned over. So by the time we got him up all Choo was saying was, "Lift my hand. Hold my hand up." I guess he was out of his head. By the time we got him up to the bus, we was going to take him into Conneaut, Ohio, which was about 12 miles, you know, and the ambulance was coming. We heard it coming. So then we took him out and held him till the ambulance came, and then we put him in the ambulance and took him on in, and Cab would call back every day and check him out, and they would always say -- well, this was a Monday morning, so they said, "He didn't regain consciousness yet." Tuesday, the same thing. Wednesday -- and he'd tell us, you know, because we'd be playing one nighters. Toronto, Kitchener, London, Ontario, and different places. And we got to Montreal about Thursday. After we finished playing on

that Thursday, he said, "Well, Chu died. I didn't want to tell you all before playing tonight, but Chu died today." Oh, man, talk about a drag. And we sent and got MacRae, you know, to fill in for him. So then Mac Rae stayed awhile. But Chu had a nice book there, you know. He had practically everything.
It's an extraordinary thing it would have to be somebody like Chu, isn't it?
Yes. Just seems impossible almost, you know.
Yeah. And a big career ahead of him.

And here comes Illinois Jacquet. Here comes the wrecking crew starting in now. He's had gentlemen in the band all the time had been pretty good. Now they get Illinois Jacquet. Well, "Flying Home" Illinois - this thing. Everybody owns it. Hamp says it's his. Arnett Cobb says it's his, Illinois says it's his. So he comes in the band. So now you've got to make "Flying Home" for him. But Jacquet comes in arguing. "I've got to have something to play, Cab." "I ain't going to sit there like that, like Shad and Jonah and them other guys that don't play nothing. I've got to have something to play." You know. So they made him a number -- Buster made an arrangement, called, "Rhythm Cocktail," which is only "Flying Home," you know, with the same solo they used. You know, same thing. So he goes on with this for about six, seven, eight months. Finally Cab said, "Rhythm Cocktail," is out. Jacquet said, "Oh, no. That's it. I'm giving him my notice. That's it. That's it. 'Rhythm Cocktail' is out, I give my notice in." So they went

in the room and talked and everything, and then finally they come out, and "Rhythm Cocktail" was back again. But no sooner than he got a chance, you know, they found somebody, you know, like Sam Taylor, Quebec, you know, Ike, out he went. He wouldn't let you hold no stick over his head, you know. I think that was mostly the reason why the guys didn't play much, like Johnny with Duke and Lawrence Brown and them, because he didn't want that to get out of hand to where he wasn't in control. I think he felt like Duke wasn't in control of the thing, you know, with Ben and them.
At the mercy of the guys.

Yeah. You know, like a guy wanted to take a solo, and then everybody was going to be asking for them, you know. And that was a drag for him, you know. He was the big -- this is Cab, Cab Calloway, you know. Sure. So he made it when he had less talented musicians, you know. But he liked to have good ones around him all the time. He liked to brag you about the band, you know. He liked the people to brag about it, you know.
Yeah.
You know, when I did some interviews with some of Basie's guys, like Snooky Young, I don't think Basie liked them very much....
Yeah, could be.
because you'll see an article in Down Beat where they'd say "a little more money."
Yeah, well that's it too, see? That's it too. See the guy wakes up to how great he is, you know. He

wakes up. Just like the drummer we're having trouble with now, see. I think one of them must have told him, "Cozy was getting this. Cozy was getting so and so." Because Sammy said, I don't have anything to do with it. So the guy's a good drummer, beautiful, you know, and what he did, he said, "Sammy, ain't I worth as much as Cozy? Don't I do as good a job as Cozy." He said, "Yeah, but who knows you?" And all that, you know. I don't know from that. Keep that away from me, you know. So the guy got a little ticked off about it, you know. Because he was doing a hell of a job. Doing a hell of a job, you know. And then Sam don't think like musicians, you see. He thought about -- we asked Basie over there, I think it was in the Hague or something. "We've got a drummer that used to play with you." Because this guy's -- all the different guys he's played with, you know, Count Basie and --
Who is he?
Clyde Lucas is his name.
Oh, yeah.

And he says -- so, you know, Sammy finds out things, he went and told Basie, "We've got a drummer that used to play with you," you know. He says, "What's his name?" "His name's Clyde Lucas." He says, "I don't know about it. Maybe he did." You know, he said, "Guys come and go. I don't care who's there." You know. Let's go and play "One O'clock Jump."
(Laughter)

But sure, you see, the thing about these guys, they get up a little bit, you know, if they're featured, then they want more bread, like Johnny. You know Johnny always wanted more bread. And different other guys wanted more bread too, you know. Everybody wants more. Even the leader wants more, you know. But there has to be a stopping point somewhere, and you've got a big band like that, it gets pretty expensive.
Well, of course one of the troubles was that they would not keep their mouths shut when they got more.
No, they'd tell the other guys. Yeah, then here he comes, you know.
That's right.

Sure. It's just like the drummer. He comes in and he says, "Now, how do you know what Cozy was getting?" And he knows just what he was getting. He said, "I should get as much as Cozy." You know, right away, he starts to make a thing about it. So he'd have to wind up giving it to him.
well. He got a very good piece.
I think Johnny over the years did get his up very well.
Well, he should. He should have.
He deserved it.

That was the greatest band I ever heard in my life. It went on through the years, and they're bringing guys like Lawrence Brown. And before Lawrence, Tricky and Tizol, you know. And they bring in Lawrence Brown. That was a big asset. That was in 1932. Everybody was wondering who

is this trombone coming, you know. That was all through the music circles, whether you was in New York or not. They were saying, 'Lawrence Brown? Who did he play with?' So we had a record that he had made out there with a guy in California. We was in Buffalo at this time, but we had this record. We said yeah, this guy can get over with that horn, you know. So -- and with men in there like Barney Bigard. Where are you going to get a man like that? Or -- and the baritone, Harry Carney.
Carney, yeah.

This guy was the band. This was the cushion. What give it that sound. I still thought there was a possibility, after Mercer had kept -- you know, after Carney was still there, I said, well, it's a chance, you know, with Carney, with that bottom still there, and maybe he can build something from there, you know. So -- but now all of them's gone. All of them's gone. So I think -- I think he would have made the biggest change in the band there ever was, if Carney had come out before the rest of them, had he left first, you know. Because if you listen to them records you hear that baritone moving through there, and you hear -- like you're on a cushion or something.
Yeah. Well, especially the way he wrote for the --
Yeah, the way he wrote for that thing. Oh, God, what a band.
Yeah.
Well, when did you eventually leave Cab, then?

I left Cab -- my last engagement was at Birdland, around about February or March or something like that, that was the last. Because we had reorganized again and made the -- after having the four pieces we had raised it back up to a big band again, which we went down to Uruguay, Montevideo, and played all down in there, you know, for the carnival, you know. And so he had had the guys, Doc Cheatham come back, and different guys he had, and Shad and all of them. And Ike, Ike Quebec, and Sam, you know, Sam the man Taylor. And Jeff.
Did Ike Quebec and Sam the Man sort of do any battling, you know, like Basie's two tenors, or --

I think on one number there. They weren't featured too much, but I think they had one number. But there was an argument down there too, because they would come to me and tell me, because Cab a lot of the time would come to me and say, "We're going to enlarge the band again. So who do you think," you know? So I'd always ask for Shad. A lot of guys didn't like Shad, because Shad would keep you upset. See, he was one of them kind of guys, he wouldn't speak all day. He'd come in and he wouldn't say a word, you know, but he played good. I like the way he plays, you know. And I liked him, so I'd get him. But they'd say, "What are you bringing him for all the

time?" Evil, you know. Oh, don't pay him no mind. He'd come in in the morning, go up there and sit down and never say a word, you know. Go out, eat, come back, second show, not a word, third show, not a word, fourth show -- by the middle of the fourth show he'd say, "Let's hang out tonight."
That's funny.

"Let's hang out tonight," he said. And then if we would go and hang out, he'd say, "Okay." You know, that was always all right. Anything to get along, you know. So now we go somewhere, some bar or something, on 47th Street or somewhere, fooling around, and DuSable, -- drinking and having fun, and he'd say, "Man, I'm sorry the way I acted today." I'd say, "Oh, pay it no mind, man. You don't feel like talking, don't talk, you know, what the heck. You give me a good rest. I didn't feel like talking either." But another habit he had when you made a bad note, he'd always take his mo knock on his derby, and sit back and sit back and look like he did nothing, you know, or you'd run the wrong the chord, he would sit back, knock on the derby, and nobody liked that. It got everybody nervous. Because Jeff, a nice boy, you know, Jeff was a nice fellow.
I know he was.
And Jeff was up there and he'd be playing, like, "Danny Boy" or something, and maybe he'd make a little bad --
T52V
Well, now, about leaving Cab. What made you make up your mind to leave him?
Well, he disbanded. He says, "We can't go on any longer because we're not guaranteeing. We don't get the guarantee we used to." See, we used to get something like 1,500 guarantee with a percentage.
Yeah.
You know, after they got -- because the theaters were beginning to close.
Yeah.
And that's why he disbanded in the first place, when he cut down the band to seven and then to four.
Yeah.

Then we had a chance to go to South America, to enlarge the band, and so he said he couldn't get the guarantee. Well, everything was covered, the transportation and the salaries. So he decided, rather than to gamble, just to cut out altogether and go as a single.
Yeah.
But then I laid around, doing -- well, where we're sitting now -- used to be Eddie Condon's downtown.
Yeah.
So I'd come down there and play with Eddie and them, you know. Whoever he had regularly would be off, so

he'd call me and ask would I do it. There was another guy named Bob, had a place across the street, on 2nd Avenue over here. Oh, Jack Crystal had a place called -- I forget the name -- but anyhow, I used to play down there on Friday and Saturday. Sometimes he'd use Charlie and Red Allen and different trumpet players, you know. So then Joe Bushkin called me one day and says, "I'm going into the Embers for six weeks." I could go in with him. I said, "Oh, Joe, I just finished playing with a big band, and I don't know if I can go in a small group anymore."
You were afraid you couldn't be blowing all that much?
Yeah, be blowing all night you know, with one horn.
That's right.
You know, if there had been another horn or something.
It's tough on the lip, even.

Yeah. If there had been another horn or something. So he said, "Look, don't worry about it. Just go on down with me," he says. You know how Joe is. "Don't worry about it." He says -- and you had to play with a mute in there. So I says, "Well, okay, let me think it over." And then he calls back again and he says, "I'll tell you what. Come on by the house. I'd like you to meet Fran." That's his wife.

I'd never met her. So they was living on the east side somewhere, so I went over. "Bring your wife." We went over and fooled around with them, and had snacks, and he'd play his horn awhile and then I'd play awhile, and play the piano. So he says, "I ain't worried about it. Don't you worry about it." And I said, "Now, don't expect too much out of me over there." He said, "Look, I ain't even worried, so don't you worry." All right, we opened up, we did good. We had Charlie Mingus there on bass, Jo Jones on drums, myself and Bushkin. So now --
Would Bushkin give Mingus any time to play or anything?

I don't think he gave him enough. I don't think he gave him enough, because Mingus one day Mingus come in and he put in his notice and he said, "I'm going over to the Downbeat with Billy Taylor." And so Bushkin had to find a bass player. So I tell Bushkin about I've got a man for him. Nobody knew him around here at that time, Milt Hinton. I said, "I've got a man named Milt Hinton." You notice you never heard him play anything till he got out of Cab's band. Well, I'm the one that got him started with Bushkin. He got a chance to come out and see him. So I said, "I've got a bass player." He said, "Who did he play with?" I said, "He played with Cab." He said, "Oh, no, I ain't heard nobody in there yet --," you know, Bushkin said, "I ain't heard nobody there playing nothing."

He said, "I come by the band and heard him when he was in Birdland. I didn't hear too much." I said, "Look, this guy's a good bass player. He can play any way. He can play -- he can play just with the left hand, and all that stuff," and that's what Joe liked. He liked the bass player to play the same things in his left hand. So he was a little reluctant about it, so I said, "Well, look try him. Tell him to come down one night. I'll tell him to come down one night, and that's it, you know." So he said, "Okay." He's your friend, okay. So I told Milt. I called him and told him, and I says, "Now, don't try to play too much. Just play whatever Joe's playing in his left hand." Because I'd seen Milt do that before, you know. So he said, "You know I can do that." So I said, "Okay. I'm just trying to put you on guard, you know." So -- because he didn't know who Buskin was, you know, because he come out of Chicago with Cab, and he didn't know nobody around town much, you know. So he come in there, and we finished that engagement, and he did such a wonderful job and Bushkin loved him so, he refused to even make an album unless Milt could get off to do it, wherever he was working. He refused to make that. I saw him one day, maybe a year or two after that, and I said, "What are you doing in town?" And he said, "Well, I come in to make an album, but Milt's busy." I said, "Milt's busy? What does that have to do with it?" He said, "I ain't making that album unless I can get Milt on it." I said, "Remember when I told you back there,
years ago, and you said, "Bring him in one night?" He said, "Yeah,." (Unintelligible). So then everybody had a chance to hear him in there, you know, and he got a chance to get over here and --
Yeah. He got exposure.
Yeah, you know, and people got to know him and in a year's time he was making all the records and stuff.
Yeah.

You know, doing everything. So Bushkin still gets him. They did that thing with Bing Crosby, the last Bing Crosby show, they went out there, flew out there with -- Bushkin had them come out, and they taped you know.
Yeah.
So -- then after I did that six weeks, then Fatha was getting a band together. He was getting a group together.
What year would this be?
This is the same year, '52.
Yeah.

The first of that year was Cab broke up. A little later in the year, about the spring, I went with Bushkin. And then a little later in the spring I went with Fatha. And that's when we had Art Blakey and Harold on tenor, and myself, and Tommy Potter and Benny Green and Fatha, and Ella Jones. So then we played along with this for awhile, and
I kind of liked the band, you know. And the money wasn't bad, you know.
What kind of spots were you working?

Oh, we were working at things like the Palomar Supper Club in Vancouver, and a place called the Capital Lounge, which was downtown Chicago, right across the alley from the Chicago Theater. And we played like at the Colonial Tavern in Toronto. And that type of thing. And the Oasis in Los Angeles. We'd go there and stay six weeks in the Oasis, you know.
What kind of things was Earl playing?
Well, we were playing -- well --
Was that when you said you were saying to him, "Don't play all that modern stuff?"

Well, what he was doing, he was trying to play like Monk and them, see, I think. And we asked 'what do you want to do?' And then after -- see, the thing was Art Blakey left and Harold left, because they was two good friends. That was the tenor player. They left, so we got Aaron Sachs in his place and we got Osie Johnson in Art's place. Now, Osie knows something about them chords you know, so he would have Earl's fingers bending way over there, and he'd say, "See, that's it." He's showing Earl, and Earl, he's trying to do it too, and people coming up there and asking for '57 varieties, Fatha.'
(Laughter)
"Monday Date." "You Can Depend on Me." You know? And Fatha'd say, "I ain't playing that old stuff." And Fatha's coming with those flatted fifths and things.
(Laughter)

You know. And I'd say, "Look, if people are going to come here you'll play this the rest of your life." "No, I ain't playing it." I said, "Well, look. I'll play them. Just lend them to me. I'll do them. When people come up and ask for it, I'll do it." So I sang, "Monday Date," and, "Depend on Me." I couldn't do "57 Varieties," because that's strictly a piano thing. But I couldn't see a man that didn't like to play his own stuff that made him, you know.
But we had a nice thing. And whatchamacallit was taking -- Aaron Sachs was taking his wife along, Helen Merrill is her name.
Oh, yeah. Right, I know her.
Well, they have a kid. The kid was very small then, about a year old or something, because we'd all take turns carrying him in our arms, if we were on a plane.
No kidding. Really?

So now what he does, he's got some heck of an ideas, Earl has, and he would get us singing together. He'd have Eddie, me and Benny Green over here, have Eddie in the middle, and then he'd have Helen Merrill over here, in the middle, and Aaron Sachs, and Aaron, Aaron would be there, and

Tommy Potter, and then we'd be singing, (Singing), "Beside a shady nook --," it was something nice. It sounded nice. But Helen isn't even on the payroll. She's just going along with Aaron, you know. "Come on," they'd say to her. We didn't have no room for two singers. We had Etta Jones. But he put her in there, because she'd do that one number, you know.
(Laughter)
(Singing) "Beside a shady --," he had some ideas, you know.
He was thinking of a production...
Yeah, production type of stuff. And it would go over nice. Once, you know, not too much.

When I first talked with him he was playing all the time he's "Lullaby of Birdland" by George Shearing, "Canadian Sunset" by Eddie Heywood, playing the medley of peer piano players "Satin Doll," by Duke, and so forth. And I said the same thing. I said, "Why the hell don't you play your own things?"

It's funny. It's a funny thing. He thinks they're too old, you know? He's got to think that, because a man can't go along all the time and never fall back on things and wake up and say, "This is me. I did this. I wrote it. I set this up." You know, through the years. People know me by this thing, you know. But he'd say, "Oh, man, I'm not going to play them." And I said, "Okay, give them to me." So I'd play them and it was good band, I liked it.
How long were you with it?

Oh, I guess I stayed in there, oh, about six months, because the next year -- see, I stayed in there, say, from about April. Maybe a little longer than that. April to -- I think it was around April I went in there. From April to about January or February, when "Porgy and Bess" was getting ready to open up, because Cab had wrote me a letter when we was in California at the Oasis, asking me. Or another place we played with Earl called -- at Bush and Powell, The Hangover. It was Doc Dougherty's place. We played out there. And that's before he went out and become a house band there. Two or three years later he went back and stayed there. But we -- Cab had wrote me he was doing Sportin' Life. He wrote me a letter asking me would I be interested in playing in the pit band for "Porgy and Bess", at the Ziegfeld Theater, when the show opens up there. So I wrote him back and told him yes, you know. It was a challenge, like I told you at the beginning. I was taught to read, you know, pretty good. So I said yes. So he told me, "Well, I'm trying to get about eight men." He said they've got about 40 pieces, they're going to use about 40 pieces in the pit band, "and I'm trying to get at least eight blacks in there." So I went to Smallens already who was conducting the show, and I asked him did he object to having black musicians in the band. But Smallens said, "No, I don't care what color they are as long as they can read my music and play my music right." So Cab said, "All right, I have some men I like." I imagine he had

Milt in mind, and somebody else, you know. But when you got back here, when the show got back -- now we -- I'm still with Earl while this is going on, and what Earl is doing, he starts me out at a salary -- he started me out at 250.00. Well, I was happy because I liked to play with Earl and I liked his piano and everything, and I can make both ends meet then, you know. So now he comes up and he says, "Well, I'm going to have to cut you 25.00." So I said okay. I said it was kind of rough on me, and so and so, but I still like it. And now this makes me think more of the thing of "Porgy and Bess" thing, you know. And we were out in California then, so Benny Green comes in and he says, "Did you get a cut?" I said yeah, and he said, "I did too, you know." So what the heck, I said, it's still pretty good, you know. It's not bad.

So then, when we get to Chicago, he says, "I'm going to have to cut another 25.00." So I says, well, okay, what can I say, you know. Then we left Chicago, the Capital Lounge, and we're coming into Snookey's on 46th Street, and so "Porgy and Bess" is getting ready -- is back in town, they're getting ready to open, and so I gave my notice. I told him that 200.00 -- because things had started going up now, you know. I said, "$200.00, I can't make it on that with the taxes and things, and I've got a chance to go down here in a show where I can sit down here for awhile, I can rest." So I went over there and so we rehearsed the show. No, we went in, and now it's a

big argument. The union about with the contractors. See, all them shows down there, theaters, they have contractors, and some guys has got four and five shows under his arm you know, contracting. Now, he passes these things -- jobs out, to guys that he knows and guys that have did things for him, you know.
Yeah.
See, you've got to know what you're doing.
Patronage.

Yeah, this type of thing. And we never knew too much about the pit at that time, you know, back in '53. So Dick Vance had been working, you know, a guy named ? who would hire him every now and then. He was about the first guy I know to work in a pit band. So that was way before this. And so they took this thing to the union, and they had a guy named Morris Stonzik (PHONETIC). He's got the show. He's got the Winter Garden, he's got the Ziegfeld and a lot of others. So now the thing comes, run head on until it hits the top man in the union, and they say, "Cab wants eight men." Stonzik says, "Who's the contractor, me or Cab?" "You know, Cab's an actor in the show. I'm the contractor." So finally they argued so much about it until it reached a compromise. Use four. Use four out of the 40. So all right, I was there, Buster Bailey, a guy named Al Brown played the viola. Very good. He was only 19 at the time, you know, but just out of Julliard. It was beautiful. The other viola players was crazy about --
What happened to him?

Huh? He's still around now. He's a contractor now. Sure, I run into him every now and then. He's a contractor. We reminisce about that. And we had another guy, now, that's playing in the Radio City Music Hall pit, named Winston Collimore. Those two I didn't know before. I knew Buster but I didn't know these two.
Cab knew them, huh?
No, not Cab. These come from another source. See, the guys that Cab got was me. Now, I don't know, Buster might have come around some way else. I don't know, come through Cab or what, you know.
Yeah.
Then these other guys was probably picked -- maybe they didn't want the guys that Cab wanted, you know.
Yeah.
Because he's got to show he's running this thing.
Yeah.
So these guys were picked by some other people.
Yeah, I understand. Yeah.
Because you never know what's goin on, with 40 pieces there, you know. You don't know what's going on over here, you know.
No.

Everything -- everybody's in here. So now I go to rehearsal and I play, and I found out, well, I've got to brush up a little. I've got a little 20 year old Jewish boy, Don Reinberg, I'll never forget him. This guy could play the thing down like he'd been playing it for years. He just got out of the Army, and his father was a cellist in Seattle -- no, in San Francisco. And he could play this legit music, oh, God. He'd run down it, and he'd get a little frightened on the high notes, but otherwise, he was straight. But what happened is -- he was a wonderful kid. I used to take him around with me at night, because I got so that playing that thing every night, it's beautiful, and you hear beautiful music every night, but you start to wonder if I can play jazz anymore, you know?
Yeah.

And then I would go out. Sometimes I would go and sit in with Earl, over on 46th, at Snookie's. You know, just when I'd get off, when the show let out. The let out at 11:15, and I'd take him with me. And he couldn't understand that. Don Reinberg would say, 'I can't understand how you can walk into another band like that, close your eyes and start playing 'Stardust,' with no music or nothing.' And he said, 'Them notes that you play all night, how do you think them things up?' See, he never played any jazz or anything. Everything was just legit, you know, and stuff. And he enjoyed that. And right now, if he sees I'm playing somewhere and that
band is travelling, coming through town, he'll stop by to see me and say hello, or else he'll leave a note in my box.
Jonah, where was Snookie's on 46th?
46th Street close to 6th Avenue. I don't know what it's called now, but it was closer to 6th Avenue than it was 7th.
The north or south side?

On the south side. So we went in there and he got a change around, he got a trumpet player -- and I forget his name now, but I think this fellow had played with him before. Oh, I liked Earl. I liked the way he played, you know. I liked the way he played behind you, you know, and stuff. I'd never played with a piano player that played like that before. A whole handful of notes, you know, and you could hear everything. And now I get in here, so I stay -- I stay in there for a year. The show runs for a year. At first the guy's on me, I can tell while I'm sitting there. Stonzik is the cello player, he's the one that's the contractor. There's about three or four cellos back there, and I remember once -- you know, after you play about six months you know the music, you know. So I had my book laying down on the floor. I didn't have to pick it up. So finally the drummer's name was Grubb. And he says --
Morris.
Yeah, Morris. I think it was Morris Grubb.
I think so. He played with the Philadelphia Symphony.
Yeah.

Yeah, with him. He plays everything, chimes, bells, marimbas and tom-toms and kettle drums and everything. He's got a whole space there, big as this room, for him, down in the pit. And he said, "Don't let him catch you with that book laying on the floor." And Stonzik says, "What? Get that book off the floor and put it back on the rack." See, you had to put it up there and play like you were reading it anyhow. See, you have to put it up there and look at it and turn pages anyhow, whether you know it or not. You know, that's the way -- that's one of their things. And another thing, you have to learn these little things they have, like when you go in there you get the A from the English horn player. He was from NBC and he played the English horn and the oboe. You'd take your A from him. Now, after you play along for a half hour, the heat from the people's bodies warms up everything in the theater, and it also makes the strings go up. So now you've got to find a place in there to get you another A. Not much, but just up a little, or else you don't do that and they know you don't belong in there, you know. Because you've got to find this place without everybody knowing it. Now, after that half hour's up, intermission. Throw open the doors and everybody goes out. Now, they come back and you get another A. See, start over again. And then after a half hour --
It happens again.
You get another one. You find another one somewhere, because the heat from the bodies makes it --
Well, how do you find another one? What do you do?
Well, you listen real close. You listen real close, and especially if you see the other trumpet player do it, you come up. You pick you out an instrument in there, you know --
You're going to tune to it.
And you do it where nobody will know it, nobody can hear it, not even hardly in the band, you know.
Yeah.

So we come out of that thing, and he liked me so much after that. Stayed in there a year and the guy looked like he just hated us before, you know. Oh, God, he just hated us. And you know after that he was calling here all the time. "Where can I get a trumpet player that's going to carry himself like you guys in the pit?" And, "Where can I get -- I need a banjo player, or I need a guitar."
That's progress really, in a way, isn't it?
Yeah, you know. I never worked for him again. And so --
But that opened his eyes.

Yeah, uh-huh. He called me back many a time for another show, you know, but then I was doing something else, because after that closed, then Delaunay [Charles] was writing to me all the time about come over, and [Hugues] Panassie was saying don't come. Because Panassie was supposed to be my boy. And so he was giving me the writeups and things.
And he didn't want you to --

He was giving me writeups when I was back with Louis Armstrong, and when he was featuring me as Louis II, he was giving me the writeups too, you know. He was sending them Hot Clubs of France books and I'd never met him, you know. Then he come, when I moved to New York he come over, and so we had him up to a big chicken dinner thing, and Madeleine was talking about that this year, you know. He said, "I never yet tasted chicken like you cooked it." We killed him up here, you know. It was quite some time ago. So he was asking me to come over, and Pernassi was saying no. Not putting you with the right group. But anyhow, I wrote back to him, I told him anything he's offering me, and he's guaranteeing me this, you know, for six weeks -- no he's guaranteeing for four weeks. That meant I played the week of the festival at the Salle Pleyel. Now, he had to pay me three weeks' money whether he got something for me or not over there, you know. And I was by myself. Gerry Mulligan had his band, with Bob Brookmeyer and Mitchell and them, and Monk was by himself. So he got me a band named Andre Rivialte and

1 French discographer, author-compiler of Hot Discography. 1st edition 1936.
2 French jazz critic-historian, author of Jazz Hot; editor of Jazz Hot.

I laid off a week and he paid me just the same. Then the next two weeks I worked at the Olympic Theater there, downtown, Boulevard des Capucines. And I went in there, and this was something I'd never seen before. All kinds of acts, the show going on for hours, horses and everything on the stage. And I'm closing the bill. I said, "What is this?"
(Laughter)

I peeped out the curtain to see if the people were still there. I said, "I know these people aren't going to stay around here all this time, waiting for me." And they stayed there. They stayed for about a four hour stage show, four hours, horses and things was running up and down and doing somersaults and stuff, and then here I come out. Here I come out with "Struttin'" with Some Barbecue." I didn't know whether to run or stay there. But they were really enjoying it. You know, they stayed there. Oh, it was great, you know.
You've got good reviews?
[Bechet]

Yeah, beautiful. And Sidney come in next. He come in after me, and you know, he just packed that thing. He just packed it. And now he says, "Now I want you to go down in Belgium." He sent me down there to Cornat la Zee for 10 weeks at the same salary, which was a pretty good salary. Better than I ever got here.
You didn't go home. You stayed --
No, I stayed. Stayed after the theater.

Stephane Grappelli was nice. I had another week off which, after the two weeks I did there. That was really finishing all that he had promised me, the four weeks. I had another week off. Stephane Grappelli got a picture together. He got a picture and he got me in there to make the records. We made the records for the picture and everything. And you know, they take their time over there. At least at that time they did. And instead of them shooting the picture, they're going to shoot the picture later. They'll let you know when they get ready to shoot the picture. So when they got ready to shoot the picture, I was on my way in Belgium, you know. And so it just happened that Ray Robinson come in town. And oh, he's got this big entourage with him, and June Clark happened to be with him. And it looked like they was giving him short money or something, so I would take him to dinner while I was there, you know.
Take who, June?

June, yeah. Well, June had been around a long time, and he had it rough. He was just like one of the hangers on, you know. He was used to having all this money they'd give him to eat off of and stuff. I said, 'Don't worry about that.' I was taking him francs and stowing them away in the safe deposit box in the hotel, because I found out what to do. Now, you take all this stuff, all these francs. The francs was a whole lot. You got a whole lot of francs for a dollar, you know, and take it to Belgium and send it right on
over here. See, you couldn't take it out of France.
Oh, I see.
But I could take it to Belgium and they change it up for you and send it right here, and the next morning she would have it.
How about that.

But all the records I did over there, and when I got paid, I just sent it to Belgium because I was going there anyway, so I did that. And when we got to Belgium, we stayed there 10 weeks. It was nice, beautiful. With this same band, Andre Rialte, and Guy Leon was playing the trumpet, and we had a wonderful time. And I met King Farouk there and we had a big argument with him about the -- he wanted me to have champagne. The waiter came and said, 'The King would like for you to have a drink.' And I didn't even know him. He said have a drink with him, so I said okay. I was drinking that Heineken's over there, so I said a draft, so he said okay, and I went over there and I said, 'Bring me a glass of Heineken's.' He said, 'Heineken's? Bring him champagne.' I said, 'I don't want no champagne. I drink beer, you know.' He said, 'Oh, beer. Champagne.' I said, 'Look, you asked me to have a drink. You want me to have a drink.' The waiter said, 'Go ahead and have champagne. That's King Farouk.' I said, 'I don't care who he is. I drink beer. I don't drink champagne. I've got another show to do.' So he said, 'Okay, bring him beer.' So

he brought me a thing of beer, you know, and then the next day he called me at the hotel about 10:00 o'clock in the morning. Another run-in. I said, "Who is this?" I don't get up till about 1:00, you know. So he said, "This is Farouk." I said, "What do you want, man, at this time of the morning?" He said, "I've got a cabana down here," on the thing. Wanted me to come down and get some sun and everything. I said, "I'll be down about 2:00 o'clock." He said, "No, come down now." I said, "No, uh-uh. I can't come down until 1:00 o'clock." So then I told the lady, I said, "Don't wake me up till 1:00 o'clock. That goes for every day, you know." Mrs. Simmons. She was nice woman. And I went down about 2:00 o'clock. He had the cabana there and he had me a little keg of beer, sitting in the bucket of ice. And I really enjoyed that gig, you know, and people got so they liked me around there, was giving parties, a little town, you know. And people would give a party for me, a Jonah Jones party, you know. I met people and got real intimate with them, and they wanted to know about Jackie Robinson, and why didn't they allow you to play baseball in America, you know. And I said, "They played baseball but they had their own leagues," and Jackic is not the first to play baseball. He's the first to get in the American Leagues, you know, to integrate it. So you have to go through all of that with them, because they want to know about all of that.
Then after that I come back, and now they're trying to
get me to go down to The Cave. This was where Bill Coleman worked, where Andre was working. It's where I heard Andre on the piano, and where Peanuts works and another guy named Nelson Williams.
Well, you'd better put that name in there.
So Nelson Williams --
Ray Persiani (PHONETIC).
Oh, yeah, Andre Persiani.
You just said Andre.

Andre Persiani, yeah. So now, I liked it very much, but the same woman that runs this place -- well, in the first place the guys were getting a bit peeved. Nelson said, "Now, it is going to be awful over here now. I hear the woman wants you to come down here and work." I said, "Yeah, she found a sound -- but you all don't have to worry about it." "No," he says, "it's too many, man. She'll be getting us for nothing pretty soon. Everybody she brings in, she'll get you cheaper." I said, "Well, I have a price, and Delaunay told me to set a price for these records and make no dates unless you get that price and don't go and play noplace else." Even Porgy and Bess was coming over there again, and the guys that was running it sent me a telegram, a long one. "Stay there and play and we'll give you the same salary that you got here." Uh-uh, I didn't want that over there, because that was less than Delaunay was giving me, see?
Yeah.

So I could have stayed over much longer, you know, because the show was coming back to Europe, and they wanted somebody that knew the show to play it, and they wouldn't have to worry, you know, about nothing.
That's right.

And I also knew the part on the stage that Howard Roberts had. You know, he had a trumpet part. He'd go out there and play a little jazz (Singing). Well, I would come out of the pit in the Ziegfield and go up on the stage and do that. And I even made them guys pay me for that, because they come up and said, 'Can you do that?' I said, 'Yeah.' He said, 'Well, okay, we'll give you $25.00 more.' I said, 'Uh-uh. You can get Bill Dillard. He can do that.' I knew they had got to pay him scale, you know. And finally they said, '50.00.' Finally they said, '75.00.' Finally they come up and Cab -- asking Cab, 'Can he go up there and play it?' He said, 'Yeah, there ain't nothing to it. He can do that with his eyes closed.' So I went up on the stage and Cab [said] 'Go on out there and blow that same thing you used to blow.' So I went on up there and did that. So I was getting almost double salary down there, you know. So that's what I wanted over there. So they wouldn't come up on that, so I just come on back home. Come on back, and it was a great thing, you know, 10 weeks there and 4 weeks there, and I enjoyed it and got out before I'd have to go in The Cave and play where they're going to cut you five dollars and the next guy, they're going to cut him five more, and the

next -- uh-uh. So Delaunay had told me everything, you know, that's how come I like him so much. Said, "Don't be going out there and working cheap and everything, because you come over here, you get straight, go on home. That's where so many of them make a mistake. Go home, and then when you come back again, maybe you can get your money again. But if you stay here it's got to go down." I wound up helping some of them guys out over there.

Then I come back, things are very bad. I see Lips Page, he's playing for the political thing, you know, going up Seventh Avenue. I walk down Seventh Avenue, here's Bushell and all of them, Johnny Letman and Lips and everybody, and I'm up there looking, because I've been so high over there, you know. Over there I was an artiste, you know.
Yeah.

Getting invitations to the Painters' Exposition and stuff. Bill Coleman said, "What's this? I ain't going to this." He said, "Go to that. Be sure you don't miss that." So he was getting me straight. But I got back and things was really bad then. It was the end of '54. And I'm thinking about getting a job, because are getting up in size, so I said I have to have something coming in regular. So I had nothing but this little thing where we were going to Rochester and play. So we'd do that on the weekend. That was 250, and she'd pay your way down. Jan Morey, down at Ridgcrest, in Rochester. So she'd have one guy to come. She already had a rhythm section
there. So that wasn't nothing. You do that one week, then you had to wait another month or two before you'd go again.

So I run into Sammy on Broadway, Sammy Burke. And Sammy Burke said, "What you doing?" I said, "Well, things are kind of rough. I don't know, I'm thinking about getting a day job and working on the weekend, just playing my horn." Because I'd been playing with Lester Lanin, too, and Meyer Davis, and me and Urbie Green , you know, we played along with the big band, then we'd come down in front and do, "Basin Street," or, "I Got Rhythm," or something, while the band was on intermission. And it paid pretty good. When they were working, you know. Around the holidays was the best time. And so Sammy says, "Well, I'll tell you what --,"
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

P R O C E E D I N G S
Well, I was walking -- yeah, I was walking down the street --
All right, now hold it a second. There we go now.

So, you know, like everything else, a lot of people, what you do, somebody's going to say something against it. So I had -- so a lot of guys say, "Oh, Jonah's gone commercial," when records started to hit and things like that, you know. But I don't look at it like that. I look at it like I enjoyed doing what I was doing. I don't think I limited myself in any way in the records that I played. You know, like those things, "On the Street Where You Live," and, "Baubles, Bangles and Beads." I played them the best I could play them. I didn't know them. The chords wasn't something that I did all the time, like, "Georgia Brown," and stuff. So I heard some guys. I just wanted to clear that up.

Now we'll go back to how when we come back from Europe things were bad, and so now Lips Page and all those guys are playing, so Lips said, "I know all about that ______. I was there. I know all about France, so don't stand there and look at us. Just get your horn and come up here on this truck and get this 12.50 right along with us." (Laughter). You know how Lips is. He's crazy. And there we go and play to 145th Street, and then we'd go down to 135th Street and they would go

in front of the Theresa, you know. So I just couldn't get with it right away, you know. I had to wait. I knew I had to come in sooner or later, but I had to wait. So while I'm thinking about it, I get this contact down there with this lady in Rochester. That was nice. Paid your way down on the train, three days and back, you know, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. And that was -- kind of helped you a little bit. And with Lester Lanin and Meyer Davis and them, going out on gigs, and now I'm looking at this paper they called The Chief, I'm looking for a job, because I run into Ham Davis. This is another trumpet player. He played with Don Redmon. I don't know if you remember him.
I don't know him.
Ham Davis. You should know him, Stanley.
Yeah, I know him.

Been around a long time. From St. Louis. Played a good horn. And he had been -- got a job and he was living up in my neighborhood, so he was telling me that, "Look, you get this job in the tool room in one of the project houses, and you don't have to do nothing. All you have to do is set there, check the tools out to the super, he goes, he uses them, and he checks them back in to you." I said that's the kind of job I want, you know, so I looked and I saw -- I had one of these papers they called The Chief. He told me what to do, buy a paper. I had never heard of The Chief. Buy a paper called
* newspaper published by the Civil Employees, Inc. of Civil Service Commission.
The Chief and it'll tell you all about a job. Because he had a job, you know.

So in the meantime, I had this paper and looking at it, and so, fooling around down Broadway, you know, as usual, walking around seeing the different guys, you know, making a little record here and there. I forget the guy we made the records with. We were making a lot of stuff with Coleman Hawkins and Foots Thomas, who used to be with Cab, and Barefield, and all those. Joe something was his name. Put out a whole series of eight tracks there for awhile. I mean 78s. And I'm looking for something, looking around, and I recorded for Him sometimes on Keynote, and Commodore. And I happened to run into Sammy one day, Sammy Burke. He's the guy that was Irving Mills, who was I think the biggest agent around here at one time, you know. Sammy told me they had about 100 bands, Ina Ray Hutton, Larry Clinton, Duke and Cab and a whole host of bands. Clyde McCoy, and he was booking everything in there. So I run into him, and he says, 'Hey, how you doing,' you know. I knew him from Cab and I had seen him every now and then, when I was back in the '30s with --
Stuff.

Stuff, yeah. So now we get to talking on the street, and he like loves to walk up Broadway, at that time, anyhow. I walk with him, and he says, 'Look, you know what I'd like for you to do? I'd like for you to -- I was thinking you could get you a group together, I think about three pieces. Get

about four altogether. You and bass, piano and drums." He said, "Now, forget about the big bands. It's all over. Let me see what I can do for you." He said, "You've been a nice guy. I've been watching you for years. You always carried yourself nice and never got mixed up in the dope angle and you always tried to support your family. Let me see what I can do." At this time he's with Universal, with Ben Bart. So now he said, "Let me talk to Ben. Let me talk to Ben." So he called me and said, "Ben wants you to come down and talk to him." So I come down and Ben was asking me, "What are you doing?" And I named all the bands, like I told you, out west, and different stuff, and with Cab and Lunceford and Stuff and different groups, Benny Carter, and so he says, "Well, okay. Maybe you'll hear from me. I'll see what we can do here." So I says, "All right, I'd appreciate it." So I left, and then Sammy called me and said, "Oh, nothing happened." I said, "What happened?" He said, "He come in and said, 'That guy's been around too long. He'll be asking too many questions. That guy's been around. He should be working up here. He'll ask too many questions.'" So Sammy says, "I'm going to quit, and just handle you myself." And I thought this was real great, you know, right off, starting off.
Fancy that.
Right off, you know, he says, "I'm going to quit up there and just handle you myself, nobody but you."
And I said, "Well, I appreciate anything that you can come up with, you know."
What year was that?
So he's been doing this for 23 years.
23 years now, a little better, yeah, in June, was when he got me the first job.
What did he get you?

He'd been trying to get something, and I'd call him, you know, "Anything happen yet?" "No, just have something you can put your hand on. No use rehearsing. Have something you can put your hand on in case I come up with something." I said all right. I had the guys on the block there, Hal Austin the drummer, and the bass player, John Brown, and the piano player was named Bill Austin. He used to play with Louis Jordan. So now he says, "I'm waiting on a little something over in Jersey, you know." I said good. "I don't know what's going to happen but I'm working on it." So finally he come up with a thing, he says, "Look, can you get them guys together in two days?" I said yeah. He said, "I would like you to do one night in the Empress for Ralph Watkins. I talked to Ralph Watkins about you and Ralph said, 'Oh, yeah, I know Jonah. Yeah, he played for me when I was at Kelly's Stables, with Stuff.'" And so he said, "I'm going to put you in there one night and we'll take it from there." So I went and got John Brown and
these three guys I was telling you about, and I told them how to play the room, because I knew how to play it because I played there with Joe Bushkin.
Yeah.

And I knew they liked show tunes, you know, and I knew just about what show tunes and I knew if some tune was a new show there, it's a good idea to get a couple of numbers from that show and see what you can do with it. There's only so much you can do with four pieces, but do the best you can, you know, with the four. So we started to do that, went in there with that, and the people was telling him, "This is the greatest group you ever had in here. Bring them back again." So then Ralph said, "Would you like to have a week?" I said yeah. We went in a week and stayed in there 12 weeks. After six weeks Sammy said, "Now, I'm going to move in on him." So I said, "What do you mean?" And he said, "Well, I'm going to see about some bread." See we were getting scale in there, you know. I'm happy with the scale, you know, 214.00, the men getting 107.00. I'm happy, we went in there for one night and we go on for 12, you know.
All that exposure.

Yeah, but I'm just thinking about playing, you know, being able to play. But I am worried about the mute, because this did turn me around a little because I was known to have a strong tone and everything, and in the band, and in the

bands it's high, really, like when you play the first parts, you know, because I had a nice strong tone. Now I come and I've got to close all that up, cover it up, you know. So -- but I enjoyed it. I didn't -- you know, after I got used to what I was doing. I had to go to a teacher again. I had to go back to William Vachiano, who was the first trumpet player of the New York Philharmonic, and I told him what I was doing and what I was up under, you know, because it got so my lip was getting tired, you know, doing four shows with a mute.
Yeah.

And Bobby Hackett was saying, "I don't see how you do it." And I said, "Well, you shouldn't." He says, "After two shows I'm through." And I said, "Well, they shouldn't make you play with a mute, soft as you play."
Yeah.
But they had a thing in there about open horns, you know.
Yeah.

And Charlie Shavers played some of the best open horn you can hear -- I mean the best muted trumpet you'd ever hear, because he played it with John Kirby. But they didn't go for him too much. And somebody else went in there they didn't go for. See, a certain thing you had to do for them. It was an after theater crowd coming in there and you had to be ready for them, mostly.
Yeah.
And they wanted to hear a little show tune, you know, and they wanted to hear it nice and soft, where they could talk.
Yeah.

You know, they could talk. Yeah, sure. And you know what I used to do? I used to play and build it up, you know, and build it up, louder, and it would get louder, and then I'd drop way down, and they'd be way out there by themselves, you know, and they'd fall down. But they'd applaud when we'd finish up.
Who did you have in that first Embers group?

That's what I was telling you about. It was Harold Austin on the drums and John Brown -- no, I didn't. John had to go out of town. He was my man. But he went in on a Sunday night. Harold Austin, John Brown and Bill Austin, on a Sunday night with me. Now, when they give us the regular job, John had already committed himself to the midnighter, so I had that boy that played with Duke on bass. What was his name? What is his name? He's around him now.
[To Stanley Dance]
You know the guy. I've met him. He played with Red Howard one time. You met him not long ago, a few months ago, up at --
Slim fellow.
Yeah. The bass player. Used to be with Duke. You know the guy. He's got an odd name, like a French name, or something.
Yeah. I can't think of it.
Well, you know him. We met him up at Ruth Ellington's affair not long ago.
Oh, yes.
Well, it's right here in the book. I'll find it. Well, anyway, go ahead, Jonah.

Well, I had him the next Sunday. Then John come back and after we went out, we were going out of town, I put John in there, because I couldn't pay no money, you know, for going out of town. But Sammy moved in and talked to Ralph, because he come to find Ralph was living in the same house he was living in on Long Island. So they run into each other coming out. So they get to talking. So we got us a deal in there. A five year contract, 20 weeks out of a year, but you don't do it consecutively. You do like 5 now, and then when you go out and come back for your second five, you get a $50.00 raise. Well, I'm happy, you know. What the heck. So now I go out again, come back, $50.00 raise again. Out again, 50.00 again, you know. So you got $200.00 more on a year, you know, than your scale.
Yeah.
So now, not knowing that anything is going

to happen, I'm just as happy as I could be, you know, but Sammy, he's as busy as a bee, so finally he got an album for me, talked to his friend in -- I forget his name now. He was a big man with Victor. Died, he's dead now.
Eli Oberstein (PHONETIC)?
Steve Shoals (PHONETIC)?

No. Not Eli, another one. But I'd know it the minute I'd hear it, because he was a big man there, a big man. See, we went there and they put us on an album. Nobody knew us, so he put us on an album. What was the name of it? Groove. That was about third down. Victor, Vik and then Groove. So he put us on there, and that's where we made one side show tunes and one side Dixie tunes, you know. And nothing happened much, you know. The sound wasn't either, you know, they didn't blow it up and make it sound, which they do today. So the sound was a little bit flat. So now we keep playing. I'm glad to have that, you know. I'm glad to have that album. I've got a job and Sammy's picking up little things, and we'd go out of the Embers, like the guy was there from Cleveland, Mushy Wechsler (PHONETIC), and he wanted to know could he have us, you know. Said yeah, you know, so we went in there and worked for him, went out to Cleveland, and we worked in there for four weeks. The next time he wanted us for eight weeks, you know, did a pretty good job. And then we went into Detroit at Baker's Keyboard Lounge. Didn't do too good.
Why was that?

I don't know. We went into Baker's and nobody knew us much you know, and we went into Baker's. And George Shearing used to go in there and break it up. But we went in there for the first time, you know, and no records, but Jonah Jones at the Embers, and probably nobody played it out there. So we went in and didn't do too good. Then he started booking us into -- you know Sam Goody up there -- I mean -- Goody, up in Canada, at the --
At the Colonial.

At the Colonial, yeah. So we'd do that and also -- and Quebec City. We'd play a place there called the Oyster Bell. We'd go in there and stay there about two weeks, and maybe lay off a week, and it's time to go back to the Embers, you know, for five weeks. And now '56 is coming in now, and Sammy's still -- we're still going back to Cleveland, and he's still calling the guy at Baker's, but he says, "No, never again. Don't call me about Jonah. Look, what else you got?" He said, "Well, Jonah." He said, "No, look, don't call me no more about Jonah. Don't call me no more about him. It's a nice band, but not for our place, you know. Don't call me." So, we went along, scuffling along.
Now, here comes '57, we scuffkalong through that. '57 comes, Irv Jerome, Jerry Jerome's brother, he's got Epic, which was a subsidiary to Victor at this time.
It was Columbia.
Huh?
Epic.
Yeah. What did they have as a subsidiary to Victor, sounded like Epic to me, but could have been something else.
Well, Groove was --
Groove was Victor.
Groove was Victor, but Epic was Columbia.
Well, what about Capitol?
Capitol I didn't think had one.

Yeah, they had one and Irv Jerome was head of it. I don't think it was once. Irv Jerome. Well, I know Irv good -- I mean Jerry good. Jerry used to take me on gigs, you know, me and Tyree. So now Irv come in and one night he was in and we was talking and the people was enjoying it, you know, enjoying the music, so he says, 'You know what? Dave Cavanaugh's in town from California. I'm going to have him to come in here and listen to you one night, you know. Can't ever tell what will happen, you know.' I said, 'Yeah. I remember when Dave used to play tenor sax years ago.' He said, 'Yeah, well he's with Capitol now.' So me come in and we got to talking and, 'Who are you with?' I said Victor. He said, 'Oh, yeah, I heard that album.' He says, 'Tell your agent I think that we can do a better job on you. But you know, just tell him that I think I
can do a better one. I don't know what kind of contract you've got or if you've got one. Tell him I think we can do a better job."

Now, he has to go to his boss and try to get -- so he calls Dave and asks Dave did he mean what he told me. So Dave says yeah. He says, "I think we can do a better job on him." So now Sammy's got to go to his man and tell him that Jonah wants to get out of the contract." I don't even know what's happening, you know. I'm glad to have anything, you know. He said, "Jonah wants to get out of the contract." He said, "What's the matter? We only did it once. Give us a chance to make another album." He says, "Well, he feels like he'd rather be a big fish in a little pond than a little fish in a big pond." And they talked. Well, they were boys, you know, and they knew each other for years, and he'd rather be on a smaller label, you know, he'd feel better. It's too heavy for him over here.
