And so after he talked to him, he said, "Okay. If he's not happy I'll give him his contract back." I didn't even know what they were talking about, didn't even know they was talking. But agents do these things, you know.
Yeah.
But Sammy's a great guy for coming back and telling me what he has to do --
Yeah.
-- to maneuver these things, you know.
Keeps you --
Makes me feel good about it, you know.
Sure.
The guy don't do nothing, he comes back and tells me everything, you know.
Yeah.

And that makes me die for the guy, you know. He's just one of the family to me. And now he gives it back to him, and then we start manoeuvering with Capitol to get a contract that escalates, and royalties. I've been making records all my life, never got no royalties. I took all the contracts and things that I'd signed with different records, with Angel Records, that stuff I made with Angel, never got a nickel for none of the stuff, or Commodore or nothing. So Sammy said, "All this has got to quit now. This has got to quit." So he figures out a contract escalating the money and so first they got -- I think Dave is just getting his foot in the door, but he gets Dakota Staton. So he has -- he says, "I want you to make a record date with Dakota." Okay. Van Alexander's going to make the arrangements, and Milt will be on there and O and Jimmy Cleveland, trombone player, and some old guys. So we did, we went down and made the record, Late, Late Show, and Hank Jones on piano, and big. The thing sold like anything, sold big.
They had good promotion at that time.

Oh, yeah. Sure. And it had a good sound. And they said, "Now, we're going to make one, make an album with you. We're going to call it Muted Jazz." Now, we play everything, all the things, the little arrangements, like, "Too Close for Comfort." A nice arrangement we had on there. Now we've got George Rhodes by this time. We've got George Rhodes. The other piano player, he thinks he's doing me a favor. I'm paying him the scale, but he says that, "I ain't going to help nobody build no band. That's all I did all my life, help people build bands. I ain't helping nobody else to build no band," you know. So I said, "Well, okay, whatever you think, you know. I'm giving you the scale. That's what they're paying me." So now we go down there and make all our stuff, arrangements that George Rhodes had. He wasn't working then, so he come on down with us. I found him and he come on down with us. And he said yes. So he started making little arrangements. "Too Close for Comfort." "The Man With the Golden Arm," and things like that. He had some nice little ideas, you know, to let you know the group was together, you know. It was limited with four pieces, but he played things that you knew -- make you know that the group was together, it wasn't a pickup group. And we played all our things, which we thought was great. So we had about 20 minutes to go on the album, Muted Jazz, and Dave said, "You know what I'd like to do? You've got about 20 minutes, Jonah." I said, "What?" He said,

"On the Street Where You Live." I said, "Oh, Dave, we don't know that thing." He said, "Well, I heard you do it in the club." I said, "We only do that when somebody asks for it. We just play the melody." He said, "Well, that's all I want you to do, play the melody. Play it through once and come back and play it an octave higher the second time, start from the last half." And he says, "Give it a shuffle beat." And he told the drummer just what kind of shuffle he wanted, because I had never played with a shuffle beat, so I couldn't tell him. So he said, "I want you to accent it, chunk, chunk, like that, you know." And he says, "Get an introduction." So Buster was around too, you know. He was always around me, you know. So he says, "Get a hit introduction." So Buster says, you do, (Singing). The piano goes (Singing). And again, (Singing). We played that thing and we got it through in time, in the 20 minutes or less, you know. And no, I don't know. We're up in Canada now, in London, Ontario. I forget the name of that -- Campbell's, in London, Ontario, and we used to go there every year. So while we're up there some people come in one night and say, "Jonah, why don't you play your record hit?" I said, "What's the name of it?" So she said, "What's that, On the Street Where You're Living, or something like that." I said, "Yeah?" She said, "Yeah, that's all they're playing around Cleveland and Detroit. So I looked around at the guys and I said, "Did we make On the Street Where you Live?" So they said, "I don't know." One of

them said, "I think we made it, but I forgot what we did to it, how we played it, now." I said, "Well, let's play a couple of choruses like we used to do in the Embers." So we played it, and they said, "Well, that's all right, but that's not like the record." The next day I get up, go down to the record store, the biggest one in town, ask him, "Do you have a record in here by Jonah Jones, Muted Jazz?" They said, "No, we don't have that, man. We have the one, the 78, the Rhodes one, 'On the Street Where You Live'." I said, "Well, that's what I'm looking for. Do you mind if I take it back in the booth and listen?" He said, "No." So I took it back in the booth and I played it and it all come back to me then, because it was just the head, you know. Then I went back and got the guys and I took them down there, and then we were straight then. We started playing it then. And then when we get back, we find out this thing is selling, and what they sent out to the disc jockeys at that time was "Rose Room," but the disc jockeys always liked to have a hand in things that's going, so they turned it over and said, "On the Street is the number that should be pushed." So they played it all over Cleveland, and they was using it for a theme in different shows, in WLW in Chicago.
So that in effect set your career for the rest of your life, almost.
Yeah, almost, you know. It almost did, you know, for going this long, you know.
How many did you make for Capitol?
18 albums.
And how many for Decca?
Six for Decca, but they didn't have -- they had that touch over there, for four pieces. You could play this thing and it sounded like more pieces than that, see, the way they had it.
Was it the studio or what?
They had an echo chamber.
Yeah.
Echo or something like that.
Yeah.
Dave knew just what he wanted, and he --
Well that set him up too, didn't it?

Sure. And you see with him bringing in Dakota, this thing is selling like crazy, "Late, Late Show," and then here he comes with us with this Muted Jazz, and then he rushes back about six months later and says, "Now we're going to make one called Swinging on Broadway, and we're going to use all show tunes," all the tunes around in them days, "And I want you to do things like, 'Just My Luck,' and you sing that, 'Just My Luck,' we'll have one vocal in there, because vocals are not doing too good, so we'll just sing one, and 'Till There Was you." That was a ballad (Singing). See, well, we had it going (Singing). You know, we had the --
Yeah.
With the bucket mute on it.
Yeah.
Then I started looking around for different mutes, then, you know, because one mute is getting monotonous, you know.
Yeah.

So I used the growl, plunger, and the hummer and different things. And in the studio they was calling them mutes the Jonah Jones mutes, that bucket mute. You know, I didn't get a penny out of that, because I know they was telling me, 'Well, I hope you're getting your bread out of here, because when the arrangements come up here and CBS --' on the Sullivan Show, we was doing that show and we was also doing Garry Moore's show, and so Lawrence Brown was sitting in there on the Garry Moore Show at one time. And he said, 'Look here what they've got on here. Jonah Jones mute.' I said, 'I ain't getting a quarter. That belongs to a guy in Chicago. I can't get a quarter out of it. I didn't invent it. I just started playing it.' And he said, 'Well, everybody's using them now.' Just shows you how things can happen.
Yeah.
How many different mutes do you use?
Well, now I use that buzz mute and I use the plunger, and I don't use the bucket anymore because I'm

playing open again. See, I could do that before with what I was doing in the Embers, because they said no open horns. So I made the drummer stay on brushes. That's so he won't overpower me and blow me out. But then, after I come out of the Embers and I've got Cozy too, I can't tell him to stay on brushes all night. He ain't used to playing with brushes. So he's playing with sticks, so it give me a chance to open up, see. So now I open up. I'll just play a little thing, maybe I'll start off one number, maybe I'll start one or two numbers, just start off with it. Then I'll leave the mute and go, you know, and play open. I play more open now than I did before. And everybody's playing loud today anyway, so it don't make that much difference. You don't find too many rooms like the Embers, you know. And we had a hard time, you know --
Yeah, but you know that -- there are still people who would like that.
Yeah, but where are you going to play it now?
I know.

Where are we going to play it? The London House is gone. And in fact the London House trumpet -- when you say a trumpet in the London House, I know what a hard time you had, Sammy getting us in the London House. When you say London House -- when you say trumpet to the London House they say, 'No, no trumpet. This is a piano room.' A piano room, as the
man calls it. Great people. They gave me this watch. I always wear it. Any time we went in there they always gave me a present when we finished.
Isn't that nice?

Oh, they were beautiful people. Both of them dead now, both brothers. It's closed now, all over. So we couldn't get a job in there, and this is a good room, but the trumpet, scared them to death. We said, "We play it with a mute." They said, "Well, mute is still too loud for here. We can't have that." So finally Sammy told me now, in later years, he said, "You'll never know the things that I pulled to straighten you. I talke to them so much out there at the London House, and I said, 'Look, if it don't go, you book him for two weeks, if it don't go, you don't owe me nothing.'" So he said, "So I didn't tell you." I said, "You didn't tell me." He said, "No, I didn't tell you. If I told you that you'd go out there and you'd go crazy, if you knew. You wouldn't want to play if I told you that." So he says, "That's just my gamble. You went in there and then they booked you back for six weeks, the next engagement." You know, we went in there and played nice and soft, and then we got so we were going in twice a year in there.
(Unintelligible) -- supposed to be a piano room, but it's one of the worst places for people talking.
Yeah, well it's bad like the Embers. It

was like that. That's the type of thing was happening in them days. What do you think Baker's -- Baker's, sometimes you catch it soft. But on Saturday night and things like that, when everybody's out, they start talking at Baker's, and don't speak of the Theatrical in Cleveland. They never stop talking. They wouldn't care if you had Duke in there.
Earl didn't like that one.
Who, Erroll Garner?
No, he never liked that.
No, Earl Fatha.

Oh, Fatha, Fatha Hines. Yeah. Well, they don't care who it is. They don't care if it's Paul Whiteman. They're going to talk at that bar and everything, and the people that listen to you are over across from the bar. They're over here. Now, you're in the middle, so all you do is just stand up there and just play what you're playing, that's all. And every now and then point your horn over there to the tables. Because these people around here, they're talking about the baseball game and about the football game.
Yeah. Well, listen, Stanley --
Where is your next --
Huh?
You're nearly finished this time.
Well, the next album we come up with, Dave comes back and says, 'We're going to make an album called

Swinging on Broadway." Now it's got all show tunes in there, and he brought out a number and he said, "Now, this is going to be the featured number in here. This is Baubles, Bangles and Beads." Well, I never heard of, "Baubles, Bangles and Beads." So he passed out the piano copy, he give us all four the piano copy, and I said, "Well, I've got to transpose mine a note higher." Okay, but it's a waltz. He said, "Yeah, but swing it, like you did 'On the Street Where You Live,' and get a head introduction and play the first chorus straight and jazz the second chorus," which I did, and this son of a gun was bigger than On the Street.
Is that so?
Yeah, it was bigger than, "On the Street Where You Live," sure.
And didn't you sing one of them?

I sang one, yeah. On that one I sang -- in Swinging on Broadway I sang, "Just My Luck," from the show, "Body Beautiful." But on the first album, Muted Jazz, I sang, "My Blue Heaven," and, "Mack the Knife," and, "St. James Infirmary."
Yeah.
I did three on there. And then we come back and we did Jumping with Jonah, which sold good. Sold over 500,000 albums.
No kidding.
Yeah.
Well, at least -- you know, that was very good, that music without any real gimmicks like that would sell.

Yeah, no gimmicks. A lot of guys wanted to say commercial. Well, that's me, then. That's the way I play. I mean I enjoyed it. I enjoyed playing like that, and I couldn't play much more with my mute, you know. I mean you've got the mute, it's got to slow you down some, when you stay up there with that mute in your horn all night like that. And you're trying to get there -- I don't care what you do, that's your nature, to punch. So you try to make them high notes mean something. That's what Vachiano told me. He said, "Don't be trying to hit F and things in the middle of the number, the solo. Hit them on the end."
Because it's rough on your lip.
Yeah, it's rough on your lip, see. But what success I had out of the thing, you know.
Yeah.
Oh, God, the success. The first check I got was over 27,000.00 in royalties. And then Sammy went out there and --
And you'd never had royalties before.

No. And then the thing of it is, then Fred Astaire sends for me. I don't know this guy from Adam. I knew guys like Johnny Mercer and Bing, you know, come in the Onyx. Johnny used to sing with us. I figured if something would
happen it would be one of them. I get a telegram --

So we were doing the Fred Astaire Show, and I was the most surprised guy. But it just happened. See, you've got to watch these things, because there are so many turns and things in it. And I never talked a lot about these things, but I figure it's good now, because I don't have to worry one way or the other, you know. I like to get it out. We're in there, so Dave tells me, says, "I want you to go somewhere with me after the session." I said okay. I think we'd just made an album called Swinging Around the World With Jonah Jones. Something like that. And it was in different countries. Madrid, and all that, Paris, you know, "April in Paris." So then I thought maybe we were going out for dinner. So we wind up at Joe Glaser's after we finish, you know. And Joe says, "I've got a job for you with Fred Astaire, but I'm not going to give it to you unless you sign with this office." Now, I don't know what to do.
Unless you sign with --
Unless you sign with his office, with ABC, you know.
Yeah.
So Dave is sitting on the side --
Is Sam with you?
No. Uh-uh. And he's up here, and this

guy's here and -- oh, oh -- I want this job, though, you know. It seems like it's going to be a big thing, you know, with Fred Astaire. He says, "I've got it here, right here. I'll show it to you." And he showed it to me, "I'd like to have Jonah Jones to do a show, a special. I'd like to have Jonah." He says, "Now, this come to me and I'm not going to give it to you unless you sign up with us." So I said, "Yeah, but I've already got an agent. Sam Burke." He said, "Sam Burke. What the hell -- this is a million dollar corporation up here. What can he do? What is that, Sam Burke. I mean this is a big company here, you know." I said, "Well, what do I do about Sam, you know. He brought me this far." So he says, "Look, if you like Sammy that much we'll give him 5 percent, you know. We'll give him 5 percent." So I said, "I don't know about that. I have to think that over." You know, because I want this show. It's another step, you know, being with Fred Astaire, you know. I don't know that much about him, because I always listened to musicians, you know, but I know he's somebody, you know, somebody told me he's in a picture or something, dancing. Dancers talk about him. So I didn't go back and tell Sammy about this, you know. I didn't know. I called Cab. I called up Cab, you know, and I explained it to him, what had happened, you know. And he says, "Look, I'll tell you very easy. Stick with the man that brought you as far as you have gotten this far."
Did he.

He said, "It's very easy." He said, "Stick with the same man that brought you as far as you have come." And he says, "If Fred Astaire wants you, he's going to get you. That man is no fool. He's been in this business for years. He wants you and Joe can't deliver you, --"
He'll find out who can.

"-- he'll find out who can deliver you. If he really wants you." I said, "Well, I saw the telegram." He said, "Did you see a telegram? Don't worry about it. You'll get it straight." I go along with this, but it's worrying me because I want to tell Sammy, you know, and I don't want Sammy to fly off the handle, because he'll fly off the handle in a minute. So when I kind of think I've got him into a point where I can tell him, you know, and I tell him about what happened, you know, because the show's getting ready, they're getting ready for this thing, you know, and it's kind of getting around you know, and I tell Sammy, "Well, this guy, Joe Glaser --," I told him how the story happened, "Dave took me over there and he told me he wouldn't give it to me unless --," that was it. He went over there, he like to run everybody out of the office. He shook his finger in Joe's face and said, "I'll have your license taken away from you. Who the hell do you think --," and cussed him out and everything, and Joe was backing up from him and everything, you know, and he's a wiry little cat, you

know. And he went right up to Joe and Joe started backing off, the guy started running, run to the door and all this stuff, and he's hollering out, you know. So now that's over with. So they set it up. I don't know how they set it up. I told him about it so there wouldn't be no stuff, so he could do it.

But now I'm in Detroit. Now, the guy was always telling him "Don't call me about Jonah," out at Baker's. This guy calls Sammy and Sammy laid it on him. Sammy laid the bread on him. "Well, I tried to get you to take him last year again, and you said no, so now it will cost you twice as much. If not, we've got other places to go. The records are jumping." Had a big following there. So we went in for him, at Baker's, and he's got lines up in the snow, on both sides of the street, and he's making us cut the session down to 20 minutes, and says, "You can only stay one set and you have to pay again."
20 minutes?

That's the only way he could make any money, because Sammy had charged him all this bread, and the guy -- we'd get up there and do 20 minutes, which was about two numbers. You know, we'd play one number and then play a long one, a show number, and off.
Well, what kind of cover was he charging?
Huh? Oh, he was charging like -- I think he was charging 2.50, and they'd say in there about 20 minutes, 25 at the most, and I stayed up there 25, he'd come back and
argue, he'd say, "Jonah, cut it down now. It was 25 minutes. Cut it down."
I'll bet he had some griping there.

Oh, man, what griping he had, you know, because he had all the hustlers and things come up from John A. Street, at that hotel out there, the Gotham. They would come out and buy champagne, you know. They didn't care what it was. They just stayed all night anyway. No used to talk to them about going after the one set. When they started doing that it didn't do us no good either, because some of the people wondered, "What's going on, Jonah? Stay up there." I'd say, "Well, this is orders from the boss. You have to ask him."
So this went on -- then we started going back regular then, you know, and charging him too. Sammy charged him, to make him pay. "I'm going to make him pay, because of how he was before."
For saying he didn't want you back.

Yeah, uh-huh. He said, "I'm going to make him pay." So the people that was good to us, he said, "We're going to be good to them. The people that was hard to get along with, we're going to make them pay." So the guy at the Theatrical, we never did make him go up where he should. And we just went out there this year for him, you know. Not as I like the room, but --
I think we --
Yeah, but I've got a couple of things I wanted Jonah to talk about.

But then, after that, we did that TV show for Fred Astaire, which we won nine awards. That was a great thing. That set us up all over the world, because after that I was invited to go down to Australia.
How long a show was that?
Huh?
How long a show was it?
It was an hour show. With Barrie Chase, you know, and --
What year was it, Jonah?
Yeah.
Yeah.
So they split it up between them, so Sammy got his good fair share and Joe was in on it too, huh?
No, Joe had to give up.
Oh, Joe gave up all together.
He had to give up on it.
And so Sammy approached Fred then, Fred Astaire.
Yeah, he started making the contact.
I get it. Oh, that's triumphal, isn't it.
So we did so good, and then Fred, on the

next show, why we got double money for it. See, we got double money when they wanted us back. He said we're going to do the same thing, we're going to do another one. But the next one didn't come off as good. And the third one, they got Basie, and it didn't come off as good, because he's competing with himself now, you see. That first one, he had really gotten out of show business. He told me, "I gave up show business."
Yeah. It was a comeback.

Yeah. And he said, "They kept calling me and calling me and I'd tell them no, but I got ahold of that Muted Jazz record. I don't hear no rhythm and things like that no more. Looked like I was lost." And he said, "It got so I played that thing of yours all the time, Jonah." Because I asked him. I said, "Why did you decide to send for me?" He said, "I got so I'd play that record. One day I'm sitting there playing it, and they called up and said, 'We are from the Chrysler Corporation. We want to know if you're ready to do a show.'" So he said, "Yeah, I'll do a show for you if you'll get me the people that I want." So they said, "Well, who do you want?" And he said, "I'd like to have Barrie Chase and Jonah Jones. Give me that and I'll do a show." You know?
Yeah. Yeah.
And he said, "Then they come over to the house. And they said, 'Well, these people, we don't know anything about these people you're talking about. If you want to do a

show get names.'" He says, "Look. This here is what I want to do now, if you want me to do it." So finally after about six weeks they said, "Okay. You can get them and if anything goes wrong it's your fault." So he says okay. So now what they did while I'm playing out at Baker's again, Bud Yorkin is out in the audience and I don't know it. So he was a producer, you know, or a director or something. So he was sitting out there, so I got off after the last set, and he said, "Jonah, my name is Bud Yorkin. I'm the director of the Fred Astaire show. I'd like to go by the hotel and talk to you." So I said I lived in a Soul neighborhood. So we went over there and we started talking, and I was telling him that I was a family man, you know, and I was happy that they selected me for the thing. And he said, "Well, after we selected you, after they decided on you, then Fred Astaire said, "Who knows what type of guy this guy is." So now he began, after he sold them, he said, "You'd better fly in there and check him out." We don't know if he's dopey or what, you know. So after he sat there about two hours that night, he said, "Well, when I go back I think Fred will be very happy. I don't see no needles or nothing laying around. I don't think we'll have no trouble. Because he likes to rehearse." So when I got there they had taken that "St. James Infirmary", off of the record and put it on tape, and the girls are doing all them things to my solo. (Singing). And all that kind of stuff. And I had to learn it over because I don't do it like that every time.
Yeah.

It might sound like that but I don't do it that way every time. Now, I have to learn it over like the record because he says, "You've got to do this just like the record because I've got steps going with it." And he featured me all the way through. Not like they used to throw you out there and do two numbers and that's all. I did a sketch with him. I played my hit things. And then I was in the "St. James Infirmary." "St. James Infirmary," was the big number of the show, and he was standing behind me, singing, and he said, "I'm going to be your shadow, instead of," we were turning around from Ted Lewis.
Yeah.
And I'm going through all this, you know, and rubbing and blowing on my fingers, and he's doing it behind me.
How funny.

And it was real nice. And then he took us all to the hotel and had a room with a television in each corner, because they had to play it back for the east coast. See they had to play it back. What you saw was the tape. They did it live in California. And then when it come time for it to play here -- or else they did it live here, I think. It come through here live, and for California, it had to come on --
Because of the time difference.
Yeah, on account of the time difference. And we was doing it out there, which was about 7:00 o'clock. That would have been 10:00 o'clock here or something.
Yeah.
So then for it to come into California at 10:00 or 9:00, they had to do it again, but they showed the tape, and he had a big party in this big room in a hotel.
And everybody could see it.
All the food and the TV in each corner of the room.
Yeah.
And everybody sitting there, looking at it, you know.
Yeah. That's wonderful.
And gloating over what's happening, you know.
Yeah.

Including me with my -- one of the greatest things I did. And then the next thing, Grace Kelly and Prince Rainier, they invited us over for the -- that gala they have, and they had our group and Ella Fitzgerald and Peter Ustinov and Frankie Vaughan, a singer from -- London
Yeah, I know who you mean.
And Tony Martin. So that was a good thing.
And what year was that?
That was around about '61 or '62.
Yeah.
And we went over. We did that number By this time I've got Teddy Brannon piano. I've got George Foster on drums. John Brown's still with me. But I don't have no guitar yet, see.
What happened to Teddy Brannon.
I don't know. You know, after awhile he -- you know, they all get up there and --
He was a good pianist.
He was a good pianist, yes.
Yes.
So then we did -- I thought that was a great thing. That was a big thing to happen in my life.
Yeah.
Who could ask for anything more. Then to come back and play that Inauguration for Johnson.
Yeah.
You know. And she --
Did Sammy --
-- was so wonderful. She had all my records.
Lady Bird?
No.
Oh, Grace Kelly.
Grace Kelly.
Did she?
She had them in her palace, and I said, "Oh, I see you have one of my records." She said, "We've got One? everything you ever made."
Isn't that nice.
"We keep them on there so when we go to bed at night we let them play and we go to sleep on it, see. It cuts off itself, you know."
What do you know. Isn't that tremendous.
So, it was a good feeling, you know.
Yeah, of course.

To be in with that crowd, you know, a crowd like that. And they didn't work you hard, at the Sea Club you did a thing. At the sporting club you did one thing. It's built out there over the Mediterranean, and all them Dukes and Duchesses and stuff coming, so you do that once, and then you go to the Sea Club and play once, and they don't do that sporting club every night. You do that about once or twice a week, and you stay two weeks.
Yeah. Well, that's wonderful.
And then follows you with another thing, Sinatra and all them come in. And there comes Sammy and Lena and all those. It's a big thing they have over there, you know.
Yeah, wonderful.
And I thought that was a great thing, and she sent a round trip ticket to my wife and
sent a round trip ticket to Sammy and his wife.
Oh, that's very nice. Well, listen, about the inauguration, how did Sam lay that on?
You know, I don't know how that come through.
Or maybe they came to him.

That come through that guy Symington, Stuart or something like that, see. He was a Senator. Anyhow, it come through and they wanted me to play this thing, and I'm trying to think how it come through, but anyhow we wound up playing at the Statler with a fellow who had a band at the Taft Hotel for so many years. What is his name?
Vincent Lopez?
Vincent Lopez. Yeah, we were alternating, you know.
Yeah.
And then this was a fantastic thing, you know, you'd go to the boxes where the Senators sat, you know, and all that stuff.
Yeah, sure.
And here he comes in, him and Ladybird and -- or Humphrey, and his wife, you know, Mrs. Humphrey.
Yeah.
And right away he goes over and he gets

the black cat, Hobart Taylor, he was a lawyer, and grabs his wife. He don't dance with Ladybird. He grabs his wife, a pretty brown skinned woman, and he dances like an old hustler, you know, with them big feet. And he danced there by himself for awhile, you know. Then all the others joined in.
That's nice.

Then later on I met Humphrey at the London House, and he come by. He said, "I just had to come by and see you." He said, "I never asked nobody for an autograph in my life, but I want an autograph from you. I want two, for my daughters."
Well, I never. Isn't that nice.

So, you know, things like that. And then later I had a telegram. I have it there, and an invitation for luncheon. He was entertaining the King of Cameroon, or the President of Cameroon. And you go in by the east gate and all that kind of stuff. So I thought that was --
Did you play?
No, no playing, just to go there for lunch.
Very nice. Very nice.
It's an honor. It's different from when you're hired to play.
Yeah, that's what Dr. Logan says, you know. Dr. Logan says, "That's an honor." But those were the

three highlights, was playing the Inauguration and playing for Grace Kelly and doing the Fred Astaire thing. Them was the big things. Of course I liked going to Australia, that was nice, we enjoyed that, you know. We went to Sydney and Adelaide, Brisbane and Melbourne.
Yeah. Well, that's wonderful, Jonah.
It was very nice, you know, when it happens to you like that. I'm going to argue about what's commercial and what's not commercial? I don't know myself, you know. The only thing I know is the so|d.
You're pleasing people.
Benny Goodman's so|d, that's some pretty good commercial to me.
Yeah, that's right.
I like to hear him.
Sure, yeah.
Sure, I mean, of course Fletcher But heck, what are you going to do with four pieces, you know?
Well, I mean, and it comes at a time when you weren't going to be able to offer anything.

That's right. You know, so I said this is a good way to go out, you know. You go out like this. I'm not a kid now. I've been around longer than I thought I'd be. I always thought when I was 40 years old that I would quit.
You know, when I was a young man I used to think that.
Yeah.

When I first come out of the Sunday school band, I first left, I said when I'm 40 years old I'm coming out of it. I thought that was old. Then I didn't get started till I was 45. I didn't get started till I was 45. But the great thing about it, let me say this about Sam Burke, that is the man. He did everything. He guided everything for me, right or wrong, right or wrong. I'm still with him, you know. I just listen to him, you know, because he did so much for me.
He had faith in you and he --

Yeah, a guy that'd have that much faith in you, you know. I was a trumpet player. Let's face it, I was a trumpet player out there, you know, and almost through, you know, and here's a guy come by and has enough confidence in me, and I was able. Of course I had something to do with it. Because he'd tell me that in a minute, 'I couldn't do it unless you did it.'
No.
Unless you can deliver, you know. He said, 'I couldn't make them buy them records, you know.'
I think it was great that Cab gave you that advice. I really think that was very good.
Oh, yeah. Well, that's nice. I mean we were very tight about that, so we celebrated our anniversary
last year, and by celebrating it we went on the cruise he was on, you know, a nostalgia cruise. And as I told you, Tedd King, Hildegarde, Peter Duchin and Cab and his daughter.
And you.
No, I didn't play. We just went along for the trip.
Oh, really?

So I talked to him and reminisced all the time, and we'd get upstairs late at night, up in that top bar up there, and we'd sit up there and eat hors d'oeuvres and stuff all night, you know, and sit there and reminisce about the big band, and she would be with his wife Nuffy all the time, we called her Nuffy, you know. Great people.
Yeah.

And my wife would be with her, they'd be reminiscing, you know, and they'd be given the old man the devil down there, but he did some good things, you know. Right now I always feel safe in where I can call him if I really didn't understand something, because at that time I couldn't call Sammy. Sammy would have blowed the building down, you know.
Yeah, that's right.
Right away like that. And then I didn't know whether to -- how to tell him that I'd asked Cab, because maybe he'd figured that I should have had enough confidence in
him at that time.
That's right.
I was mixed up. I had no idea about something like that hits you, if Fred Astaire wants you to come and play a show.
Yeah, sure.
Now, what the heck is that, you know what I mean? Okay --
And turn your back on that.
Well, in the first place I don't know what to say about it. This guy tells me -- I don't know nothing about this business, what agents do, you know.
Yeah.
And here's a guy says I'm not going to give it to you unless you come with this office. So now what the --
That's right.
You know, I don't know what to do. I don't want to ask Sammy.
That's right.
He's the agent, you know.
Well, he knew what he was doing. He knew what he was doing.
Yeah.
Yeah, well, that is good. Very good.
But a lot of things like that he did then. Another thing about Capitol, when we got out there and we started doing the Fred Astaire show, well the royalties was graduated up, you know, like --
Percentage higher?

Yeah, so that's what I was thinking, you know, so this guy said -- so Wally said, 'Well, we're happy to have you with the family and I hope you're happy.' So Sammy said, 'Oh, we're happy, but we could be happier.' So Wally said, 'Well, what do you mean by that, you could be happier?' He said, 'Well, if that 4 percent was moved up to 5 percent.' He said, 'Yeah, but you've got a contract.' So he says, 'Oh, but you said that if I could be happier, you know. You said you hope I'm happy. I said yeah, but I could be happier.' He said, 'I'll tell you what you do. Come by here tomorrow at 2:00 o'clock and we'll talk.' And he gave him the 5 percent.
You know, well that is really --

Here's a guy that's fighting for you. Now, he don't have to tell me all of these things, you know, but he's fighting for me, you know what I mean? All the way. Sammy says, 'Get it now, while them records are hot. Who knows what's going to be next year.'
It's the truth.
He says, 'You may be dead next year.'
And try, always try.
That's right, you know. Yeah, always try.
Also he's saying things that you wouldn't want to say, probably, you know.
Oh, yeah, and I couldn't say, and I wouldn't know how to say.
That's it.
Well, I mean Earl's the same. Earl doesn't want to do that kind of thing either.
I didn't know that the thing graduates. I didn't know nothing about that, you know.
Yeah.
If they had given me a penny I'd have been happy. It's more than I ever got.
Yeah. Jonah, I'm going to cut it off, because we've got to drive to Connecticut.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

segments.chapter: Family and Louisville childhood
segments.title: Copyright notices, title page and start of recording
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright warnings, Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Project title page, a voice check, and Helen Oakley Dance opening the interview with Jonah Jones on October 26, 1978.

segments.chapter: Family and Louisville childhood
segments.title: Birth in Louisville and his slave-born great-grandmother
segments.summary: Born December 31, 1908 in Louisville and raised by his mother, grandmother and great-grandmother, who lived to 109 and told him about slavery times. The women kept him close to home.

segments.chapter: Family and Louisville childhood
segments.title: His trumpet-playing younger brother and Cab Calloway's rules
segments.summary: Jones's brother, eight years younger, played good trumpet but would not accept band discipline; Cab Calloway offered him a job after hearing him sit in at Fort Bragg, but he refused to follow the rules on drinking.

segments.chapter: Family and Louisville childhood
segments.title: Strict upbringing, his father the fireman, and the piano at home
segments.summary: The switches kept on the mantel; his father was one of the first black firemen in Louisville, rising to lieutenant, and played piano by ear and bought him an odd reed instrument.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: First seeing the Booker T. Washington Community Center Band parade
segments.summary: At nine or ten, after the family moved to 10th Street, he saw the all-kid band in a parade; Dickie Wells was in it, and he mentions Bill Beason, who later replaced Chick Webb and went with John Kirby.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Dickie Wells organizes the Kentucky Club reunion at the Celebrity Club
segments.summary: About ten years earlier, the Kentucky musicians from the band started a club; Dickie Wells arranged space at the Celebrity Club on 25th Street with Jones's money.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Louisville band alumni in Lloyd Scott's and Furman Tapp's bands
segments.summary: Les Carr, Dickie Wells, Hal MacFerin, Bill Beason and Mac Walker came out of the Louisville kid band and played in Furman Tapp's and Lloyd Scott's bands, so half of Scott's band was from Louisville.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Who came to the Kentucky Club get-together
segments.summary: Hoggie (Harold McFerlin), Les Carr, Charlie Bloomer, Isaiah Bland and his twin brother, and Fatha Hines all showed up; they just talked.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Mrs. Bessie L. Allen and the Sunday school behind the band
segments.summary: Louis Thompson, the first member, recalls Mrs. Bessie L. Allen handing out instruments; her non-denominational Sunday school drew 500 children, and some parents distrusted her as a truant officer.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Mrs. Allen's orphanage and how she raised money from white businesses
segments.summary: She ran a home like an orphanage, put some of its children in the band (including Mac Walker), and raised money from downtown stores and professionals, some giving $500 a year.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Free training, the conductor Lockwood Lewis and the band's size and repertoire
segments.summary: A beginner's teacher for six to nine months, then placement in the band under Lockwood Lewis, who made them read overtures; the band had 45 to 60 players including many clarinets, trumpets and tubas.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: The baritone horn and euphonium; Hank Duncan's brother
segments.summary: Jones explains the baritone horn versus the euphonium, how a single baritone carries over an 80-piece band in Sousa marches, and the outstanding baritone player who was Hank Duncan's young brother.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Begging his family for a trombone
segments.summary: After seeing the parade he kept demanding a trombone at about ten or eleven, but money was scarce in hard times.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Hence Grundy's advice and being given an alto horn
segments.summary: Trombonist Hence Grundy told his mother the band would give a trombone and free lessons; at the band Jones's arms proved too short for seventh position, so Mrs. Allen gave him an alto horn.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: How the alto horn prepared him for trumpet and reading
segments.summary: He describes the alto horn's shape and size and says two years on it built his lip for trumpet and taught him to read.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: The beginners' teacher who forbade jazz
segments.summary: Students practiced reading at home; the teacher rapped fingers of anyone who added jazz notes, yet the kids liked him, and older musicians resented that the band was training their replacements.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Turnover of players and girls joining the marching band
segments.summary: Good readers were taken by big bands each year and replaced; girls aged ten to thirteen came in, played clarinet and trumpet and marched, and nobody objected.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Daily rehearsals and Sunday school playing
segments.summary: Pupils had to attend rehearsal every day after school; on Sundays the band played an overture and hymns like "Onward Christian Soldiers" for the whole Sunday school.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Playing for fraternal orders on trips, with Mrs. Allen's discipline
segments.summary: The band played marches for the Elks, Masons and United Brothers of Friendship, travelled to Chicago and St. Louis, was cheap because non-union, and was put up in dormitories under strict supervision.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Camp mischief: the tents and Raymond Tate
segments.summary: After a tape change: the girls presumably lodged elsewhere; while camping, Raymond Tate hit a tent with a stick and knocked out a saxophonist.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Henry Allen on trips; Sunday school keeps kids off the streets
segments.summary: Mrs. Allen stayed home to run Sunday school while her husband Henry went on trips; the Sunday school gave neglected kids somewhere to go, and Jones also went to church with his mother and grandmother.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Moving up to trumpet as older players leave
segments.summary: After about two years on alto horn, first-chair Matthew Holland left to play with adult bands; chairs shifted up and Jones was given fourth trumpet and quickly rose to first chair.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: The mellophone year and quick rise to first trumpet
segments.summary: Mrs. Allen bought four mellophones; he played one for a year using his alto mouthpiece, then went to trumpet and in about two years was first trumpet.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Alto and mellophone, and moving up chair by chair
segments.summary: Both were E-flat instruments playing the same parts; players moved up as others shifted to trombones or trumpets, and the kids helped one another.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: How Robert Jones became Jonah
segments.summary: Playing E-natural in the trio of the march "Our Director", the stammering conductor threw his baton and called him "Jonah" instead of Jones, and the name stuck.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Bassist Louis Thompson's career after the band
segments.summary: Louis Thompson, an early member who played bass with Louis Depp's band when Earl Hines was in it, now lives in New Jersey and works for a distiller.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: E-flat versus double-B bass, Mac Walker, and slowing down Armstrong records
segments.summary: Mac Walker could play the "West End Blues" introduction on E-flat tuba; Jones and Mac slowed Armstrong records at home to learn them, and his mother put him in the back yard to practice.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Band pranks: candle wax on a sleeper and stolen cookie boxes
segments.summary: Boys dripped wax on a big bass player's fingers in the Chicago dormitory, and a trombonist juggled stolen cake boxes at a stop on the road to Kentucky country fairs.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: The Kentucky Club becomes the Friendly 50
segments.summary: The club was meant to fund a monument to Mrs. Allen but grew by admitting non-Kentuckians, became the Friendly 50, and still meets monthly; early meetings were at a bar and at Les Carr's house.

segments.chapter: Booker T. Washington Community Center Band
segments.title: Throwing the goat George and Bill Beason's career
segments.summary: Jones taught Bill Beason his trick of flipping a goat; Beason left Louisville early for Horace Henderson's and Benny Carter's bands and later stopped playing.

segments.chapter: Louisville music and first jobs
segments.title: Under strict rule until sixteen, then playing in the joints
segments.summary: He had to report straight home until about sixteen, then was allowed to play with adults in local joints; Bob Carroll came out of there too, and he credits Mrs. Allen for Louisville's musicians.

segments.chapter: Louisville music and first jobs
segments.title: Louisville adult bands and the Lloyd Scott trombonists
segments.summary: Local bands included Winstead's Wonders, Howard Jordan's and Furman Tapp's; Dickie Wells, Bill Coleman and Frankie Newton were in Lloyd Scott's band, and his brother-in-law Russell Bowles took Dickie's place with Tapp.

segments.chapter: Louisville music and first jobs
segments.title: His wife and her brother in the band; Dickie Wells nicknamed Parkland
segments.summary: His wife fooled around with clarinet and baritone but did not stay; her brother Russell Bowles joined after Dickie left, whom they teased as Parkland for the muddy part of town he came from.

segments.chapter: Louisville music and first jobs
segments.title: Milt Robinson and playing dance gigs with Artie Jones
segments.summary: Trombonist Milt Robinson played with Andy Kirk and Benny Carter; Jones played Sunday dance jobs with trombonist Artie Jones's small band and had no trouble reading its book.

segments.chapter: Louisville music and first jobs
segments.title: The Island Queen excursion steamer
segments.summary: The sidewheeler Island Queen made daily Cincinnati excursions to Coney Island and an autumn trip to New Orleans, with a Paducah band living aboard for $40 a week room and board.

segments.chapter: Louisville music and first jobs
segments.title: Getting hired for the boat with his friend William Granger
segments.summary: The boat needed a trumpet and clarinet; Jones refused to go without his buddy William Granger, so the leader took both trumpets.

segments.chapter: Louisville music and first jobs
segments.title: Sunday school horns taken on the boat and replaced in Memphis
segments.summary: They took band horns without permission, then spent their first pay in Memphis on two $20 horns and shipped the borrowed ones back to Mrs. Allen.

segments.chapter: Louisville music and first jobs
segments.title: Parents wanted college; Mrs. Allen's Tuskegee and Fisk connections
segments.summary: He told his parents after leaving; they wanted him in college, and Mrs. Allen could send promising pupils to Tuskegee or Fisk.

segments.chapter: Louisville music and first jobs
segments.title: Down the Mississippi on the steamboat to New Orleans
segments.summary: Playing moonlight excursions at Memphis, Helena, Vicksburg and other towns with calliope and crowds, then arriving at New Orleans where rival boats saluted them.

segments.chapter: Horace Henderson band and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Sent for by Jimmy Smith's Missourians to play the Savoy
segments.summary: About 1932 he was sent for to play two weeks at the Savoy with the Missourians, part of which had split off when Cab was put in front; a tape break and false start follow.

segments.chapter: Horace Henderson band and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Playing beside young Roy Eldridge in Horace Henderson's band
segments.summary: In Horace Henderson's band Jones found the 17-year-old Roy Eldridge blowing prodigiously without reading, and Horace said Roy's improvised sax parts sounded better than the written ones; Jones absorbed jazz from him.

segments.chapter: Horace Henderson band and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Roy Eldridge leaves for Speed Webb; his brother Joe in Detroit
segments.summary: Roy went with Speed Webb's touring band; at a battle of bands in Detroit Jones first saw Roy's brother Joe in Earl Walton's band, who scolded Roy and offered help with reading.

segments.chapter: Horace Henderson band and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Roy Eldridge's range and habit of jumping on bandstands; Little Jazz
segments.summary: Roy's range grew later; the two went around sitting in everywhere, with Roy sitting on the chair edge stomping, and he earned the nickname Little Jazz, appreciated more by musicians than the public.

segments.chapter: Horace Henderson band and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Louis Armstrong's automatic influence on Roy and other trumpeters
segments.summary: Neither had met Armstrong yet everyone played like him; Jones says boppers play Louis without knowing it, doubling up the tempo.

segments.chapter: Horace Henderson band and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Taking over Roy's solos and learning to swing the first trumpet part
segments.summary: After Roy left, Jones played his solos nearly as Roy did, and learned from Roy that the lead trumpet can swing the section, as Cootie Williams did.

segments.chapter: Horace Henderson band and Roy Eldridge
segments.title: Speed Webb's band with Roy, Renald Jones and Vic Dickenson
segments.summary: Roy's next band, Speed Webb's, included Renald Jones, Vic Dickenson and alto Leonard Gay; the band left sayings on bandstand shells, and there were many good western bands around Indiana.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Little Harlem in Buffalo: the on-air battle with Stuff Smith
segments.summary: A small band grew to seven with John L. Henderson and Joe Thomas; on a radio half hour they battled Stuff Smith's band three blocks away at Little Harlem, and each copied the other's arrangements.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Sorting out dates: leaving the Vendome in 1931 when Willie Bryant came in
segments.summary: Jones clarifies that he left the Vendome after about a year when the owner brought in Willie Bryant's big band, in 1931 before the Savoy job of 1932.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Stuff Smith's small group and his earlier career
segments.summary: Stuff had Peanuts Holland, Buster Nash and Fran Sherrill; Jones recalls Stuff's earlier work with Alphonso Trent and a record date with Jelly Roll Morton or King Oliver.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Joining Jimmie Lunceford's band in 1931: members and arrangers
segments.summary: He joined Lunceford's band when it came through, replacing Paul Webster alongside Eddie Tompkins and Doug Clay; the reeds were Willie Smith, Fats and George Clark; Moses Allen and Jimmy Crawford were in the rhythm section.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Poor pay and unfulfilled share-and-share-alike promises in Lunceford's band
segments.summary: College dates paid $10 a night with gas and truck costs deducted; Lunceford promised shares but arrangers like Willie Smith and Wilcox got nothing extra, and Jones left before finding out.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Bringing his brother-in-law Russell Bowles into Lunceford's band
segments.summary: Lunceford refused New York players like Dickie Wells but let Jones's brother-in-law sit in on New Year's Eve and kept him until the band broke up.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Tommy Stevenson, the high-note man behind "Rhythm Is Our Business"
segments.summary: After Trummy Young joined, Tommy Stevenson came in as the first trumpeter Jones heard hit notes that high; mostly a high-note specialist.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Stuff Smith takes over the Vendome band
segments.summary: Eddie Tompkins and Jones were asked back but Jones had already gone with Stuff, who took over the Vendome band with pianist Jimmy Sherman, bassist Sylvester Turpin, drummer Buster Nash and trombonist Gus Wilson.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Gus Wilson, the self-doubting arranger who walked out
segments.summary: Teddy Wilson's brother Gus wrote beautiful arrangements and tore them up whenever praised, then left his trombone on the chair after a quarrel with Stuff and was never seen again.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Back to Stuff's bigger Vendome band on a steady job
segments.summary: Dance interrupts to untangle the chronology; Jones and Stuff got along well and the Vendome job was steady, until Jimmy Smith's invitation to New York came.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Quitting for the Savoy in New York at lower pay
segments.summary: Wanting to reach New York, he left Buffalo to join the Savoy band with R. Q. Dixon and Jimmy Smith, doubling at the Harlem Opera House, but then earned only $22.50 and went back to Buffalo.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Stuff's enlarged band and the sad fate of trumpeter Sleepy Tomlin
segments.summary: Back in Buffalo the band had Dick Vance and St. Louis trumpeter William 'Sleepy' Tomlin, whose daughter was murdered in St. Louis and who then lost his mind.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Stuff Smith's band stranded in Philadelphia and taken over by Lil Armstrong
segments.summary: The band played the Lafayette in New York and the Lincoln in Philadelphia, got stranded, was joined by Teddy McRae, and then Lil Armstrong took over the band, Stuff excluded.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Lil Armstrong's band: Louis the Second and Detroit
segments.summary: Lil featured him as Louis the Second, played the Graystone Ballroom in Detroit and wrote arrangements; agents disliked the tiny wife and big husband billing; irregular work and pro rata pay led him to leave.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: A short spell with the depleted McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.summary: John McKinney offered work in Detroit but the band had lost Don Redman's men, Cuba, and singer Fathead Thomas; only the arrangements remained, and Jones stayed two months.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Stuff's small group at the Silver Grill and the move to the Onyx Club
segments.summary: Back in Buffalo Stuff hired him for his quartet at the Silver Grill; Dick Stabile heard the group and arranged for them to open at the Onyx Club in New York on February 4, 1936.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: California contract trouble, returning to the Onyx and Maxine Sullivan
segments.summary: After the Onyx, the group went to the Famous Door in California, hated it and left despite a six-month contract; back at the Onyx the band grew and took off once Claude Thornhill's find Maxine Sullivan sang.

segments.chapter: Buffalo, Lunceford, Lil Armstrong and Stuff Smith
segments.title: End of the first tape and header of sides 3-4
segments.summary: The recording stops at the end of one side and resumes on sides 3-4 with a new Smithsonian header and a voice check.

segments.chapter: Riverboat to New Orleans and Horace Henderson
segments.title: The Streckfuss excursion boats and riverboat work for musicians
segments.summary: Boats of the St. Louis Streckfuss company saluted them; St. Louis musicians such as Red Allen played excursions, and Louisville had its own dance boats.

segments.chapter: Riverboat to New Orleans and Horace Henderson
segments.title: Jamming in New Orleans and the mystery trumpeter who sounded like Louis
segments.summary: After work they jammed at places like Ramona's, finding every local trumpeter played like Armstrong; one night an unidentified tall man in overalls walked through the crowd playing like Louis.

segments.chapter: Riverboat to New Orleans and Horace Henderson
segments.title: Why William Granger never pursued a career
segments.summary: Granger improvised better than Jones but lacked the initiative to push ahead and take a chance.

segments.chapter: Riverboat to New Orleans and Horace Henderson
segments.title: Stranded in Paducah and the telegram from Horace Henderson
segments.summary: After New Orleans the boat band wintered at Paducah with about one job a month, so Jones and Granger took a train home to Louisville, where a telegram from Horace Henderson arrived.

segments.chapter: Riverboat to New Orleans and Horace Henderson
segments.title: Horace Henderson's trumpet section: Red Holland, Bernice Morton and Roy
segments.summary: The band's trumpets were Roy, Bernice Morton (Spratt) and Matthew 'Red' Holland, all but Roy from the Louisville kid band; when Red left, Jones took his place, his second professional job.

segments.chapter: Riverboat to New Orleans and Horace Henderson
segments.title: Playing on percentage; Roy leaves, Granger and guitarist Luke Stewart join
segments.summary: With Horace they played for a split of the door instead of the boat's guaranteed $40; after Roy left Granger was sent for, and Louisville guitarist Luke Stewart, who later played with Stuff Smith, was also in the band.

segments.chapter: Riverboat to New Orleans and Horace Henderson
segments.title: One-nighters out of Cleveland and being stranded in Buffalo when Horace vanishes
segments.summary: The band played one-nighters through Pennsylvania and Ohio, was booked for a week at a Buffalo club that did not exist, and Horace disappeared, leaving the players stuck.

segments.chapter: Riverboat to New Orleans and Horace Henderson
segments.title: Tommy Amagon's Villa gives the stranded band beds and a grill
segments.summary: A jazz-loving club owner let them play weekends for the take and put beds in the hall; Luke Stewart earned tips at a hotel to buy groceries, and Granger grew desperate to go home.

segments.chapter: Riverboat to New Orleans and Horace Henderson
segments.title: Staying with his wife's aunt in Cleveland and going home in defeat
segments.summary: He and Granger stayed at his wife's aunt's home in Cleveland, doing dishes in exchange for greens and ribs; then they wired home for fare and returned, hearing that he should have gone to college.

segments.chapter: Midwest bands: Hardy Brothers, Helvey and Buffalo
segments.title: Horace Henderson calls again from Indianapolis; Fletcher's arrangements
segments.summary: In late 1930 Horace sought a trumpet and trombone for a band at the Walker Theater in Indianapolis; Jones joined for the music itself, since Horace played Fletcher Henderson arrangements.

segments.chapter: Midwest bands: Hardy Brothers, Helvey and Buffalo
segments.title: Fronting the Hardy Brothers pit band at the Walker Theater with Milt Robinson
segments.summary: Horace fronted a band led by Coleridge Davis and the Hardy Brothers; Jones brought in trombonist Milton Robinson, and they earned about $30 a week in the building built on Madame C. J. Walker's hair-care fortune.

segments.chapter: Midwest bands: Hardy Brothers, Helvey and Buffalo
segments.title: Theater tour and lining up work in Cincinnati with Zack White and Wesley Helvey
segments.summary: The show took them to theaters in Cincinnati, Cleveland and Detroit; Jones used the stops to contact the best local leaders, Zack White and Wesley Helvey, in case of openings.

segments.chapter: Midwest bands: Hardy Brothers, Helvey and Buffalo
segments.title: Why the kid band mattered: reading and learning together
segments.summary: Leaders wanted musicians who could read, and the community band, unlike private lessons, taught reading and let kids learn from each other, which he says was the greatest thing that happened to him.

segments.chapter: Midwest bands: Hardy Brothers, Helvey and Buffalo
segments.title: Richmond, Virginia, Johnson's Happy Pals and meeting Tyree Glenn
segments.summary: Richmond work was poor at $3.50 a night; he and Milt Robinson heard Tyree Glenn practicing with Johnson's Happy Pals, then wired Helvey for a job.

segments.chapter: Midwest bands: Hardy Brothers, Helvey and Buffalo
segments.title: Wesley Helvey's Troubadors, full of Louisville band alumni
segments.summary: Helvey's band had Jeff Cass, Milt Robinson, John L. Henderson, George Loving and drummer Charles Bloomer, all from the Louisville kid band, and paid better than Horace.

segments.chapter: Midwest bands: Hardy Brothers, Helvey and Buffalo
segments.title: The Vendome in Buffalo: tips, entertainers and playing in odd keys
segments.summary: Luke Stewart held a steady four-piece job at the Vendome for $35 a week, with the dancer sharing tips and customers requesting songs in difficult keys.

segments.chapter: Midwest bands: Hardy Brothers, Helvey and Buffalo
segments.title: Leaving Helvey's band for Luke Stewart's telegram offer in Buffalo
segments.summary: After a battle of bands in Louisville against Purdue's Pirates, he accepted Luke Stewart's wire for a 35-week trumpet opening, learning he had to go it alone sometimes.

segments.chapter: Midwest bands: Hardy Brothers, Helvey and Buffalo
segments.title: Big tips at the Vendome during the Depression
segments.summary: The Vendome paid $35 a week plus tips; the quintet never took home under $50 each a night and blew it on pool.

segments.chapter: Midwest bands: Hardy Brothers, Helvey and Buffalo
segments.title: Joe Thomas and John L. Henderson join the enlarged Vendome band
segments.summary: Joe Thomas, a former waiter picked up by Horace Henderson in Columbus and stranded in Buffalo, became a tenor man in the six-piece Vendome band that swung well.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Header of sides 5-6 and resumption
segments.summary: A new Smithsonian transcript header and a short exchange to check the recording before resuming.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Dick Stabile's Onyx Club offer and the Silver Grill's counteroffer
segments.summary: Stabile suggested the group follow Farley and Raleigh at the Onyx; the Silver Grill's manager offered to double salaries if they stayed in Buffalo, so Stuff went to New York to assemble another band.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: The Onyx owner insists on the original group, ignoring the Buffalo contract
segments.summary: Stuff rehearsed other musicians, but the owner demanded the group he had heard; the signed Buffalo contract was brushed aside and they were ordered to open on February 4.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Opening at the Onyx: tripling with the Roxy, and the seven-day week
segments.summary: They doubled at the Roxy Theater and sometimes tripled with a radio show, were booked by Consolidated Radio Artists, and worked seven days a week as nobody had days off then.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: The Onyx as studio musicians' hangout; pianist Frankie Froeba and the Spirits of Rhythm
segments.summary: Mostly studio players frequented the club; the house group was Stuff's band with pianist Frankie Froeba, sometimes alternating with the Spirits of Rhythm and for a while Billie Holiday.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Recording behind Billie Holiday with Teddy Wilson's studio groups
segments.summary: He and Cozy Cole recorded often with Billie Holiday under Teddy Wilson (Brunswick or Vocalion), with Goodman, Hodges, Carney, Ben Webster and later Lester Young sitting in on dates.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Greeting Count Basie's band at Roseland in 1936
segments.summary: John had told them about Basie's Kansas City band before it came east; when it opened at Roseland, Stuff's group went over and played a couple of numbers as greeters.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Who owned the Onyx and why musicians came: Carl Kress and the Casa Loma players
segments.summary: Joe Helbock owned the club, guitarist Carl Kress drew studio men, and the Casa Loma band came nightly; Jones and trombonist Pee Wee Hunt did spontaneous jive numbers.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Derby and top hat: the comedy routine with Stuff and "I'se a-Muggin'"
segments.summary: Jones wore a derby and Stuff a top hat in a front-line sketch that began "I'se a-Muggin'" and was Stuff's first exposure in New York.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Cozy Cole joins the Onyx band and Billie Holiday sessions
segments.summary: Johnnie Washington was the first drummer; Cozy Cole came in a few months later, and they hung out together and went to hear Billie before recording with her, including Red Allen on a Billie session.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Red Allen's feeling, singing and peak with Fletcher Henderson
segments.summary: At Stanley Dance's suggestion Jones discusses trumpeters as they come up; he admired Red Allen's soulful, unique sound, finding him greatest with Fletcher Henderson and good with Luis Russell.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Horace Henderson's small-group records with Red Allen and Hawkins
segments.summary: Jones first really listened to Red on records by a Horace Henderson group with Red, Hilton Jefferson and Benny Morton, and still owns the discs, as well as Red's own sessions with Coleman Hawkins.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: The record collection he lost in Louisville
segments.summary: He kept his Buffalo record collection but lost his earliest ones (Armstrong, Red Nichols with Rollini, Teagarden) because he moved from room to room and his mother discarded them.

segments.chapter: Onyx Club and Stuff Smith
segments.title: Every trumpeter had his own style then; Bubber Miley and Freddie Jenkins
segments.summary: Lips Page, Red Allen, Rex Stewart and Joe Smith were instantly recognizable on records, unlike today's players who imitate Dizzy; he also praises Frankie Newton, Bill Coleman, Bubber Miley and Freddie Jenkins.

segments.chapter: Trumpeters he admired and the Ellington near-miss
segments.title: Freddie Jenkins and the Christmas War Bonds from Cab's band
segments.summary: Cab and Duke were booked by the same office and Cab's band chipped in every Christmas to send ailing Freddie Jenkins, in hospital with TB, a War Bond; Jones was glad to hear he was back.

segments.chapter: Trumpeters he admired and the Ellington near-miss
segments.title: Artie Whetsol's "Mood Indigo" sound and Ray Nance
segments.summary: Nobody sounded like Whetsol on "Mood Indigo"; Dance says only Ray Nance sometimes recalled his delicate, soulful tone, perhaps because he was a violinist.

segments.chapter: Trumpeters he admired and the Ellington near-miss
segments.title: Turning down a chance to rehearse with Duke Ellington in Buffalo
segments.summary: When Ellington's band stayed at the Vendome Hotel, Sonny Greer invited him to rehearse; tired after a late night and wary of unwritten parts, he stayed away and later regretted it.

segments.chapter: Trumpeters he admired and the Ellington near-miss
segments.title: How Ellington changed every man: Al Sears, a tenor in the band, Barney Bigard
segments.summary: Duke wrote behind each player; Al Sears sounded better there than anywhere, and Jones wondered how a featured tenor would fit a band that never featured one, praising Barney Bigard's individual clarinet.

segments.chapter: Trumpeters he admired and the Ellington near-miss
segments.title: Ben Webster in Ellington's band and Johnny Hodges's influence
segments.summary: Ben Webster, who played like Coleman Hawkins, came out differently under Ellington; the saxophone section sounded like Ben on "Perdido", though Hodges's influence could be heard.

segments.chapter: Trumpeters he admired and the Ellington near-miss
segments.title: What might have been: Ellington's trumpet features and Jones's cold feet
segments.summary: He imagines what Ellington would have written for him as he did for Rex Stewart and Cootie in "Tooting Through the Roof" and "Boy Meets Horn"; he admits he had cold feet about those aloof men.

segments.chapter: Trumpeters he admired and the Ellington near-miss
segments.title: Fletcher's band jammed after hours; Ellington's players rarely did
segments.summary: When Fletcher Henderson came to Buffalo jam sessions followed, with Rex and Hawkins getting Jones up at night, but Duke's men seldom took out their horns apart from Ben Webster.

segments.chapter: Trumpeters he admired and the Ellington near-miss
segments.title: Ellington finds something for every player
segments.summary: Duke would listen to a player and then write something just right for him, as he would have for Red Allen, and the New Orleans sound was in his band.

segments.chapter: Trumpeters he admired and the Ellington near-miss
segments.title: Individual trumpet styles: Mason, Peanuts Holland, Shad Collins, Basie's trumpeters
segments.summary: He praises lesser-known trumpeters Gus Mason and Peanuts Holland and Shad Collins; Dance observes that Basie's Buck and Sweets were less dominant than Rex, Armstrong, Red and Cootie.

segments.chapter: Trumpeters he admired and the Ellington near-miss
segments.title: Bunny Berigan: jamming uptown and hating studio work
segments.summary: Jones jammed after hours with Bunny Berigan on Lenox Avenue, was asked by him if he was white, and Berigan disliked the light classical studio calls and could not stop drinking.

segments.chapter: Leaving Stuff Smith; Benny Carter and Fletcher Henderson
segments.title: His own heart tremor in 1940 and Stuff Smith's reaction to sobriety
segments.summary: A doctor told him to quit 100-proof whiskey and marijuana; later when he and Cozy Cole stopped drinking, Stuff put them up front anyway to play with a derby and high hat.

segments.chapter: Leaving Stuff Smith; Benny Carter and Fletcher Henderson
segments.title: Chicago hotel jobs in 1940, sharing a stand with Eddie Condon's band
segments.summary: After the Onyx and California the Stuff Smith group played the Three Deuces, La Salle, Sherman and Cincinnati's Netherlands Plaza; at the Sherman Condon's band, with Bud Freeman, shared the stand.

segments.chapter: Leaving Stuff Smith; Benny Carter and Fletcher Henderson
segments.title: Stuff spends the payroll on a car; the band demands separate checks
segments.summary: Stuff bought a car with a whole payroll, the Chicago union intervened, and Jones asked the booking agent to send individual checks, which Stuff agreed to and then resented.

segments.chapter: Leaving Stuff Smith; Benny Carter and Fletcher Henderson
segments.title: After Stuff: Benny Carter's band, then the whole band goes to Fletcher Henderson
segments.summary: Stuff left for Buffalo after Blatt's Beer Garden; Jones joined Benny Carter's irregular band, then the entire band left for Fletcher Henderson at Roseland without giving notice.

segments.chapter: Leaving Stuff Smith; Benny Carter and Fletcher Henderson
segments.title: Cab Calloway's repeated calls; sending Dizzy Gillespie to the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Cab had asked Jones and Cozy to join since the Stuff days; Jones had sent Dizzy Gillespie down to try out instead, and while with Fletcher he now got Cab's third call.

segments.chapter: Leaving Stuff Smith; Benny Carter and Fletcher Henderson
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson asks him to stay; Cab sends money anyway
segments.summary: Fletcher offered recording work and a welcome back; Jones said he owed Fletcher $200, and Cab sent about $300 to settle it. Jones praises Smack as an easy leader, in contrast to Horace.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Joining Cab Calloway in Pittsburgh and Cab's three rules
segments.summary: He joined Cab at Pittsburgh's Stanley Theater on February 21; Dizzy warned the show was fixed for a year, and Cab asked only that he be on time, play the music and wear the uniforms; he stayed eleven years.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Spitballs with Dizzy during the Cab Drivers' number
segments.summary: While Cab changed costumes, Jones, Dizzy and Chu Berry shot paper wads at Cozy Cole during the Cab Drivers' spot, a game repeated across theaters until Cab saw it.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Why Cab outdrew Ellington: visual versus sound
segments.summary: Despite Ellington's music, Cab's band played better theaters and drew more because audiences wanted to see him sing "hi-de-ho"; the two bands shared an office and travelled in similar fashion.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: The Dizzy Gillespie and Cab Calloway knife incident
segments.summary: Cab thought he saw Dizzy's hand throw a spitball; the quarrel ended with Dizzy scratching Cab's hand and Cab hurting his thigh on a trunk lock, which Down Beat blew up.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Defending Dizzy to Cab and Mills's manager; Charlie Barnet refuses him
segments.summary: Jones told Cab it was him throwing paper wads, but the manager insisted Diz be fired; Charlie Barnet refused to hire Diz as the man who cut Cab.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Dizzy shows him bebop harmonies; Cab bans it
segments.summary: After the firing Diz practised intensively and raved about Charlie Parker's chord substitutions; when both tried the ideas on "Some of These Days" Cab threatened to fire them, so Jones stuck to his commercial style, as he had a family.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Cab directs every solo: the high F lesson on "Geechee Joe"
segments.summary: At a morning Strand Theater show Jones skipped his usual high F ending and Cab, who directs each soloist's ending with his stick, scolded him; he says late nights are no excuse.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Cab's valets and the ammonia stick after late nights
segments.summary: Cab had three valets; after a night out his valet Rudolph put him in a cold shower and held ammonia under his nose in the wings during "Minnie the Moocher".

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Chicago South Side: the Jones brothers, Sewell brothers, Joe Louis and the baths
segments.summary: Cab went out with Tyree and Jones to see Chicago numbers men Jones brothers and the oil-rich Sewell brothers at the baths with Joe Louis, joking about who had money.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Cab's strict discipline: no drinking or pot, and firing the clique
segments.summary: Cab sniffed dressing rooms for marijuana because he feared headlines linking him to his men's habits, fired offenders with two weeks' pay and fare home, and said he would fire any clique.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Ellington and Calloway: opposites who came up with Irving Mills
segments.summary: The two leaders were completely different and not close, only connected through Mills, with perhaps some jealousy between them.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Cab's arrangers: Andy Gibson, Buster Harding and the endings dispute
segments.summary: Cab always kept an arranger on hand, first Andy Gibson, then Buster Harding, for films like Stormy Weather; Andy's fade-out endings drew Cab's demand for a real ending.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Cab's pay and paid August and Christmas vacations
segments.summary: Cab paid better than others and gave four weeks off in August and two at Christmas with full pay and fare, something Jones had never known.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: Turning down Cab and Tommy Dorsey; Bud Freeman and Davey Tough say "get Jonah"
segments.summary: Before joining Cab he had refused calls because he was with Stuff, and about 1938 Dorsey's trumpeter Bunny Berigan failed to show, so Bud Freeman and Davey Tough suggested Jonah (the story resumes after the tape change).

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band
segments.title: End of side 8 and header for sides 7-8 recording
segments.summary: Recording break, a new Smithsonian transcript header and a voice check before the interview resumes.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Why Stuff's band disliked California and the Famous Door contract
segments.summary: Dance asks how long he stayed with Stuff; he explains that he and Cozy found California dead, tried to give two weeks' notice, and were told a six-month Consolidated Radio Artists contract bound them.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Back in New York while John Kirby's group at the Onyx rises with Maxine Sullivan
segments.summary: They left despite a call from union official Bernard Baker, and found the Onyx business slow until Claude Thornhill's find Maxine Sullivan made Kirby's sextet take off.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Expelled by the musicians' union and seeking help from Weber and Petrillo
segments.summary: A month later the national federation expelled them for leaving the California job; the New York local refused to help and the national president Weber ordered them to finish the contract.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Agent Rosenberg's 15 percent claim and the court seizing the band's cars
