segments.summary: A manager signed by Stuff for 15 percent sued them, taking cars and instruments from the others, while the judge spared Jones because he had children; the Famous Door owner barred Rosenberg from the club.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Working off the fare back to California at the Silver Grill, then the Famous Door closes
segments.summary: Penniless, they were allowed to earn fare money for two weeks at the Silver Grill in Buffalo, returned to California for two more months, and were stranded when the club closed early.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Why the Famous Door lost business after the band left
segments.summary: Film stars like Kay Francis and Bette Davis packed the club until they left; Fats Waller's small group did not draw, nor did they when they returned.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Looking back: the Duke Ellington road not taken
segments.summary: Everything changes; he wonders what would have happened had he built his name sooner by sitting behind Ellington, but he was afraid.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Stuff walks out alone in California; Eddie Barefield fronts; the band all leaves together
segments.summary: When Stuff left for New York the union sent him back; Jones brought in Eddie Barefield, and in the end the band left together, went to Buffalo to pay their way back, and found Kirby's group in the Onyx.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Breaking every rule at Chicago's La Salle Hotel
segments.summary: Despite signs banning drinking and sitting with customers, the band filled their lockers with bottles, sat at tables, played loud at dinner and packed the room for five months instead of four weeks.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Stuff's tear gas gun in the hotel kitchen
segments.summary: Stuff fired a tear gas gun in the kitchen next to the dressing room, making cooks and waiters cry; the manager told Jones he would fire them all but for the business.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Dedicating numbers to Petrillo's mayor and Petrillo's party in Room 1432
segments.summary: Petrillo ordered the Chicago bands to dedicate a number to his candidate, annoying the Republican manager; Petrillo later hosted a hotel-room party and had each man given a bottle of whiskey.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Stuff arrives late for the coast-to-coast NBC broadcast
segments.summary: Stuff and his bassist were at a ball game while the band went on air without them; Stuff arrived five minutes before the end in riding clothes.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Stuff never worried: ignoring the union and skipping out on rent in Milwaukee
segments.summary: Stuff avoided union meetings, learned numbers instantly, but at Blatt's Beer Garden in Milwaukee sneaked a trunk out of his rooming house to avoid $15 rent.

segments.chapter: Famous Door, the union dispute and Stuff Smith's last years
segments.title: Stuff Smith the violin genius who inspired Jones and Cozy Cole
segments.summary: On violin Stuff had perfect pitch and tireless drive; he and Cozy swung more with him than ever, and Stuff was never happier than with that group, with spontaneous head arrangements.

segments.chapter: Tommy Dorsey's offer
segments.title: Header of sides 9-10 and resumed recording
segments.summary: A new Smithsonian header and voice check at the start of sides 9-10.

segments.chapter: Tommy Dorsey's offer
segments.title: Filling in for Bunny Berigan with Tommy Dorsey and the $3,750 offer
segments.summary: Jonah sat in at Dorsey's Newark gig when Berigan was drunk and was heckled by Chick Webb at the Savoy; later in Los Angeles Dorsey offered a job, sending a ticket but never naming a salary until a letter offered $3,750 a year.

segments.chapter: Tommy Dorsey's offer
segments.title: Visiting Dorsey backstage in Cleveland and the hundred-dollar bill
segments.summary: A year later Jones explained he earned $125 with Stuff and so never answered the letter; Dorsey gave him $100 and Dance remarks that Benny Goodman was tight with money too.

segments.chapter: Tommy Dorsey's offer
segments.title: Sy Oliver's arrangements and the sound of Dorsey's band
segments.summary: Charlie Shavers said arrangements for Jones were written for Dorsey, whose band had big tones but did not swing, perhaps because Dorsey wanted to be the show.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: Cab's instrumental records and feature numbers: "Ghost of a Chance", "Ebony Silhouette"
segments.summary: Cab made good instrumental records such as "Ghost of a Chance" with Chu Berry, "Ebony Silhouette" and "Willow Weep for Me" for Hilton Jefferson, and Buster wrote a feature, "Jonah Jones and Cab".

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: Rotating features and Cab dropping Cozy Cole's drum number
segments.summary: Features were rotated every six months and Cab cut shows by telling Cozy only on stage that his drum number was out, which made Cozy furious; the number had originally been Stuff's.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: Telling Cab off over the high note in "I Can't Give You Anything but Love"
segments.summary: Jealous bandmates grumbled about Cab's featuring Jonah in a singing number; at a Sherman Hotel rehearsal he saved his lip, Cab insisted he play the high note, and Jones muttered a rude reply that Cab overheard.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: Cab offers loans to buy a horn through road manager Mr. Wright
segments.summary: Cab afterwards behaved perfectly and offered advances to buy an instrument interest-free, repaid weekly; Jones used it for an Olds trumpet and learned other leaders refused such loans.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: Eleven years with Cab: weekly salary from $110 to $250
segments.summary: Cab paid about $90 when others paid $70; Jones began at $110 in 1941, reached $125, and was on $250 in 1952, working every week, with Hilton Jefferson there throughout.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: Cab's group cut to seven and four; J. C. Heard replaces Cozy
segments.summary: Cab cut the band to seven and then four (Panama Francis, Dave Rivera, Milt Hinton and Jones as the one horn to growl on "Minnie the Moocher"), touring Cuba; J. C. Heard succeeded Cozy and Buster Harding played arranger's piano.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: The night Chu Berry died in a car crash on the way to Canada
segments.summary: Chu Berry's car overturned near Youngstown on the way to the Peace Bridge; the bus found him, he died days later and Cab announced it in Montreal; Ike Quebec's predecessor Mac Rae filled in.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: Illinois Jacquet, "Rhythm Cocktail" and Cab keeping control of soloists
segments.summary: Jacquet demanded a feature and got "Rhythm Cocktail", a version of "Flying Home"; Jones thinks Cab limited solos so he would not lose control as Duke did.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: Sidemen who learn their worth demand more money: Johnny Hodges, Clyde Lucas
segments.summary: Stanley Dance and Jones discuss how soloists learn what others earn and ask for raises, citing a current drummer who wanted Cozy's pay and Basie's indifference to drummer Clyde Lucas.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: Ellington's greatest band: Lawrence Brown, Barney Bigard and Harry Carney
segments.summary: He calls Ellington's the greatest band, recalls the stir over Lawrence Brown's arrival in 1932, and says Harry Carney's baritone was the cushion of the sound.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: Final Cab band: Birdland and the Uruguay carnival tour
segments.summary: His last engagement was at Birdland; Cab had enlarged the band again for a carnival tour of Uruguay with Doc Cheatham, Shad Collins, Ike Quebec and Sam Taylor, Hilton Jefferson.

segments.chapter: Cab Calloway's band, features and small groups
segments.title: Shad Collins's silences and Cab's derby knock
segments.summary: Jones always asked for Shad Collins despite his sulky silence all day until the fourth show; Cab's habit of knocking his derby when someone made a mistake made the band nervous.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Bushkin and Earl Hines
segments.title: Cab disbands the big band in 1952 as theater guarantees disappear
segments.summary: Cab broke up the band because theaters were closing and the guarantee, about $1,500 plus percentage, could not be assured for the South American tour; he went out as a single.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Bushkin and Earl Hines
segments.title: Freelancing downtown, then Joe Bushkin's invitation to the Embers
segments.summary: He sat in at Eddie Condon's and other spots; Joe Bushkin invited him into the Embers for six weeks, and Jones feared playing one horn all night with a mute, until Bushkin reassured him at home.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Bushkin and Earl Hines
segments.title: Playing the Embers with Bushkin, Mingus and Jo Jones; getting Milt Hinton the bass job
segments.summary: The quartet had Mingus and Jo Jones; when Mingus left for Billy Taylor, Jones persuaded Bushkin to try Milt Hinton, who impressed so much that Bushkin later refused to record without him.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Bushkin and Earl Hines
segments.title: Joining Earl Hines's group in spring 1952
segments.summary: After Cab broke up in early 1952 and the Bushkin job in spring, he joined Hines with Art Blakey, Tommy Potter, Benny Green and Etta Jones, playing clubs from Vancouver and Chicago to Toronto and Los Angeles.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Bushkin and Earl Hines
segments.title: Earl Hines refuses to play his old hits; Jones sings them instead
segments.summary: Hines was trying to play like Monk and bristled at requests for "57 Varieties"; with Osie Johnson and Aaron Sachs in the band, Jones offered to sing "Monday Date" and "Depend on Me" himself.

segments.chapter: After Cab: Bushkin and Earl Hines
segments.title: Hines's production ideas, Helen Merrill singing along, and Dance on his own tunes
segments.summary: Aaron Sachs's wife Helen Merrill and baby travelled with the band, and Hines arranged ensemble vocals; Stanley Dance and Jones agree Hines wrongly thought his own compositions too old.

segments.chapter: Porgy and Bess on Broadway
segments.title: Cab's letter about the Porgy and Bess pit band and Smallens's answer
segments.summary: After six months with Hines, a letter from Cab (playing Sportin' Life) asked him to join the Ziegfeld pit band and Cab wanted eight black musicians; conductor Smallens said colour did not matter if they could read.

segments.chapter: Porgy and Bess on Broadway
segments.title: Earl Hines cuts his pay twice, so he gives notice
segments.summary: Hines started him at $250, cut $25 in California and another $25 in Chicago; he gave notice at Snookie's to take the Porgy and Bess job.

segments.chapter: Porgy and Bess on Broadway
segments.title: The contractor fight that cut Cab's eight men to four in the pit
segments.summary: Contractors hand out jobs by patronage; the union brokered four black musicians out of forty rather than Cab's eight, namely Jones, Buster Bailey, violist Al Brown and Winston Collymore.

segments.chapter: Porgy and Bess on Broadway
segments.title: Young trumpeter Don Reinberg and sitting in at Snookie's
segments.summary: Brushing up his reading with 20-year-old Don Reinberg, a legit player amazed that Jones could play "Stardust" without music; after the show Jones sat in with Earl Hines at Snookie's on 46th Street.

segments.chapter: Porgy and Bess on Broadway
segments.title: Pit etiquette: keeping the book on the stand, retuning as the house heats up
segments.summary: The cello-playing contractor insisted music stay on the rack, and the pit musicians took their A from the English horn and sneakily retuned as body heat raised pitch; the contractor came to respect them.

segments.chapter: Europe in 1954
segments.title: Delaunay brings him to Paris for the Salle Pleyel festival, Panassie objecting
segments.summary: Charles Delaunay invited him over while Hugues Panassie advised against; Jones had been Panassie's favourite since Louis the Second days, and got four weeks guaranteed, playing the festival at Salle Pleyel.

segments.chapter: Europe in 1954
segments.title: Closing the bill at the Olympia in a four-hour music-hall show
segments.summary: At the Olympia he followed circus acts with horses to close the bill with "Struttin' with Some Barbecue" and won good reviews; Sidney Bechet followed him, and Delaunay sent him on to Belgium.

segments.chapter: Europe in 1954
segments.title: Grappelli's film records, Sugar Ray Robinson's entourage, and francs to Belgium
segments.summary: He recorded for a Grappelli film that was shot after he left; in Paris he took June Clark to dinner and found a way to send francs to Belgium and then home.

segments.chapter: Europe in 1954
segments.title: Ten weeks in Belgium and run-ins with King Farouk over beer
segments.summary: At the coast resort he refused champagne offered by King Farouk, who also phoned him at ten a.m. to join him at his cabana; locals held Jonah Jones parties and asked about Jackie Robinson and segregation.

segments.chapter: Europe in 1954
segments.title: The Cave in Paris and local musicians' fear of cheap competition
segments.summary: The Cave's owner wanted him, but local players like Nelson Williams worried she would pay less each time; Jones followed Delaunay's advice to hold to his price.

segments.chapter: Europe in 1954
segments.title: Refusing cut-rate offers and the Porgy and Bess stage solo pay dispute
segments.summary: Porgy and Bess producers offered to hire him again at his old salary, and he had earlier bargained from $25 to $75 extra to play Howard Roberts's stage trumpet spot; Delaunay told him to go home rather than work cheaply.

segments.chapter: Return to New York and the Embers
segments.title: Back in New York in late 1954: hard times, Lips Page's parade, thinking of a day job
segments.summary: Having been treated as an artiste in Paris, he came home to find Lips Page and Bushell playing political parades; he took weekend Rochester jobs and society gigs with Lester Lanin and Meyer Davis and considered a day job.

segments.chapter: Return to New York and the Embers
segments.title: Header of sides 11-12
segments.summary: A new Smithsonian header and a short exchange to restart the recording.

segments.chapter: Return to New York and the Embers
segments.title: Answering the charge that Jonah went commercial
segments.summary: He rejects claims that he went commercial; he enjoyed the songs like "On the Street Where You Live" and played them as well as he could.

segments.chapter: Return to New York and the Embers
segments.title: Lips Page's truck parade gig and the Rochester weekends
segments.summary: Lips Page invited him on a truck for a $12.50 street parade; he was also making short Rochester trips on the train and gigs with Lester Lanin while looking for a regular job.

segments.chapter: Return to New York and the Embers
segments.title: Ham Davis's tip about a housing-project tool-room job
segments.summary: Trumpeter Ham Davis told him of an easy city job checking out tools and told him to buy the paper The Chief to find it.

segments.chapter: Return to New York and the Embers
segments.title: Sammy Burke proposes a small group and Ben Bart turns him down
segments.summary: Recording around Broadway for small labels, he met agent Sammy Burke, who advised forming a quartet; Universal's Ben Bart refused him as too experienced, so Burke quit his job to manage him personally.

segments.chapter: Return to New York and the Embers
segments.title: First quartet job at the Embers for Ralph Watkins
segments.summary: In June 1955 Burke got him one night in the Embers with Hal Austin, John Brown and Bill Austin; they played show tunes, were kept for 12 weeks and Burke moved to renegotiate.

segments.chapter: Return to New York and the Embers
segments.title: Learning to play muted: Vacchiano lessons and the Embers crowd
segments.summary: Playing four shows a night with a mute tired his lip and changed his strong tone; he went back to Vacchiano, noted Hackett's and Charlie Shavers's muted playing, and learned to build and drop volume for the after-theater crowd.

segments.chapter: Return to New York and the Embers
segments.title: Embers lineup, bass-player search and the five-year contract
segments.summary: John Brown could not stay and another bassist filled in; Burke found Watkins lived in his building and negotiated a five-year deal of 20 weeks a year with $50 raises.

segments.chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
segments.title: The Groove album for Victor and touring Cleveland, Baker's Keyboard and Canada
segments.summary: Burke secured an album on Victor's Groove label, which sold little; the group worked Cleveland, flopped at Baker's Keyboard Lounge in Detroit, and played the Colonial in Toronto and Quebec City.

segments.chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
segments.title: Getting out of the Victor contract to sign with Capitol's Dave Cavanaugh
segments.summary: Irv Jerome brought Dave Cavanaugh to hear him; Burke got Victor to release him as 'a big fish in a small pond', and Jones notes how agents maneuver without telling musicians.

segments.chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
segments.title: Escalating Capitol contract with royalties and the Dakota Staton date
segments.summary: Burke wrote a royalty-bearing contract, as Jones had never been paid royalties on earlier records, and Capitol had him accompany Dakota Staton on the hit "The Late, Late Show".

segments.chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
segments.title: Making Muted Jazz and the shuffle-beat "On the Street Where You Live"
segments.summary: With George Rhodes's arrangements, Dave Cavanaugh asked for the last twenty minutes to be filled with "On the Street Where You Live" played in a shuffle beat; Jones and the band did it from the melody.

segments.chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
segments.title: Learning in London, Ontario that the record was a hit
segments.summary: Fans in London, Ontario asked for his record hit; he bought the 78 to relearn what they had done, and disc jockeys flipped over "Rose Room" to push "On the Street", which set his later career.

segments.chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
segments.title: Eighteen Capitol albums, Decca's echo chamber and Swinging on Broadway
segments.summary: He made 18 albums for Capitol and 6 for Decca, whose echo chamber made four pieces sound bigger; Dave Cavanaugh followed Muted Jazz with a show-tune album, Swinging on Broadway.

segments.chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
segments.title: The bucket mute, the "Jonah Jones mute" and playing open again
segments.summary: He varied mutes (growl, plunger, hummer), the bucket mute got his name in the studios without payment, and with Cozy Cole he now plays open more than in the Embers days.

segments.chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
segments.title: Quiet rooms: the London House, the Embers and clubs where the crowd talks
segments.summary: Few rooms like the Embers remain; Sammy Burke gambled to get a trumpet into Chicago's piano-only London House, and Jones comments on talking crowds at Baker's and the Theatrical.

segments.chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
segments.title: "Baubles, Bangles and Beads" outsells the first hit; vocals; Jumping with Jonah
segments.summary: Cavanaugh handed him "Baubles, Bangles and Beads", a waltz he did not know, and he swung it into a bigger hit; he sang "Just My Luck" and earlier songs, and Jumping with Jonah sold over 500,000.

segments.chapter: Capitol Records and "On the Street Where You Live"
segments.title: No gimmicks and the rough work of playing high notes with a mute
segments.summary: Dance praises that straight music sold without gimmicks; Jones accepts the 'commercial' label, says the mute slows a player, and recalls Vacchiano telling him to save high notes for the end of a solo.

segments.chapter: Fred Astaire and the high points
segments.title: First big royalty check; Fred Astaire's special and Joe Glaser's ultimatum
segments.summary: His first Capitol royalty check was over $27,000; Astaire's telegram asked for him on a TV special, but agent Joe Glaser said he would only release it if Jones signed with his office, offering Sammy 5 percent.

segments.chapter: Fred Astaire and the high points
segments.title: Cab advises loyalty to Sammy Burke, who confronts Glaser
segments.summary: Cab told him to stick with the man who brought him this far; when Jones confessed, Burke stormed into Glaser's office threatening his license and the job was arranged.

segments.chapter: Fred Astaire and the high points
segments.title: Baker's Keyboard Lounge pays more and limits him to twenty-minute sets
segments.summary: The Detroit club owner who once refused him now paid Burke double and held him to 20-minute sets so hustlers kept buying champagne, while Burke made difficult clubs pay.

segments.chapter: Fred Astaire and the high points
segments.title: The 1958 Fred Astaire show and how Astaire chose him
segments.summary: The hour show with Barrie Chase won nine awards and led to an Australian tour; Astaire, retired, had listened to Muted Jazz and asked Chrysler's sponsors for Barrie Chase and Jonah Jones.

segments.chapter: Fred Astaire and the high points
segments.title: Director Bud Yorkin checks him out in Detroit
segments.summary: Astaire wanted him vetted, so director Bud Yorkin visited him in Detroit and was satisfied there were no needles lying about.

segments.chapter: Fred Astaire and the high points
segments.title: Rehearsing "St. James Infirmary" with Astaire as his shadow
segments.summary: Astaire built a dance number to the recorded "St. James Infirmary" solo, featured Jones throughout and stood behind him copying his gestures; a hotel party watched the tape on televisions in every corner.

segments.chapter: Fred Astaire and the high points
segments.title: Grace Kelly and Prince Rainier's gala in Monaco
segments.summary: The group, with Ella Fitzgerald, Peter Ustinov and Tony Martin, played the Monaco gala around 1961-62; Princess Grace owned all his records, and she sent plane tickets for his wife and Sammy Burke and wife.

segments.chapter: Fred Astaire and the high points
segments.title: Playing Lyndon Johnson's inauguration; Hubert Humphrey
segments.summary: He alternated with Vincent Lopez at the Statler; Humphrey danced with the wife of lawyer Hobart Taylor, later asked him for autographs for his daughters and invited him to a White House luncheon.

segments.chapter: Reflections and Sammy Burke
segments.title: Career highlights, Australia, and what 'commercial' means
segments.summary: The Astaire show, Monaco and the Inauguration were the high points, with Australian tour cities; Jones asks who decides what is commercial, citing Benny Goodman's sound, and says he once expected to quit at forty.

segments.chapter: Reflections and Sammy Burke
segments.title: Sam Burke's faith in him, starting at forty-five
segments.summary: His career really started at 45; Jones credits his manager Sam Burke, who believed in a nearly finished trumpeter and told him he could not make people buy the records alone.

segments.chapter: Reflections and Sammy Burke
segments.title: Cruise with Cab and the dilemma of asking Cab instead of Sammy
segments.summary: On a nostalgia cruise with Cab and his wife they reminisced; Jones explains he could not ask Sammy about Glaser's offer, since Sammy might have exploded, and Dance says Sam knew what he was doing.

segments.chapter: Reflections and Sammy Burke
segments.title: Burke gets Capitol to raise his royalty from four to five percent; end of tape
segments.summary: After the Astaire show, Burke argued for a higher graduated royalty and won 5 percent; Jones, who never knew royalties escalate, was happy with a penny, and Dance ends the session to drive to Connecticut.
